0.9% saline: Isotonic sodium chloride solution; a crystalloid that expands circulating volume.
0.9% sodium chloride: Normal saline: the standard IV fluid used first to rehydrate in DKA.
1-alpha-hydroxylase: Kidney enzyme that makes active vitamin D (calcitriol).
1-alpha-hydroxylation: The kidney step that converts vitamin D into its active form, calcitriol.
12-lead ECG: A standard recording of the heart's electrical activity from 12 views; first-line after any blackout.
16-gauge: Large-bore cannula size used for needle decompression.
1:1000: Adrenaline strength of 1 mg in 1 ml, used for IM injection.
1st MTP: First metatarsophalangeal joint, at the base of the big toe; the classic site of gout.
2-week wait: NHS urgent suspected cancer referral, seen within two weeks.
2-week-wait: The NHS urgent referral pathway for suspected cancer.
21-hydroxylase: Adrenal enzyme; antibodies against it mark autoimmune Addison's.
24-hour pH monitoring: A probe measuring oesophageal acid over a day to prove reflux.
25-OH vitamin D: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form measured to assess vitamin D status.
25-hydroxyvitamin D: The storage form of vitamin D measured to check vitamin D status.
2WW: Two-week-wait: NICE urgent referral pathway for suspected cancer.
2x2 table: Grid of test result against true disease status giving TP, FP, FN and TN.
3-2-1 rule: Lynch screen: 3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 diagnosed under 50.
4 F's: Classic gallstone risk profile: female, fat, forty and fertile.
4-2-1 rule: Criteria for severe NPDR: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1.
4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate: Concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X for urgent warfarin reversal.
4AT: Two-minute bedside delirium screen; a score of 4 or more suggests delirium.
4Hs and 4Ts: The reversible causes of arrest to look for during CPR.
4th generation: HIV test detecting both p24 antigen and antibody, so it turns positive earlier.
5-alpha-reductase: Enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent DHT.
6 Ps: Pain, pallor, pulseless, perishingly cold, paraesthesia and paralysis: the signs of acute limb ischaemia.
6CIT: Six-item Cognitive Impairment Test, a short screen used in primary care.
72-hour supervised fast: Diagnostic test for insulinoma: fasting in hospital with bloods taken when glucose drops.
99th centile: The upper reference limit for troponin; values above it indicate myocardial injury.
9am cortisol: Morning cortisol taken at its natural daily peak; the first test for adrenal insufficiency.
A CHEST 92: Mnemonic for life-threatening asthma: altered consciousness, cyanosis, hypotension, exhaustion, silent chest, tachy/bradyarrhythmia, PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%.
A wave: JVP wave from right atrial contraction; large in pulmonary stenosis.
ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: the structured emergency assessment.
ABG: Arterial blood gas: measures pH, PaO2, PaCO2 and bicarbonate in arterial blood.
ABO incompatibility: Transfusion of red cells carrying A or B antigens that the recipient has antibodies against.
ABPA: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: allergic reaction to Aspergillus in asthma, with eosinophilia and high IgE.
ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle over arm systolic pressure; below 0.9 suggests peripheral arterial disease.
ABPM: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring: a cuff worn for 24 hours, the NICE-preferred way to confirm hypertension.
ABVD: Standard Hodgkin chemotherapy: doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine.
ACA: Anterior cerebral artery: supplies the medial cortex including the leg and bladder areas.
ACE: Angiotensin-converting enzyme; made by granulomas, so raised in active sarcoidosis.
ACE inhibitor: A blood pressure drug such as ramipril that blocks angiotensin II formation and dilates the efferent arteriole.
ACE2: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2: the cell receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter.
ACLS: Advanced cardiac life support: the standard algorithms for treating cardiac arrest and arrhythmias.
ACPGBI: Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland, which issues colorectal surgery guidance.
ACR: Albumin:creatinine ratio on a urine sample; the first-line test for kidney damage.
ACS: Acute coronary syndrome: unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI caused by a sudden fall in coronary blood flow.
ACT: Artemisinin-based combination therapy; first-line for uncomplicated falciparum.
ACTH: Adrenocorticotropic hormone from the pituitary; drives cortisol production.
ACTH-dependent: Cortisol excess driven by too much ACTH, from the pituitary or an ectopic tumour.
ACTH-independent: Cortisol made autonomously by the adrenal or given as a drug; ACTH is suppressed.
AChE inhibitors: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine.
AChR: Acetylcholine receptor; the nicotinic receptor on the muscle end-plate targeted in myasthenia.
ADAMTS13: Enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor; deficiency causes TTP.
ADCC: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity: immune cells kill antibody-coated cells.
ADEM: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis: demyelination after an infection or vaccination.
ADH: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin): makes the kidney reabsorb water in the collecting duct.
ADP: Adenosine diphosphate: released by activated platelets to recruit more platelets.
ADPKD: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease: inherited cysts that enlarge the kidneys.
AEIOU: Dialysis indications: Acidosis, Electrolytes (K+), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia.
AERD: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, also called Samter's triad.
AFB: Acid-fast bacilli, seen on sputum staining in tuberculosis.
AFP: Alpha-fetoprotein: a tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and germ-cell tumours.
AGE: Advanced glycation end-products: proteins damaged by glucose that impair nerve and vessel function.
AGEs: Advanced glycation end-products: glucose-modified proteins that damage vessels and nerves.
AHI: Apnoea-hypopnoea index: apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep; 5, 15 and 30 mark mild, moderate and severe.
AIDS: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome: CD4 below 200 or an AIDS-defining illness.
AIDS-defining illness: An infection or cancer that signals advanced HIV with severe immune loss.
AIH: Autoimmune hepatitis: chronic immune attack on liver cells.
AIHA: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: antibodies attack the patient's own red cells.
AKI: Acute kidney injury: a sudden fall in kidney function shown by rising creatinine or reduced urine output.
ALL: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: the commonest childhood cancer, peaking at 2 to 5 years.
ALP: Alkaline phosphatase; rises in bile duct obstruction.
ALS: Advanced life support: the hospital algorithm of shocks, drugs and reversible causes.
ALT: Alanine aminotransferase; a marker of liver cell damage.
AMA: Anti-mitochondrial antibody, the marker of primary biliary cholangitis.
AML: Acute myeloid leukaemia: mostly over 65s; Auer rods on the film.
AMTS: Abbreviated mental test score, a 10-point confusion test; 7 or less counts as confused in CURB-65.
ANA: Antinuclear antibody, an autoantibody against cell nuclei; positive in type 1 AIH and lupus.
ANCA: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, found in small-vessel vasculitis that can cause glomerulonephritis.
APB: Abductor pollicis brevis: thenar muscle that abducts the thumb, supplied by the median nerve.
APC: Tumour suppressor gene whose loss starts the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
APML: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia: AML subtype with t(15;17), prone to DIC.
APS: Antiphospholipid syndrome: autoimmune clotting disorder needing anticoagulation.
APTT: Activated partial thromboplastin time; used to monitor unfractionated heparin.
ARA criteria: American Rheumatism Association (now ACR) classification criteria used to define SLE for diagnosis and research.
ARB: Angiotensin receptor blocker, such as losartan; acts like an ACE inhibitor on the kidney.
ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome: leaky lung capillaries causing severe hypoxia and bilateral shadowing.
ARNI: Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, such as sacubitril-valsartan.
ART: Antiretroviral therapy: the drug combination used to treat HIV.
ASCVD: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, e.g. angina, MI, stroke.
ASIS: Anterior superior iliac spine, the bony point at the front of the hip.
ASMA: Anti-smooth muscle antibody, the autoantibody most consistent with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis.
ASO titre: Antistreptolysin O antibody level, raised after a recent streptococcal infection.
AST: Aspartate aminotransferase: liver (and muscle) enzyme, typically at least twice ALT in alcoholic hepatitis.
AST:ALT ratio: AST divided by ALT; a value of 2 or more is the hallmark of alcohol-related liver injury.
ATN: Acute tubular necrosis: death of tubular cells from ischaemia or toxins; the commonest intrinsic AKI.
AV block: Delayed or failed conduction from atria to ventricles through the AV node.
AV node: Atrioventricular node: conducts impulses from the atria to the ventricles.
AV node block: Delayed or blocked conduction from atria to ventricles, seen on ECG as heart block.
AVN: Avascular necrosis: bone death from lost blood supply.
AVNRT: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia; the commonest type of SVT.
AVP: Arginine vasopressin, another name for ADH.
AVS: Adrenal venous sampling: lateralises the source of excess aldosterone.
AXR: Abdominal X-ray, the key diagnostic test for volvulus.
Abducens: The sixth cranial nerve, which moves the eye outwards; often stretched by raised ICP.
Abscess: A walled-off collection of pus that needs drainage.
Absence: A brief generalised seizure with blank staring, typical in children.
Acanthosis nigricans: Velvety, dark skin in the neck and armpits; a sign of insulin resistance.
Acetaldehyde: Toxic first breakdown product of alcohol that damages liver cells.
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies: Serum IgG against the AChR; the first test for myasthenia.
Acetylcholinesterase: Enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: A drug that blocks acetylcholine breakdown, such as donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine.
Achilles tendonitis: Inflammation of the Achilles tendon, causing heel pain.
Aciclovir: Antiviral drug for herpes simplex and varicella zoster infections.
Acitretin: Oral retinoid for severe psoriasis; teratogenic and causes dry mucous membranes.
Acoustic neuroma: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve, causing hearing loss and sometimes facial numbness.
Acromegaly: Excess growth hormone in adults, causing enlarged hands, feet and jaw.
Activated charcoal: Oral powder that binds drugs in the gut; useful within 1 hour of ingestion if the airway is safe.
Actrapid: Soluble short-acting human insulin, used in the IV infusion for DKA.
Acupuncture: Fine-needle treatment that NICE suggests considering to prevent chronic tension-type headache.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden rise in eye pressure causing a painful red eye, haloes, vomiting and reduced vision.
Acute chest syndrome: Sickle cell emergency: chest pain, breathlessness, hypoxia and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray.
Acute haemolytic reaction: Rapid destruction of transfused red cells, usually from ABO mismatch; the most serious acute reaction.
Acute limb ischaemia: Sudden loss of arterial blood supply to a limb, threatening its survival within hours.
Acute on chronic: A sudden worsening on top of a long-standing problem; in blood gases, low pH with raised bicarbonate.
Acute oncology: The hospital team that manages emergencies in patients with cancer.
Acute tubular necrosis: Death of kidney tubular cells from prolonged low blood pressure, sepsis or nephrotoxins.
Acute urticaria: Urticaria lasting less than 6 weeks, often triggered by infection, food or drugs.
Acute-phase response: Liver shift towards making inflammatory proteins such as CRP during illness.
Addison's disease: Primary adrenal insufficiency; can cause normal gap acidosis with hyperkalaemia.
Addisonian crisis: Life-threatening acute adrenal insufficiency with shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia.
Adenosine: IV drug that briefly blocks the AV node; terminates most SVTs.
Adenovirus: DNA virus that is the commonest cause of viral conjunctivitis.
Adhesins: Bacterial surface proteins that let bacteria stick to host tissues.
Adipokines: Hormones and signals released by fat tissue, such as adiponectin and leptin.
Adiponectin: Fat-derived hormone that improves insulin sensitivity; low in obesity.
Adjusted calcium: Serum calcium corrected for the albumin level.
Adjuvant: Treatment given after surgery to reduce recurrence.
Adrenal cortex: Outer layer of the adrenal gland that makes aldosterone, cortisol and androgens.
Adrenal crisis: Acute, life-threatening cortisol deficiency needing immediate hydrocortisone.
Adrenal insufficiency: Too little cortisol from the adrenal glands, as in Addison's disease.
Adrenal venous sampling: Sampling blood from each adrenal vein to see whether one or both glands make excess aldosterone.
Adrenaline: Emergency drug for anaphylaxis, given intramuscularly into the thigh.
Advance decision: A legally binding refusal of specific treatment, made while the person had capacity.
Adverse features: Shock, syncope, heart failure or ischaemia, which mandate urgent cardioversion.
Afferent arteriole: The small artery bringing blood into the glomerulus.
Afterload: The pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.
Agonal gasps: Occasional, ineffective gasping breaths seen in cardiac arrest.
Agranulocytosis: Severe loss of neutrophils, a side effect of co-trimoxazole.
Air bronchogram: Dark, air-filled airways visible inside a white consolidated area on X-ray, showing the alveoli around them are filled.
Air-fluid levels: Horizontal lines on an erect film where gas sits above fluid in obstructed bowel.
Airway clearance techniques: Physiotherapy breathing methods that help shift and cough up sputum.
Albumin: Main blood protein made by the liver; falls in sepsis.
Alcohol dehydrogenase: Liver enzyme that converts ethanol to acetaldehyde.
Alcoholic hepatitis: Acute inflammation of the liver caused by heavy alcohol use, often after a binge.
Aldose reductase: The enzyme that converts glucose to sorbitol in the polyol pathway.
Aldosterone: Mineralocorticoid that makes the kidney retain sodium and excrete potassium.
Alendronic acid: Weekly oral bisphosphonate; first-line treatment for osteoporosis.
Alert card: A card carried by asplenic patients telling clinicians they are at high risk of sepsis.
Alfacalcidol: Activated (1-alpha-hydroxylated) vitamin D that does not need the kidney to work.
Allergen: A normally harmless substance, such as pollen or milk protein, that triggers an allergic reaction.
Allergic contact dermatitis: Delayed itchy rash where skin touched an allergen such as nickel, latex or hair dye.
Allergic rhinitis: IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal lining causing sneezing, itch and a runny, blocked nose.
Allodynia: Pain from something that should not hurt, such as bedsheets touching the feet.
Allopurinol: First-line urate-lowering drug that inhibits xanthine oxidase.
Alopecia: Hair loss, often patchy or diffuse thinning in active lupus.
Alpha-1: Adrenoceptor causing vasoconstriction, which raises BP and reduces swelling.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin: A liver-made antiprotease protecting alveoli from neutrophil elastase.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: Inherited lack of a protease inhibitor causing early emphysema and cirrhosis.
Alpha-1 receptor: Adrenergic receptor on vessels that causes vasoconstriction.
Alpha-blocker: Drug such as tamsulosin that relaxes prostate smooth muscle to improve urine flow.
Alpha-fetoprotein: Blood tumour marker raised in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Alpha-synuclein: The protein that misfolds into Lewy bodies in DLB and Parkinson's disease.
Alpha-thalassaemia trait: Carrier state for alpha-thalassaemia: mild microcytosis, normal ferritin and normal electrophoresis.
Alteplase: A thrombolytic drug used for massive PE and stroke.
Alveolar macrophages: Immune cells in the alveoli that engulf dust and microbes.
Alzheimer's disease: The commonest dementia: gradual memory-led decline from amyloid plaques and tau tangles.
Amaurosis fugax: Painless, temporary, curtain-like loss of vision in one eye from retinal artery ischaemia.
Ambulatory oxygen: Portable oxygen used while walking or active.
Aminoglycoside: Antibiotic class (e.g. tobramycin, gentamicin); inhaled forms suppress Pseudomonas.
Aminoglycosides: Antibiotics such as gentamicin that impair neuromuscular transmission and worsen myasthenia.
Aminophylline: An IV theophylline salt used in refractory acute asthma; narrow therapeutic range.
Amiodarone: Class III antiarrhythmic used for stable VT and rhythm control in AF.
Amitriptyline: A tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for neuropathic pain; anticholinergic side effects.
Amphibole: The straight, needle-like asbestos fibre group (crocidolite, amosite) most linked to mesothelioma.
Amphotericin B: Antifungal used with flucytosine to induce treatment of cryptococcal meningitis.
Amylase: Pancreatic enzyme; more than 3 times normal suggests pancreatitis, a mild rise occurs in perforation.
Amyloid-beta: A protein fragment that clumps into plaques outside neurons in Alzheimer's.
Amyloidosis: Deposition of abnormal protein (AA amyloid in chronic inflammation) in organs such as the kidney.
Anaemia: A haemoglobin level below normal, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
Anaemia of chronic disease: Normocytic anaemia in long-term inflammation with low serum iron but normal or high ferritin.
Anaerobes: Bacteria that grow without oxygen, common in ear, sinus and dental infections.
Anaerobic glycolysis: Breaking down glucose without oxygen, producing acid; in empyema it lowers the pleural fluid pH.
Anaerobic metabolism: Energy production without oxygen, which makes lactate.
Anal crypt: A small pocket in the anal canal lining at the dentate line, where anal glands open.
Anal fissure: A tear in the anal canal lining causing sharp pain and bleeding on defecation.
Anal fistula: A chronic abnormal tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin.
Anal tone: Resting tightness of the anal sphincter on rectal examination; reduced in cauda equina.
Anal verge: The outer edge of the anal canal where it meets perianal skin.
Anaphylactoid reaction: An allergy-like reaction not caused by IgE antibodies, common with NAC; it settles when the infusion is stopped.
Anaphylaxis: Severe, life-threatening systemic allergic reaction with airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
Anaplastic large cell lymphoma: T-cell NHL that can be aggressive with extranodal disease.
Anasarca: Severe generalised oedema affecting the whole body.
Anastrozole: Aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal ER-positive breast cancer.
Anechoic: Black on ultrasound because it contains fluid that reflects no echoes.
Aneurysm: A permanent abnormal dilation of an artery.
Angioedema: Swelling of deeper skin layers, often lips, tongue or eyelids.
Angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery with a balloon via a catheter, often with a stent.
Angular stomatitis: Cracks at the corners of the mouth, seen in iron deficiency.
Aniline dyes: Industrial dyes containing aromatic amines; linked to bladder cancer.
Anion gap: (Na + K) minus (Cl + HCO3); a raised gap means extra unmeasured acid such as ketones.
Ankle reflex: The ankle jerk (S1); reduced or absent in diabetic neuropathy.
Ankylosing spondylitis: Chronic inflammatory arthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints that can fuse them over years.
Ann Arbor: Older name for the lymphoma staging system now updated as Lugano.
Annulus: The fibrous ring that supports a heart valve.
Anopheles: Genus of mosquito whose females transmit malaria.
Anosmia: Loss of the sense of smell.
Antalgic gait: A limp in which the patient spends less time on the painful leg.
Antecubital fossa: The hollow at the front of the elbow.
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy: Infarction of the front of the optic nerve, causing sudden painless visual loss.
Anterior mediastinum: The front part of the space between the lungs, where the thymus sits.
Anterior rhinoscopy: Looking into the front of the nose with a light and speculum.
Anterior uveitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body causing a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision.
Anterolateral thigh: Front and outer side of the thigh; the recommended IM adrenaline site.
Anti-CCP: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody; the most specific blood test for RA.
Anti-GBM: Antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane, found in Goodpasture's disease.
Anti-La: Anti-SSB antibody that, with anti-Ro, can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus.
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: Autoimmune encephalitis from antibodies to the NMDA receptor, often with an ovarian teratoma.
Anti-PLA2R: Autoantibody against the phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes; marker of membranous nephropathy.
Anti-Ro: Anti-SSA antibody linked to photosensitive rash, cytopenias and neonatal lupus with congenital heart block.
Anti-Smith: Antibody against Smith nuclear protein; highly specific for SLE but less sensitive.
Anti-TPO: Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase, an enzyme that makes thyroid hormone; positive in about 90% of Hashimoto's.
Anti-TPO antibodies: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies, a marker of autoimmune thyroid disease.
Anti-dsDNA: Antibody against double-stranded DNA; highly specific for SLE and rises with disease activity and nephritis.
Anti-histone antibodies: The hallmark antibodies of drug-induced lupus.
Anti-parietal cell antibodies: Antibodies found in pernicious anaemia; sensitive but less specific than intrinsic factor antibodies.
Anticholinergic: Blocks acetylcholine; causes confusion, dry mouth and urinary retention.
Anticoagulation: Drugs that reduce blood clotting to prevent stroke in AF.
Antifibrotic: Drug that slows the laying down of scar tissue.
Antihistamines: Drugs that block histamine H1 receptors to relieve itch, sneezing and hives.
Antimuscarinic: Drug blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, e.g. oxybutynin, to relax the detrusor.
Antiplatelet: A drug such as clopidogrel or aspirin that stops platelets clumping.
Antistreptolysin O titre: Blood test for antibodies to streptolysin O, showing recent strep infection.
Antithrombin III: A natural anticoagulant that inactivates thrombin and factor Xa; heparin boosts it.
Anusol: A soothing topical haemorrhoid preparation suitable in pregnancy.
Aortic dissection: A tear in the aortic intima letting blood split the wall, causing tearing chest pain.
Aortic regurgitation: Leaky aortic valve; causes an early diastolic murmur.
Aortic root abscess: Infection spreading from the aortic valve into surrounding tissue, which can damage the conduction system.
Aortic root dilation: Widening of the first part of the aorta, which stretches the valve and causes regurgitation.
Aortic root replacement: Open surgery replacing the dissected aortic root and ascending aorta with a graft.
Aortic sclerosis: Thickening of the aortic valve without obstruction; ESM that does not radiate, normal S2 and pulse.
Aortic stenosis: Narrowing of the aortic valve, obstructing blood leaving the left ventricle.
Aortocaval compression: The pregnant uterus pressing on the aorta and vena cava, reducing venous return.
Aortoiliac: The lower aorta and the iliac arteries that it divides into.
Apex beat: The lowest, most lateral point where the heartbeat can be felt; displaced when the ventricle dilates.
Apical fibrosis: Scarring of the upper zones of the lungs, an extra-articular feature of AS.
Apical-radial deficit: Apex rate exceeds radial pulse because some beats are too weak to reach the wrist.
Apixaban: A DOAC (factor Xa inhibitor) used for stroke prevention in AF.
Aplastic anaemia: Failure of bone marrow stem cells, causing low red cells, white cells and platelets.
Apnoea: A pause in airflow during sleep, usually defined as lasting at least 10 seconds.
Aromatase inhibitor: Drug blocking conversion of androgens to oestrogen; used in postmenopausal ER-positive cancer.
Aromatic amines: Chemicals in dyes, rubber and smoke that are excreted in urine and damage urothelium.
Arousal: A brief shift to lighter sleep or waking that restores airway muscle tone.
Arterial calcification: Calcium in the artery wall making it stiff and non-compressible.
Arterial ulcer: Painful, punched-out ulcer on the toes or foot from poor arterial supply.
Arteriolosclerosis: Thickening and hardening of small arteries caused by long-standing high blood pressure.
Arthrocentesis: Needle aspiration of fluid from a joint.
Arthropathy: Joint disease; in haemochromatosis, typically 2nd/3rd MCPs and large joints.
Articular cartilage: Smooth tissue covering bone ends inside a joint, allowing frictionless movement.
Asbestos: A naturally occurring fibrous mineral once widely used for insulation, lagging and building materials.
Asbestosis: Interstitial lung fibrosis caused by inhaled asbestos fibres.
Ascending cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, often from obstruction; classic fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
Ascites: Fluid in the peritoneal cavity, often from portal hypertension.
Ascitic tap: Diagnostic paracentesis: a small sample of ascitic fluid sent for cell count and culture.
Aseptic loosening: Loosening of a joint replacement without infection; the commonest reason for hip revision.
Aseptic technique: Methods that prevent contamination when inserting or handling devices.
Aspirate: The fluid or cells drawn out by a needle.
Aspiration: Drawing pus out of the abscess with a needle, usually via a burr hole.
Aspiration pneumonia: Pneumonia from inhaling stomach contents or mouth bacteria, often with anaerobes, usually after stroke, alcohol or reduced consciousness.
Asplenia: Absence of the spleen, surgical or functional.
Asterixis: Flapping tremor of outstretched hands, seen in hepatic encephalopathy.
Asthma action plan: Written plan telling the patient how to adjust treatment and when to seek help.
Asthma-COPD overlap: Persistent airflow obstruction with features of both asthma and COPD.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms.
Asystole: No electrical activity of the heart; a flat line.
Atelectasis: Collapse of small airways, common after surgery, causing low-grade fever in the first 48 hours.
Atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty plaques in artery walls, causing narrowing.
Atlantoaxial subluxation: Instability between C1 and C2 that can compress the cervical cord.
Atonic: A seizure with sudden loss of muscle tone causing a drop attack.
Atopic dermatitis: Chronic itchy inflammatory skin disease linked to atopy; same as atopic eczema.
Atopic march: The typical progression from infant eczema to food allergy, asthma and allergic rhinitis.
Atopic triad: Eczema, asthma and allergic rhinitis occurring together.
Atopy: An inherited tendency to make IgE to allergens, causing eczema, asthma and hay fever.
Atorvastatin: Statin used at 20 mg for primary and 80 mg for secondary prevention.
Atrial fibrillation: An irregularly irregular heart rhythm in which clots can form in the left atrium.
Atrial flutter: A regular atrial re-entry rhythm with sawtooth waves, often 2:1 conduction.
Atrial kick: The extra ventricular filling from atrial contraction, lost in AF.
Atropine: Antimuscarinic drug that speeds the heart; first-line for unstable bradycardia.
Atypical pneumonia: Pneumonia from organisms without a typical bacterial cell wall, such as Mycoplasma or Legionella, often with systemic features.
Audiometry: Formal hearing test; normal in BPPV.
Auer rods: Rod-shaped clumps of granule material in myeloblast cytoplasm; a hallmark of AML.
Aura: A warning sensation at the start of a focal seizure, such as an epigastric feeling.
Aural fullness: A feeling of pressure in the ear, typical of Ménière's disease.
Auspitz sign: Pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is scraped off.
Austin Flint murmur: A mid-diastolic apical rumble in severe AR, from the jet stopping the mitral valve opening.
Auto-injector: A spring-loaded pen that delivers a fixed IM dose of adrenaline, such as an EpiPen.
Autoimmune adrenalitis: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex; the commonest cause of Addison's in the UK.
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: Breakdown of red cells by the body's own antibodies, linked to Mycoplasma through cold agglutinins.
Automatisms: Repetitive purposeless movements during a seizure, such as lip-smacking or fiddling.
Autonomic neuropathy: Damage to the nerves controlling automatic functions such as blood pressure, gut, bladder and erections.
Autonomy: The patient's right to make their own decisions about their care.
Autosomal dominant: Inheritance where one faulty copy causes disease; each child has a 50% risk.
Autosomal recessive: Inheritance needing two faulty copies to be affected; carriers are usually well.
Autosplenectomy: Shrinking and loss of function of the spleen from repeated infarction in sickle cell disease.
Axillary node clearance: Removal of the axillary nodes for proven nodal spread; risks arm lymphoedema.
Axonal loss: Death of nerve fibres after repeated demyelination; causes permanent disability.
Azathioprine: Immunosuppressant used as a steroid-sparing agent in myasthenia.
Azithromycin: Macrolide used long term to prevent bronchiectasis exacerbations.
Azithromycin prophylaxis: Long-term low-dose azithromycin to reduce exacerbations in selected patients.
Azole: Antifungal class that blocks ergosterol synthesis.
Azoospermia: No sperm in the semen; a reversible side effect of sulfasalazine.
B lymphocytes: Antibody-producing white cells; the cells EBV infects.
B symptoms: Fever above 38°C, drenching night sweats and weight loss over 10% in 6 months.
B-scan ultrasonography: Ultrasound of the eye used to see the retina when blood blocks the view.
B12: Vitamin needed for blood cells and nerves; deficiency causes tiredness and anaemia.
BAL: Bronchoalveolar lavage: washing a lung segment through a bronchoscope and analysing the fluid.
BAPEN: British Association for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition; developed MUST.
BASHH: British Association for Sexual Health and HIV, which writes UK sexual health guidelines.
BCG: Live attenuated mycobacterium instilled into the bladder as immunotherapy for high-risk tumours.
BCR-ABL: Fusion gene making a permanently active tyrosine kinase; drives CML.
BEP: Bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin: chemotherapy for non-seminoma.
BHIVA: British HIV Association, which publishes UK HIV guidelines.
BHL: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy: enlarged lymph nodes at both lung roots.
BISAP: A bedside pancreatitis severity score: BUN, Impaired mental state, SIRS, Age, Pleural effusion.
BLS: Basic life support: recognition, calling for help, CPR and defibrillation.
BM: Bedside capillary blood glucose reading from a finger-prick test.
BMD: Bone mineral density: how much mineral is packed into bone, measured by DEXA.
BMI: Body mass index: weight in kg divided by height in metres squared.
BMI percentile: Where a child's BMI sits compared with children of the same age and sex.
BNP: B-type natriuretic peptide, released by stretched ventricles; a low level makes heart failure unlikely.
BPH: Benign prostatic hyperplasia: non-cancerous prostate enlargement, the commonest cause of post-renal AKI.
BPPV: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: brief vertigo from loose inner ear crystals, triggered by head movement.
BRCA1: Tumour suppressor gene for DNA repair; mutations give the highest relative breast cancer risk.
BRCA2: Tumour suppressor gene for DNA repair; mutations raise breast, ovarian and male breast cancer risk.
BSA: Body surface area affected; above 10% means moderate-to-severe psoriasis.
BSACI: British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology, which publishes UK urticaria guidance.
BSH: British Society for Haematology: publishes UK haematology guidelines.
BSR: British Society for Rheumatology, which publishes PMR and GCA guidance.
BTS: British Thoracic Society, which publishes the UK pneumothorax guidelines.
Babinski: Upgoing big toe on stroking the sole, a UMN sign.
Babinski sign: Big toe extends upwards when the sole is stroked: an UMN sign.
Bacillus cereus: Spore-forming bacterium that can contaminate platelet units.
Baclofen: GABA-B agonist muscle relaxant used for spasticity.
Bacterial translocation: Gut bacteria crossing the bowel wall into lymph nodes, blood or ascites.
Bacterial vaginosis: Overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella, giving thin fishy discharge and raised pH.
Bacteriostatic: Stops bacteria multiplying rather than killing them outright.
Bag-valve mask: A hand-squeezed bag and face mask used to ventilate a patient with oxygen.
Baker's cyst: A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee; rupture mimics DVT.
Balloon pericardiotomy: A balloon catheter makes a window in the pericardium, used for malignant effusions.
Balloon valvuloplasty: Widening a narrowed valve by inflating a balloon across it through a catheter.
Ballooning degeneration: Swelling and breakdown of virus-infected keratinocytes that splits the epidermis into blisters.
Bamboo spine: Late X-ray appearance of a fused spine bridged by syndesmophytes.
Band ligation: Endoscopic placement of rubber bands around varices to stop or prevent bleeding.
Bariatric surgery: Weight-loss surgery such as gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy.
Barking cough: A harsh, seal-like cough typical of croup.
Baroreceptor: Pressure sensors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that slow the heart when BP rises.
Barrett's: Columnar metaplasia of the lower oesophagus caused by chronic reflux; premalignant for adenocarcinoma.
Barrett's oesophagus: Replacement of oesophageal squamous lining by columnar cells due to reflux; premalignant.
Bart's hydrops fetalis: Alpha-thalassaemia major: severe fetal anaemia and oedema, incompatible with life.
Barthel Index: Scale of independence in activities of daily living after stroke.
Basal ganglia: Deep brain nuclei that control the initiation and scaling of movement.
Basal insulin: Long-acting background insulin that covers needs between meals and overnight.
Baseline creatinine: The patient's usual creatinine before the illness, used to define and stage AKI.
Basement membrane: Thin layer under the epithelium; breaching it makes a cancer invasive.
Basophil: A blood white cell similar to a mast cell, which also carries IgE and releases histamine.
Basophilic stippling: Blue dots in red cells from leftover ribosomal RNA; seen in thalassaemia and lead poisoning.
Bat wing: Perihilar shadowing on CXR caused by alveolar pulmonary oedema.
Bayes' theorem: Rule linking pre-test probability and test accuracy to post-test probability.
Beck's triad: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds: the signs of cardiac tamponade.
Behavioural weight management programme: Structured group or individual programme supporting diet, activity and habit change.
Behçet's: Vasculitis with oral and genital ulcers and bilateral uveitis.
Behçet's syndrome: Vasculitis with mouth and genital ulcers; a cause of pericarditis.
Bell's palsy: Acute, one-sided lower motor neurone weakness of the facial nerve with no other cause found.
Bell's phenomenon: The eyeball rolls upward when the patient tries to close the eye.
Bell-Clapper deformity: Abnormally high attachment of the tunica vaginalis, so the testis hangs freely and can rotate.
Below-knee amputation: Removal of the leg below the knee for an unsalvageable limb.
Bence Jones protein: Free immunoglobulin light chains found in the urine in myeloma.
Bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic used for hypertension that reduces urate excretion and can trigger gout.
Beneficence: Acting in the patient's best interests; doing good.
Benign: Not cancerous; does not invade or spread.
Benserazide: Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor combined with levodopa as co-beneldopa.
Benzodiazepine: Sedative drug class acting on GABA receptors, such as lorazepam.
Benzylpenicillin: IV penicillin used for Strep. viridans endocarditis.
Best interests: The basis for decisions for adults lacking capacity, using their wishes, values and the views of those close to them.
Beta-1: Adrenoceptor in the heart that increases rate and force of contraction.
Beta-2: Adrenoceptor causing bronchodilation and reducing mediator release from mast cells.
Beta-adrenergic receptors: Receptors for adrenaline on heart and other cells; increased by thyroid hormone.
Beta-blockers: Drugs such as propranolol that block adrenaline receptors; can trigger psoriasis.
Beta-haemolytic: Bacteria that completely break down red cells on blood agar, leaving a clear zone.
Beta-hydroxybutyrate: The main ketone body in DKA, measured by capillary blood ketone meters.
Beta-lactam: Antibiotic class including penicillins and cephalosporins that blocks cell-wall synthesis.
Beta-lactamase: A bacterial enzyme that breaks down penicillins.
Beta-thalassaemia major: Both beta genes faulty: severe anaemia in infancy needing lifelong transfusion.
Beta-thalassaemia trait: Carrier state for beta-thalassaemia: often no symptoms, very low MCV, HbA2 above 3.5%.
Betahistine: A drug used in Ménière's disease to reduce attack frequency.
Betamethasone: Potent topical corticosteroid, combined with calcipotriol in psoriasis.
BiPAP: Bilevel positive airway pressure (NIV); also helps blow off CO2 in hypercapnia.
Bibasal crackles: Crackles heard at both lung bases; fine and end-inspiratory in fibrosis.
Bicarbonate: The main blood buffer (HCO3); it is used up by ketoacids, so a low level shows acidosis severity.
Bicuspid aortic valve: A congenital aortic valve with two leaflets instead of three, which stenoses decades early.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes at both lung roots; the classic X-ray sign of sarcoidosis.
Biliary colic: Pain from a stone transiently blocking the gallbladder outlet, without fever or jaundice.
Bilirubin: Yellow breakdown product of haemoglobin, cleared by the liver; high levels cause jaundice.
Billroth I: Partial gastrectomy with the stomach remnant joined directly to the duodenum.
Biofilm: A slime layer of bacteria on a device surface that shields them from immunity and antibiotics.
Biologic: An antibody-based drug targeting a specific immune molecule.
Bioprosthetic valve: A tissue (animal) valve that does not need lifelong warfarin but wears out.
Biopsy: Taking a tissue sample to confirm the type of cancer under the microscope.
Biphasic T wave: A T wave with an up and a down part; seen in Wellens syndrome.
Biphasic reaction: A second wave of anaphylaxis hours (typically 4 to 6) after the first, without re-exposure.
Birefringence: How a crystal bends polarised light; positive or negative birefringence helps identify the crystal type.
Bisoprolol: Cardioselective beta-blocker used for AF rate control.
Bisphosphonate: Drug that binds bone mineral and kills osteoclasts, slowing bone loss.
Bisphosphonates: Drugs that bind bone mineral and kill osteoclasts, reducing bone resorption.
Bite cells: Red cells with a 'bite' taken out where the spleen removed Heinz bodies.
Bladder diary: A record over at least 3 days of fluid intake, voids, leaks and triggers.
Bladder irrigation: Continuous washing of the bladder with saline to clear clots.
Bladder retraining: Gradually lengthening the time between voids to reduce urgency; first-line for urge.
Blasts: Immature white blood cell precursors; at least 20% in the marrow means acute leukaemia.
Bleomycin: Chemotherapy drug, used in testicular cancer, that causes pulmonary fibrosis.
Blood cultures: Blood bottles incubated to grow and identify bacteria in the bloodstream.
Blood film: A stained smear of blood examined under the microscope.
Blood-brain barrier: Tight junctions in brain capillaries that stop most substances leaking from blood into brain tissue.
Board-like: Describes a rigid abdomen that feels hard like a board, classic of a perforated viscus.
Bolus: A set volume of fluid given quickly, e.g. 500 ml stat in a hypotensive patient.
Bone biopsy: Sampling bone tissue for histology and culture; the gold standard in osteomyelitis.
Bone marrow biopsy: Aspirate and trephine sample of marrow; gold standard for diagnosing leukaemia.
Bone marrow failure: Marrow cannot make enough normal blood cells, causing anaemia, infection and bleeding.
Bone marrow oedema: Excess fluid in the marrow, an early MRI sign of osteomyelitis.
Bone marrow transplant: Replacement of a failed or diseased marrow with donor stem cells.
Bone mineral density: Amount of mineral per area of bone, measured by DEXA.
Bone profile: Blood panel of calcium, phosphate, ALP and albumin.
Borchardt's triad: Severe epigastric pain, retching without vomiting and inability to pass an NG tube: gastric volvulus.
Bosentan: An oral endothelin receptor antagonist used in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Botulinum toxin: Injected into the bladder wall for refractory urge incontinence to paralyse the detrusor.
Bouchard's nodes: Hard bony swellings of the PIP joints in osteoarthritis.
Boutonnière deformity: Finger with flexed PIP and hyperextended DIP.
Bovine cough: A weak, breathy cough from inability to close the vocal cords or generate force.
Bradyarrhythmia: An abnormal heart rhythm with a rate below 60 bpm.
Bradycardia: Heart rate below 60 bpm; in DKA it may signal raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema.
Bradykinesia: Slowness of movement with progressive loss of amplitude on repetition.
Bradykinin: A peptide normally broken down by ACE; its build-up on ACE inhibitors causes a dry cough.
Brain abscess: A walled-off collection of pus inside the brain tissue.
Brain metastases: Secondary cancer deposits in the brain that have spread from a primary tumour elsewhere.
Brandt-Daroff: Home exercises of repeated side-lying to settle BPPV.
Breast abscess: Collection of pus in the breast, usually when breastfeeding, with fever.
Breast cyst: Benign fluid-filled sac in breast tissue, common in women aged 30 to 50.
Breast mouse: Nickname for a fibroadenoma because it slips away under the fingers.
Breast ultrasound: Imaging with sound waves; shows whether a lump is fluid or solid.
Breast-conserving surgery: Removing the tumour with a margin while keeping the breast; also called wide local excision.
Brisk reflexes: Exaggerated tendon reflexes, suggesting upper motor neurone or CNS involvement.
Bristol stool chart: Seven-point scale of stool form: types 1 to 2 constipated, 6 to 7 liquid.
Broad-spectrum: An antibiotic or regimen covering many types of bacteria before the organism is known.
Broca's: Expressive aphasia from an inferior frontal gyrus lesion: non-fluent speech with preserved understanding.
Bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds heard over consolidated lung, because solid lung carries airway sounds to the chest wall.
Bronchial challenge test: Inhaling methacholine or histamine to provoke airway narrowing; shows hyperresponsiveness.
Bronchiectasis: Permanent dilatation of the bronchi with poor mucus clearance and recurrent infection.
Bronchiolitis: RSV infection of the small airways in infants under 1, causing wheeze and crackles.
Bronchodilator: Drug that opens the airways, such as salbutamol.
Bronchorrhoea: Excessive watery secretions from the airways.
Bronchoscopy: A camera passed down the airways to look inside and take samples.
Bronchospasm: Tightening of the airway smooth muscle causing wheeze.
Bronze diabetes: Diabetes plus bronze skin from iron in the pancreas and skin.
Brudzinski sign: Neck flexion causing involuntary hip and knee flexion, a sign of meningism.
Brudzinski's sign: Passive neck flexion causes the hips and knees to flex.
Brugada: An inherited sodium channel disorder with a coved ST pattern in V1–V2 and risk of sudden death.
Bruit: Whooshing sound heard with a stethoscope from turbulent blood flow.
Buccal midazolam: A benzodiazepine given inside the cheek when there is no IV access.
Buccal mucosa: The lining inside the cheeks; pigmented patches here suggest Addison's.
Budd-Chiari syndrome: Hepatic vein obstruction causing hepatomegaly, abdominal pain and high-SAAG ascites.
Budding yeast: Yeast cells reproducing by small outgrowths, seen on microscopy in candidiasis.
Bulbar: Muscles of speech, chewing and swallowing, supplied by the brainstem.
Bull's eye retinopathy: Ring-shaped macular damage caused by hydroxychloroquine.
Bullae: Large air spaces in emphysematous lung that can mimic a pneumothorax.
Bundle of Kent: The accessory pathway in WPW linking atria and ventricles, bypassing the AV node.
Burkitt's lymphoma: Very aggressive EBV-associated B-cell NHL driven by MYC; high tumour lysis risk.
Burr hole: A small hole drilled in the skull to drain fluid or pus.
Bursitis: Inflammation of a bursa, a fluid-filled sac that cushions tendons near joints.
Bypass graft: A vein or synthetic tube routing blood around a blocked artery.
Bypass surgery: Using a vein or graft to route blood around a blocked artery.
C-V wave: A merged, giant systolic wave in the JVP seen in tricuspid regurgitation.
C-peptide: Fragment released with insulin; low in type 1 diabetes because insulin production has failed.
C. difficile: Clostridioides difficile: spore-forming Gram-positive anaerobe causing antibiotic-associated colitis.
C282Y: The classic HFE mutation; homozygosity causes most hereditary haemochromatosis.
C3: Complement component 3; falls when consumed by immune complexes, so low levels mean active lupus.
C4: Complement component 4; like C3, low levels indicate active lupus.
C9orf72: A gene whose repeat expansion causes frontotemporal dementia and ALS.
CA 19-9: A tumour marker linked to pancreatic cancer, used mainly to monitor disease.
CA125: Tumour marker for ovarian cancer, checked in women with IBS-like symptoms.
CABG: Coronary artery bypass graft: open-heart surgery that uses a vein or artery to bypass blocked coronary arteries.
CAGE: Four-question alcohol dependence screen: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; two or more yes answers is significant.
CAP: Community-acquired pneumonia: starts outside hospital or within 48 hours of admission.
CAS: Clinical Activity Score for thyroid eye disease activity.
CAUTI: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection, usually E. coli.
CBD: Common bile duct, carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
CBG: Capillary blood glucose, the bedside finger-prick reading.
CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy: a talking therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviours.
CCB: Calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine); first-line for age 55 or over or Black patients.
CCBs: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine; can reduce intestinal motility.
CCU: Coronary care unit: ward with continuous cardiac monitoring.
CD20: Surface protein on B cells targeted by rituximab.
CD21: Complement receptor 2 on B cells; the entry receptor for EBV.
CD4: Surface marker on T-helper cells that HIV uses to enter cells.
CD4 count: Number of helper T cells; below 200 cells/µL defines AIDS.
CD8+: Marker of cytotoxic T cells that kill virus-infected cells.
CEA: Carcinoembryonic antigen; tumour marker used to monitor colorectal cancer treatment.
CFS: Chronic fatigue syndrome: disabling fatigue with post-exertional malaise for at least 3 months, not explained by another condition.
CFTR: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, an epithelial chloride channel.
CGM: Continuous glucose monitoring with a sensor under the skin.
CGRP: Calcitonin gene-related peptide: a neuropeptide driving neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation in migraine.
CHA2DS2-VASc: Score estimating stroke risk in AF to decide anticoagulation.
CHARTS: Mnemonic for upper lobe fibrosis: coal, histiocytosis/HP, ankylosing spondylitis, radiation, TB, silicosis/sarcoid.
CHOCOLATE: Mnemonic for migraine triggers: chocolate, hangovers, orgasms, cheese/caffeine, oral contraceptives, lie-ins, alcohol, travel, exercise.
CIN: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: pre-cancerous change graded I to III.
CIS: Carcinoma in situ: flat, high-grade, non-invasive cancer of the lining.
CK: Creatine kinase: a muscle enzyme that is very high in rhabdomyolysis.
CK-MB: A heart-specific creatine kinase enzyme that falls quickly after MI, making it useful for spotting reinfarction.
CKD: Chronic kidney disease: kidney damage or reduced function lasting 3 months or more.
CKD-mineral bone disease: Bone and mineral problems in CKD: abnormal calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D, fractures and calcification.
CLL: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, a common cause of warm AIHA.
CML: Chronic myeloid leukaemia: defined by the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22); massive splenomegaly.
CMPA: Cow's milk protein allergy: an immune reaction to the proteins in cow's milk.
CMV retinitis: Cytomegalovirus infection of the retina causing floaters and visual loss when CD4 is below 50.
CN V: The trigeminal nerve, the fifth cranial nerve.
CN VII: The facial nerve: moves the face and carries taste, tear, saliva and stapedius fibres.
CO2 retainer: A patient with chronically raised pCO2 who risks worsening with uncontrolled oxygen.
COCP: Combined oral contraceptive pill; its oestrogen raises clotting risk.
COMT inhibitor: Drug such as entacapone that slows peripheral levodopa breakdown and prolongs each dose.
COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; the most important cause of respiratory acidosis.
COX-1: Cyclooxygenase-1: enzyme that makes thromboxane in platelets and protective prostaglandins in the stomach.
COX-2: Inducible cyclooxygenase involved in inflammation; also blocked by aspirin.
CPAP: Continuous positive airway pressure via a tight mask; keeps alveoli open in pulmonary oedema.
CPP: Cerebral perfusion pressure: MAP minus ICP; the pressure driving blood through the brain.
CPPD: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, the umbrella term that includes pseudogout.
CPR: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions and rescue breaths.
CRAB: HyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions: myeloma end-organ damage.
CRB-65: CURB-65 without the urea, used in the community where blood results are not available.
CRP: C-reactive protein; a blood marker of inflammation used to guide antibiotics in acute cough.
CRT: Cardiac resynchronisation therapy: a biventricular pacemaker that makes both ventricles contract together.
CRT-D: A CRT device that is also an implantable defibrillator.
CSF: Cerebrospinal fluid, which surrounds the brain and spinal cord.
CT: Computed tomography: cross-sectional X-ray imaging used to find and stage cancer.
CT CAP: CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, used to find a primary tumour or other spread.
CT KUB: Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder; the standard test for stones.
CT angiogram: CT scan with IV contrast showing the aorta's size, shape and leaks; used to plan EVAR.
CT angiography: CT scan with IV contrast that maps the arteries and shows blockages or aneurysms.
CT aortic angiogram: Contrast CT timed for the aorta; the gold-standard test, showing the false lumen.
CT colonography: CT 'virtual colonoscopy' after bowel preparation and gas insufflation.
CT coronary angiography: CT scan with contrast showing coronary narrowing; first-line test for stable angina.
CT sinuses: A CT scan of the facial sinuses, used in severe, recurrent or complicated disease.
CT urogram: CT with contrast timed to show the kidneys, ureters and bladder lining.
CT-guided biopsy: Needle biopsy of a lung lesion using CT to guide it; used for peripheral masses.
CTCA: CT coronary angiography: first-line non-invasive scan of the coronary arteries.
CTEPH: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, caused by unresolved pulmonary emboli.
CTPA: CT pulmonary angiogram; timed for the pulmonary arteries to look for PE, not dissection.
CURB-65: Pneumonia severity score: confusion, urea over 7, RR 30 or more, low BP, age 65 or over.
CYP2C19: Liver enzyme that activates clopidogrel; inhibited by omeprazole and esomeprazole.
CYP2E1: Cytochrome P450 enzyme induced by chronic drinking; metabolises alcohol and makes free radicals.
CYP450: Liver enzyme family that breaks down many drugs, including warfarin.
CYP450 inducer: Drug that speeds up CYP450, lowering levels of drugs like warfarin.
CYP450 inducers: Drugs such as rifampicin and carbamazepine that speed up liver breakdown of other drugs.
CYP450 inhibitor: Drug that slows CYP450, raising levels of drugs like warfarin.
Caecal volvulus: Volvulus of a mobile caecum; gives right iliac fossa pain and a small bowel obstruction picture.
Caeruloplasmin: Copper-carrying protein; low in Wilson's disease.
Calcineurin inhibitor: Drug that blocks T-cell activation; used topically in eczema to avoid steroid side effects.
Calcipotriol: Topical vitamin D analogue that slows keratinocyte growth.
Calcitriol: The active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made in the kidney.
Calcium gluconate: IV calcium given to stabilise the heart muscle in severe hyperkalaemia; it does not lower potassium.
Calcium pyrophosphate: The calcium salt that forms the rhomboid crystals of pseudogout.
Callus: Thickened skin over a pressure point; a warning sign of ulcer risk in a neuropathic foot.
Cameron ulcers: Linear erosions in a hiatus hernia at the diaphragmatic pinch, causing occult bleeding.
Campylobacter: Commonest UK bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea, often from undercooked chicken.
Campylobacter jejuni: Gut bacterium whose infection commonly triggers GBS.
Candesartan: An angiotensin receptor blocker used as second-line migraine prophylaxis.
Candida albicans: The commonest Candida yeast; normal flora of mouth, gut and vagina.
Candidiasis: Infection caused by Candida yeasts, usually Candida albicans.
Cannon A waves: Large JVP waves when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.
Capacity: The ability to make a specific decision at a specific time, judged by the four-stage test.
Capillary: Finger-prick sample used at the bedside for glucose and ketone measurements.
Capillary leak: Fluid escaping from damaged small vessels into tissues, causing oedema and low circulating volume.
Caplan syndrome: Rheumatoid lung nodules in people exposed to coal, silica or asbestos dust.
Capnography: Continuous measurement and waveform of exhaled CO2; confirms the tube is in the trachea.
Capsule: The fibrous wall that forms around a mature abscess.
Caput medusae: Dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus, a sign of portal hypertension.
Carbamazepine: A second-line AED for focal seizures; an enzyme inducer that weakens hormonal contraception.
Carbidopa: Peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor given with levodopa.
Carbimazole: Antithyroid drug that blocks hormone synthesis; used for hyperthyroidism, never for hypothyroidism.
Carcinoma in situ: High-grade cancer cells confined to the lining, not yet invasive.
Cardiac MRI: Magnetic resonance scan of the heart; the gold-standard test for myocarditis.
Cardiac arrest: Sudden cessation of cardiac output, so circulation stops.
Cardiac cirrhosis: Liver scarring from long-term venous congestion in right heart failure.
Cardiac output: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume: blood pumped per minute.
Cardiac sarcoidosis: Granulomas in the heart causing heart block, arrhythmias or heart failure.
Cardiac tamponade: Blood or fluid in the pericardium compressing the heart and stopping it filling.
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lungs from raised pressure in an overloaded or failing heart.
Cardiogenic shock: Low blood pressure and poor perfusion because the heart cannot pump enough.
Cardiomegaly: An enlarged heart shadow on CXR: cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 on a PA film.
Cardiomyopathy: Heart muscle disease; iron causes restrictive or dilated forms.
Cardiotoxicity: Drug damage to the heart muscle, such as heart failure from trastuzumab.
Cardiotropic: Having a tendency to infect heart tissue.
Carney complex: Rare inherited syndrome of adrenal nodules, skin pigmentation and heart myxomas.
Carotid endarterectomy: Surgery to remove plaque from the carotid artery to reduce stroke risk.
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: Syncope from pressure on the neck (shaving, tight collar), usually in older people.
Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist causing tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers.
Carpometacarpal joint: Joint between wrist bones and hand bones; the first one is at the base of the thumb.
Carrier: A person with one faulty copy who is usually unaffected but can pass it on.
Carvallo's sign: A right-sided murmur that gets louder on inspiration.
Carvedilol: Non-selective beta-blocker with alpha-blocking action, used to prevent first variceal bleeds.
Casal's necklace: Hyperpigmented band of dermatitis around the neck in pellagra.
Cascade screening: Testing relatives of someone with an inherited condition.
Cascade testing: Testing the relatives of someone with an inherited condition such as FH.
Caseating: With central cheesy necrosis; typical of TB granulomas.
Catecholamines: Adrenaline and noradrenaline; cortisol keeps blood vessels responsive to them.
Cauda equina: The bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord, resembling a horse's tail.
Cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, retention and LMN leg signs.
Cavitation: A hollow, air-filled space forming inside an area of lung destroyed by infection, typical of S. aureus or Klebsiella.
Cefalexin: Oral cephalosporin used for UTI in late pregnancy and complicated UTI.
Cefotaxime: A third-generation cephalosporin used in infants and with amoxicillin in Listeria risk groups.
Ceftriaxone: Third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used IV to treat SBP.
Cefuroxime: IV cephalosporin used for pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
Ceiling of care: The agreed upper limit of treatment escalation for a patient.
Celecoxib: A COX-2 selective NSAID with less stomach irritation.
Cell-mediated immunity: T-cell driven immunity that controls fungi, viruses and intracellular organisms.
Cellulitis: Acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually of one lower leg.
Centor: Short for the Centor criteria, the sore throat score used to decide antibiotics.
Centor criteria: Four-point score (exudate, tender anterior nodes, fever over 38°C, no cough) estimating the chance of Group A strep.
Central clearing: Paler centre to a lesion with a red edge.
Central sensitisation: The spinal cord and brain become over-responsive to pain signals, so pain is felt more easily.
Central sleep apnoea: Pauses in breathing because the brain stops sending the signal to breathe, usually without loud snoring.
Central venous catheter: A line placed in a large central vein for drugs, nutrition or monitoring.
Central vertigo: Vertigo from the brainstem or cerebellum, e.g. stroke; often with neurological signs.
Centrilobular necrosis: Death of liver cells around the central veins (zone 3), the pattern of paracetamol injury.
Cerebellar stroke: Infarction of the cerebellum; a dangerous central cause of vertigo with ataxia.
Cerebral hypoxia: Lack of oxygen to the brain, causing injury within minutes.
Cerebral lupus: Neuropsychiatric lupus: brain involvement causing psychosis, seizures, severe headache or confusion.
Cerebral oedema: Brain swelling, a rare but deadly DKA complication in children, linked to rapid osmotic shifts during treatment.
Cerebral perfusion: Blood flow to the brain; consciousness is lost when it falls too low.
Cerebritis: Early, poorly defined inflammation of brain tissue before an abscess capsule forms.
Cervical lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck.
Cervical spine: The neck vertebrae; injury is a concern after trauma, so the neck is not tilted.
Charcot foot: Neuropathic joint destruction: a warm, swollen foot that collapses into deformity.
Charcot neuroarthropathy: Progressive destruction of foot bones and joints in a foot without protective sensation.
Charcot's triad: RUQ pain, jaundice and fever: the classic presentation of cholangitis.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth: Autosomal dominant inherited neuropathy with distal weakness and foot drop.
Chelation: Using a drug that binds a metal so it can be excreted.
Chest drain: A tube placed through the chest wall to drain fluid, pus or air from the pleural space.
Child-Pugh score: Severity score using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy, graded A to C.
Chlamydia trachomatis: Sexually transmitted organism that can cause neonatal conjunctivitis.
Chloramphenicol: Topical broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic; first choice for bacterial conjunctivitis.
Chlordiazepoxide: Long-acting benzodiazepine used to cover alcohol withdrawal.
Chlorphenamine: A sedating H1 antihistamine; supportive only in anaphylaxis.
Cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, usually behind an obstruction.
Cholecystectomy: Surgical removal of the gallbladder, offered after recovery to prevent recurrence.
Cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder from an impacted stone, with pain and fever but usually no jaundice.
Choledocholithiasis: Gallstones in the common bile duct.
Cholestasis: Reduced bile flow, causing raised conjugated bilirubin, ALP and GGT.
Cholinergic: Relating to acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter for attention and memory.
Cholinergic crisis: Weakness, sweating, salivation and diarrhoea from too much acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.
Chondrocalcinosis: Calcium deposits visible in joint cartilage on X-ray, typical of pseudogout.
Chromaffin cells: Catecholamine-producing cells of the adrenal medulla, the origin of phaeochromocytoma.
Chronic bronchitis: Chronic airway inflammation with mucus hypersecretion and productive cough.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria: Chronic urticaria with no external trigger, often driven by autoantibodies against mast cells.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hyperte: Pulmonary hypertension from unresolved clots scarring and blocking the pulmonary arteries.
Chronic tophaceous gout: Long-standing gout with tophi and joint damage from years of high urate.
Chronic urticaria: Recurrent wheals on most days for 6 weeks or more, usually with no identifiable trigger.
Chrysotile: White, curly serpentine asbestos; less carcinogenic than amphiboles.
Chvostek's sign: Twitching of the face when the facial nerve is tapped in front of the ear.
Ciclosporin: An immunosuppressant used after transplant; causes gum overgrowth, excess hair and nephrotoxicity.
Cilia: Tiny hair-like projections on lining cells that beat to move mucus.
Ciprofloxacin: Oral fluoroquinolone antibiotic that covers Pseudomonas.
Circinate balanitis: Painless lesions on the glans or prepuce of the penis in reactive arthritis.
Circle of Willis: The ring of arteries at the base of the brain linking carotid and vertebrobasilar circulations.
Circumflex: Branch of the left coronary artery supplying the lateral wall.
Cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with nodules, causing portal hypertension and liver failure.
Cisplatin: Platinum chemotherapy used for advanced or metastatic bladder cancer.
Citrullinated proteins: Proteins in which arginine has been converted to citrulline; targets of anti-CCP.
Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic used when a patient is penicillin allergic.
Class II compression stockings: Medium-pressure stockings worn after healing to stop venous ulcers recurring.
Class III antiarrhythmic: Drug that blocks potassium channels, prolonging action potential and refractory period.
Claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking a set distance, relieved by rest.
Clean-contaminated: An operation entering the gut, airway or urinary tract under controlled conditions, such as appendicectomy.
Clindamycin: Antibiotic for penicillin allergy; carries a high risk of C. difficile diarrhoea.
Clinical Activity Score: Seven-point score of pain, redness and swelling; 3 or more means active thyroid eye disease.
Clobetasol propionate: A very potent topical corticosteroid; avoid on the face and in children.
Clobetasone butyrate: A moderate-potency topical corticosteroid (0.05%); not to be confused with clobetasol.
Clonic: The rhythmic jerking phase of a seizure.
Clopidogrel: P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet given with aspirin in ACS.
Closed-loop obstruction: Obstruction where a segment of bowel is blocked at both ends, so pressure rises fast.
Clostridioides difficile: Spore-forming anaerobe that causes diarrhoea and colitis after antibiotics.
Clostridium perfringens: Anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod that causes gas gangrene.
Clot retention: Inability to pass urine because blood clots block the bladder outlet.
Clotrimazole: Topical or vaginal azole antifungal; the pessary is used in pregnancy.
Clubbing: Loss of the nail-bed angle and bulbous fingertips, seen in asbestosis and lung cancer.
Cluster headache: Severe unilateral headache around the eye lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, with a red watery eye.
Cluster of grapes: Groups of cystic dilated bronchi on HRCT in severe bronchiectasis.
Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid; first-line IV antibiotic for cholangitis.
Co-codamol: Combination tablet of codeine (an opioid) and paracetamol; 30/500 means 30 mg codeine and 500 mg paracetamol.
Co-trimoxazole: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole; treats and prevents PCP.
Coagulase: Enzyme that clots plasma; separates Staph. aureus (positive) from Staph. epidermidis (negative).
Coagulase-negative staphylococci: Skin staphylococci such as S. epidermidis that colonise lines and form biofilms.
Coagulation cascade: Chain of clotting factor reactions ending in fibrin formation.
Coagulation screen: Blood tests of clotting: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and platelet count.
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from coal dust in miners, with upper zone nodules and fibrosis.
Coarctation: A congenital narrowing of the aorta causing radio-femoral delay and upper limb hypertension.
Coarctation of the aorta: Congenital narrowing of the aorta causing arm hypertension and weak, delayed femoral pulses.
Cobblestone papillae: Large bumps on the inner eyelid seen in allergic conjunctivitis.
Coccobacillus: A bacterium shaped between a sphere and a rod, such as Haemophilus influenzae.
Cockcroft-Gault: A formula using age, sex, weight and creatinine to estimate creatinine clearance for drug dosing.
Codeine: A weak opioid painkiller; in overuse headache it is withdrawn gradually.
Coeliac disease: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy that can cause functional hyposplenism.
Coffee bean sign: AXR appearance of sigmoid volvulus: a huge dilated loop with a central dividing line.
Cognitive reserve: The brain's ability to cope with insults before function declines.
Cognitive stimulation therapy: Group activities and exercises that keep memory and thinking active in mild to moderate dementia.
Cogwheel rigidity: Jerky, ratchet-like resistance to passive movement from rigidity plus tremor.
Colchicine: Anti-inflammatory drug for acute gout that blocks microtubules; causes diarrhoea and vomiting.
Cold agglutinins: Antibodies that clump red cells at low temperatures, produced in Mycoplasma infection.
Cold sore: Recurrent HSV blisters on or around the lip.
Colecalciferol: Vitamin D3 supplement used for bone protection.
Colicky: Pain that comes and goes in waves.
Collagen: A strong structural protein in the aortic wall that resists rupture.
Collapsing pulse: A pulse that rises fast then falls away abruptly; also called water hammer pulse, typical of AR.
Collateral circulation: Alternative small vessels that bypass a gradually narrowing artery.
Collateral vessels: Small alternative arteries that grow around a blockage.
Collection: A pocket of fluid or pus within tissues or a body space.
Colles' fracture: Dorsally displaced fracture of the distal radius after a fall on an outstretched hand.
Colour desaturation: Colours, especially red, look faded in one eye; an early sign of optic nerve disease.
Combined oral contraceptive pill: Oestrogen plus progestogen pill; contraindicated in migraine with aura because of stroke risk.
Commissural fusion: Leaflets stuck together at their edges, narrowing the valve; typical of rheumatic MS.
Commissure: The junction where two valve leaflets meet.
Common cold: A mild viral URTI of the nose and throat, usually rhinovirus.
Common peroneal nerve: Nerve winding round the fibular neck; injury causes foot drop.
Compartment syndrome: Raised pressure in a muscle compartment that cuts off its blood supply.
Compensated: Cirrhosis with no ascites, bleeding, jaundice or encephalopathy.
Compensated respiratory acidosis: Raised CO2 with normal pH because the kidneys have raised bicarbonate.
Complement: Blood proteins that, once activated by antibody, damage cell membranes.
Complete heart block: Third-degree block: atria and ventricles beat independently.
Compliance: How easily the lungs stretch; low in fibrosis.
Complicated UTI: UTI in men, pregnancy, abnormal urinary tract, catheters or systemic illness.
Compressive optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from swollen orbital contents pressing on it; sight-threatening.
Concentric hypertrophy: Even thickening of the ventricular wall with a small cavity, from pressure overload.
Concordant: All three parts of triple assessment agree.
Conduction aphasia: Inability to repeat words, from an arcuate fasciculus lesion.
Confidentiality: The duty to keep patient information private unless a recognised exception applies.
Confusion screen: Blood tests to find reversible causes of confusion, such as thyroid, B12, calcium and glucose.
Congenital heart block: Complete heart block present at birth, from maternal anti-Ro/La damaging the fetal AV node.
Coning: Herniation of the brainstem through the foramen magnum due to raised pressure, which can be fatal.
Conjugated bilirubin: Water-soluble bilirubin processed by the liver; appears in urine when bile is blocked.
Conjunctiva: Thin membrane covering the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids.
Conjunctival: Relating to the conjunctiva, the thin membrane covering the white of the eye.
Conjunctival injection: Redness of the conjunctiva from dilated blood vessels.
Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, causing a red eye with discharge and irritation.
Conn's syndrome: Primary hyperaldosteronism: high sodium, low potassium and hypertension; the opposite of Addison's.
Consolidation: Lung where the air spaces have filled with fluid, pus or cells, so it looks solid and white on X-ray.
Constrictive pericarditis: Stiff, scarred pericardium restricting heart filling, raising venous pressure and causing ascites.
Constructional apraxia: Inability to copy or draw shapes, such as interlocking pentagons, despite normal strength.
Contact tracing: Finding and testing people exposed to an infectious patient.
Contaminated: An operation with gross spillage or acute inflammation, such as a perforated appendix.
Contiguous: Spreading to the next adjacent node group in order.
Contiguous spread: Spread of infection directly from a neighbouring infected structure.
Contralateral: On the opposite side of the body to the lesion.
Conus medullaris: The tapered lower end of the spinal cord, at about the L1 vertebra.
Convulsions: Involuntary jerking movements; brief ones can occur in faints as well as seizures.
Coombs test: Another name for the direct antiglobulin test.
Cor pulmonale: Right heart failure caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
Core biopsy: Wider needle sample of tissue for histology.
Core needle biopsy: A wide needle takes a tissue core for histology and receptor testing.
Corneal reflex: Blinking when the cornea is touched; tests V1 sensation and CN VII.
Coronary angiogram: Invasive X-ray of the coronaries with contrast via a catheter; the gold standard.
Coronary ostia: The openings of the coronary arteries in the aortic root.
Corrigan's sign: Visible bounding pulsation of the carotid arteries in aortic regurgitation.
Cortical destruction: Erosion of the hard outer bone layer, visible on X-ray later in infection.
Cortical spreading depression: A slow wave of neuronal depolarisation then suppressed activity across the cortex; the cause of aura.
Corticospinal tract: The main motor pathway running from the cortex down the spinal cord to the motor neurones.
Corticosteroids: Steroid hormones and drugs that suppress inflammation and the immune response.
Cortisol: Main glucocorticoid; maintains blood pressure, glucose and the stress response.
Coryza: Inflammation of the nasal lining causing a runny, blocked nose and sneezing.
Costochondritis: Inflammation where ribs join the sternum; reduces chest expansion in AS.
Costophrenic angle: The angle where the diaphragm meets the chest wall on CXR; blunted by an effusion.
Costovertebral angle: Angle between the 12th rib and the spine, over the kidney.
Court order: An instruction from a court, which can legally require disclosure of patient information.
Courvoisier's law: In jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones.
Courvoisier's sign: Painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignancy not stones.
Covid-19: Illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, ranging from a cold to severe pneumonia.
Cow's milk protein allergy: Immune reaction in infants to cow's milk proteins, either IgE or non-IgE mediated.
Coxiella burnetii: Organism causing Q fever in farmers and abattoir workers; a culture-negative cause.
Coxsackie: An enterovirus that commonly causes viral pericarditis and myocarditis.
Coxsackievirus A16: Enterovirus causing hand, foot and mouth disease.
Coxsackievirus B: Enterovirus that is the most common cause of viral myocarditis.
CrCl: Creatinine clearance, an estimate of kidney function.
Crackles: Short popping sounds on inspiration as fluid-filled small airways and alveoli open.
Creatine kinase: Muscle enzyme that rises when muscle fibres are damaged.
Creatinine: A muscle breakdown product cleared by the kidneys; a rising level means falling kidney function.
Creon: Pancreatic enzyme replacement capsules taken with meals.
Crepitations: Crackles heard with a stethoscope; coarse in bronchiectasis, fine in fibrosis.
Crepitus: Crackling felt under the skin from gas in the tissues.
Crescendo-decrescendo: A murmur that builds up then fades, typical of outflow obstruction.
Critical limb ischaemia: Severe chronic ischaemia with rest pain, ulcers or gangrene.
Critical mass: Enough myocardium depolarised together to stop chaotic activity.
Crocidolite: Blue asbestos, an amphibole and the most carcinogenic type.
Crohn's disease: Inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gut, including the anus.
Crossmatch: Testing donor blood against the patient's blood so units are ready for transfusion.
Croup: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis in young children causing a barking cough and stridor.
Cryptococcal meningitis: Fungal meningitis from Cryptococcus neoformans, usually when CD4 is below 50.
Cryptococcus neoformans: Encapsulated yeast causing meningitis in immunocompromised patients.
Cryptoglandular: Arising from the anal glands that open into the anal crypts at the dentate line.
Cryptosporidiosis: Parasitic infection causing chronic watery diarrhoea in advanced HIV.
Crystal arthropathy: Joint disease caused by crystals depositing in and around the joint, mainly gout and pseudogout.
Crystalloid: Clear salt-based IV fluid such as 0.9% sodium chloride.
Culture-negative endocarditis: Endocarditis with negative blood cultures, from prior antibiotics or hard-to-grow organisms.
Cupula: A jelly-like flap in each canal that bends with fluid movement to signal rotation.
Curschmann spirals: Spiral mucus plugs from small airways seen in asthmatic sputum or histology.
Cushing's disease: Cushing's syndrome caused specifically by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
Cushing's syndrome: Clinical state caused by prolonged excess cortisol from any source.
Cushing's triad: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing from brainstem compression; a late sign.
Cyanocobalamin: A form of vitamin B12 used as a supplement.
Cyanosis: Bluish skin or lips from low blood oxygen.
Cyanotic congenital heart disease: Heart defects present from birth that shunt deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, such as tetralogy of Fallot.
Cyclopentolate: Anticholinergic eye drop that dilates the pupil and relaxes the ciliary muscle, easing uveitis pain.
Cyclophosphamide: Chemotherapy drug whose metabolite (acrolein) irritates the bladder and raises cancer risk.
Cycloplegic: Drug that paralyses the ciliary muscle, relieving spasm.
Cystic fibrosis: Autosomal recessive CFTR defect causing thick secretions in lungs, pancreas and gut.
Cystine: Amino acid forming stones in a genetic condition (cystinuria).
Cystitis: Infection or inflammation of the bladder; lower UTI.
Cystoscopy: Looking inside the bladder with a camera through the urethra.
Cytogenetics: Study of chromosomes in cancer cells to find translocations that guide prognosis and treatment.
Cytokine: Signalling protein from immune cells; TNF-alpha and IL-6 drive sepsis.
Cytokine storm: Excessive release of inflammatory signalling proteins that damages tissues throughout the body.
Cytokines: Inflammatory signalling proteins released during infection or surgery.
Cytology: Looking at cells under the microscope; often non-diagnostic for mesothelioma in pleural fluid.
Cytopenia: A low count of any one blood cell type.
Cytotoxic oedema: Swelling of brain cells themselves from energy failure, as in stroke; steroids do not help it.
D-dimer: Fibrin breakdown product; raised in clotting and often in Covid-19.
DAA: Direct-acting antiviral; drugs that block hepatitis C proteins and cure most patients.
DAMN: Drugs to stop in AKI: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Metformin, NSAIDs.
DANISH: Mnemonic for cerebellar signs: dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred speech, hypotonia.
DAPT: Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, usually continued for 12 months after ACS.
DAS28: Disease Activity Score using 28 joints, ESR/CRP and patient score; remission is under 2.6.
DAT: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, which detects antibody or complement on red cells.
DCIS: Ductal carcinoma in situ: malignant duct cells with an intact basement membrane, often seen as microcalcification.
DCM: Dilated cardiomyopathy: dilated, poorly contracting ventricle causing heart failure.
DCT: Distal convoluted tubule of the nephron.
DEXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry: a scan measuring bone mineral density.
DH: Dermatitis herpetiformis: the itchy blistering skin manifestation of coeliac disease.
DHFR: Dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme blocked by methotrexate.
DHT: Dihydrotestosterone: a potent androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase; drives prostate growth.
DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting that uses up platelets and clotting factors.
DIP: Distal interphalangeal joint, the finger joint nearest the fingertip.
DKA: Diabetic ketoacidosis: hyperglycaemia, ketones and metabolic acidosis from insulin deficiency.
DLB: Dementia with Lewy bodies: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
DLCO: Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide; reduced in emphysema.
DMT: Disease-modifying therapy: a drug that reduces relapse rate in MS.
DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban, used to prevent clots in AF.
DOACs: Direct oral anticoagulants: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban and dabigatran.
DPP-4 inhibitor: Gliptin (e.g. sitagliptin) that prolongs incretin action; weight neutral.
DRAGON score: Predicts 3-month outcome after thrombolysis with alteplase.
DRE: Digital rectal examination: feeling the prostate through the rectal wall.
DSM-5: The American Psychiatric Association's manual of diagnostic criteria for mental disorders.
