Labetalol: An IV alpha and beta-blocker used first to lower heart rate and BP in dissection.
Labyrinthitis: Inflammation of the labyrinth: continuous vertigo with hearing loss.
Lactate: A product of anaerobic metabolism; its level reflects how much tissue is ischaemic.
Lactational: Related to breastfeeding or milk production.
Lactulose: Osmotic laxative that reduces ammonia absorption, used for hepatic encephalopathy.
Lacunar: A small deep infarct from occlusion of a perforating artery, often from hypertension.
Lagger: A worker who wraps pipes and boilers with insulation, historically asbestos.
Lagophthalmos: Inability to close the eyelids fully.
Lambert-Eaton: Lambert-Eaton syndrome: presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, often with small cell lung cancer; strength improves with effort.
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: Anti-VGCC antibody syndrome: proximal leg weakness that improves with exertion, linked to small cell.
Lamina papyracea: The paper-thin bone between the ethmoid sinus and the orbit.
Lamotrigine: A sodium channel blocking AED, preferred in pregnancy; can cause a serious rash.
Lanosterol 14α-demethylase: Fungal CYP450 enzyme making ergosterol; the target of azoles.
Lanz incision: A transverse right iliac fossa incision used for open appendicectomy.
Laparotomy: Open abdominal surgery through a large incision.
Laplace's law: Wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius, so wider aneurysms are under more tension.
Large-volume paracentesis: Draining several litres of ascites to relieve tense distension, given with albumin cover.
Laryngeal mask airway: A supraglottic airway that sits over the larynx; quick to insert but does not protect against aspiration.
Laryngotracheobronchitis: Inflammation of the larynx, trachea and bronchi: the formal name for croup.
Lasting power of attorney: A legal document letting a chosen person make health or financial decisions if the patient loses capacity.
Latchkey incontinence: Urge leakage triggered by arriving home and putting the key in the door.
Late gadolinium enhancement: Bright areas on cardiac MRI after contrast showing scar or inflammation.
Latency: The time between exposure and disease appearing; decades for asbestos.
Lateral lumbar flexion: Side-bending of the lower spine; reduced early in AS.
Least restrictive option: Under the MCA, the choice that limits the person's rights and freedom the least.
Leflunomide: DMARD that can raise blood pressure; teratogenic.
Left atrial appendage: A pouch off the left atrium where clots form in AF.
Left lateral tilt: Tilting a pregnant patient about 15° to the left to relieve aortocaval compression.
Left sternal edge: The area just left of the breastbone where aortic regurgitation is best heard.
Length-dependent: Damage that affects the longest nerves first, so the feet before the hands.
Leptin: Fat-derived satiety hormone; obese people become resistant to its effect.
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: Rare X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism causing high urate, gout, self-injury and developmental delay.
Letrozole: Aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal ER-positive breast cancer.
Leucocyte esterase: Enzyme from white cells detected on a dipstick; marker of pyuria.
Leucopenia: A low total white cell count (alternative spelling of leukopenia).
Leukoerythroblastic: Blood film with immature white and red cells, from marrow infiltration or stress.
Leukopenia: A low total white cell count.
Leukoplakia: A white oral patch that cannot be scraped off; potentially premalignant.
Leukostasis: Very high blast counts clogging small vessels, causing headache, visual change and breathlessness.
Leukotrienes: Lipid mediators from mast cells that cause prolonged bronchoconstriction and vascular leak.
Levetiracetam: Anti-epileptic drug commonly used for seizures caused by brain tumours.
Levodopa: Dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier; the most effective Parkinson's drug.
Levothyroxine: Synthetic T4 tablet, first-line replacement treatment for hypothyroidism.
Lewy bodies: Clumps of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein inside neurons.
Lewy body dementia: Dementia with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
Lhermitte's sign: Electric shock sensation down the spine or limbs on neck flexion; a cervical cord lesion.
Lichenification: Thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated markings from chronic scratching.
Lid lag: The upper lid is slow to follow the eye down; can occur in any thyrotoxicosis.
Lid retraction: The eyelid sits higher than normal, exposing sclera above the iris.
Lidocaine: Antiarrhythmic used as an alternative to amiodarone in refractory VF.
Lilliputian: Hallucinations of small people or animals, classic in Lewy body dementia.
Limbic encephalitis: Autoimmune inflammation of the limbic system causing memory loss and seizures.
Line sepsis: Bloodstream infection arising from a central venous catheter.
Liothyronine: Synthetic T3; faster acting and not first-line for hypothyroidism.
Lipase: Enzyme that breaks down dietary triglycerides so fat can be absorbed.
Lipid peroxidation: Free-radical damage to fats in cell membranes, injuring hepatocytes.
Lipid profile: Blood test measuring total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides.
Lipiduria: Fat in the urine, seen as fatty casts or oval fat bodies.
Lipodermatosclerosis: Chronic hardening and brown-red discolouration of lower-leg skin from venous disease.
Lipolysis: Breakdown of stored fat into free fatty acids and glycerol, switched on when insulin is absent.
Lipooligosaccharide: The meningococcal endotoxin that triggers DIC and shock.
Lipoprotein lipase: Enzyme on vessel walls that breaks down triglyceride-rich lipoproteins.
Liraglutide: Daily GLP-1 mimetic used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes.
Listeria: A bacterium causing meningitis in over-60s, pregnancy and immunosuppression; needs amoxicillin.
Listeria monocytogenes: A Gram-positive rod spread by soft cheese and unpasteurised milk.
Lithium: Mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder that can cause hypothyroidism and goitre.
Little's area: The anterior-inferior nasal septum where Kiesselbach's plexus lies; source of most nosebleeds.
Liver biopsy: Taking liver tissue for histology; the gold standard for cirrhosis, contraindicated if INR above 1.5.
Lobar pneumonia: Pneumonia filling one whole lobe of a lung, classically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Lobule: A milk-producing unit of the breast.
Locked-in syndrome: Basilar artery occlusion causing quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.
LogMAR: Visual acuity scale where 0.0 is normal and higher numbers mean worse vision.
Loin: The side of the back between the ribs and the hip.
Long QT: QTc above 440 ms in men or 460 ms in women; risks torsades.
Long-term oxygen therapy: Oxygen for at least 15 hours a day for chronic hypoxia, which slows pulmonary hypertension in COPD.
Looser's zones: Pseudofractures: radiolucent transverse bands with sclerotic edges, often at the hip.
Loratadine: A non-sedating oral antihistamine; first line for mild allergic rhinitis.
Lorazepam: Benzodiazepine used for sedation when antipsychotics must be avoided, and for rapid tranquillisation.
Loud P2: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, suggesting pulmonary hypertension.
Low voltage complexes: Small QRS complexes on the ECG, seen with myocardial oedema or effusion.
Lucozade: A glucose drink used as oral fast-acting glucose.
Lugano staging: Lymphoma staging system (stages 1 to 4) based on the diaphragm and organ spread; replaced Ann Arbor.
Lumbar puncture: Needle sampling of CSF from the lower back; dangerous when a mass lesion raises intracranial pressure.
Lumpectomy: Breast-conserving removal of a tumour with a clear margin.
Lung abscess: A pus-filled cavity inside the lung, often after aspiration, seen as a cavity with a fluid level.
Lung volume reduction surgery: Removing hyperinflated emphysematous lung to improve mechanics.
Lupus nephritis: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis in SLE causing proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension and rising creatinine.
Lupus pernio: Purple, indurated rash on the nose and cheeks in sarcoidosis; not related to SLE.
Luteal phase: Second half of the menstrual cycle, after ovulation, when progesterone is high.
Lyme disease: Tick-borne Borrelia infection that can cause facial palsy, sometimes bilateral.
Lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes, such as in the axilla.
Lymphangitis: Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, seen as red streaks tracking towards lymph nodes.
Lymphoblasts: Immature lymphoid blasts, seen in ALL.
Lymphocyte-depleted: Rarest Hodgkin subtype with the worst prognosis; older or HIV patients.
Lymphocyte-predominant: Hodgkin subtype with the best prognosis, often found early.
Lymphocytosis: Raised lymphocyte count; in CSF, suggests a viral or autoimmune cause.
Lymphoedema: Swelling from damaged lymph drainage, often of the arm after axillary surgery.
Lymphoma: Cancer of lymphocytes arising in lymph nodes or other lymphatic tissue.
Lymphopenia: Low lymphocyte count, a common blood finding in active SLE.
Lynch syndrome: Autosomal dominant mismatch repair defect causing early right-sided colorectal and endometrial cancers.
Lytic lesion: An area where bone has been destroyed, appearing as a dark hole on X-ray.
Löfgren's syndrome: Acute sarcoidosis with fever, BHL, erythema nodosum and polyarthralgia; good prognosis.
M cells: Specialised epithelial cells over Peyer's patches that sample gut contents; S. typhi enters through them.
M protein: Another name for the paraprotein band on electrophoresis.
M1: Screening grade for maculopathy needing referral, such as exudates near the fovea.
M3 receptor: Muscarinic receptor on the detrusor that mediates bladder contraction.
MAHA: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia: red cells sheared in small damaged vessels.
MAO-B inhibitor: Drug such as selegiline or rasagiline that slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.
MAP: Mean arterial pressure; the target in shock is usually 65 mmHg or above.
MART: Maintenance and reliever therapy: one ICS/formoterol inhaler used regularly and as needed.
MCA: Mental Capacity Act 2005, the framework for adults who lack capacity.
MCH: Mean cell haemoglobin, the average amount of haemoglobin per red cell; low in iron deficiency.
MCP: Metacarpophalangeal joint, the knuckle joint; typical in rheumatoid arthritis.
MCV: Mean cell volume; a raised MCV (macrocytosis) is common with heavy alcohol use.
MDF: Maddrey's discriminant function, the severity score that guides steroid use.
MDMA: Ecstasy: a stimulant drug that can cause hyperthermia and serotonin toxicity.
MDRD: An eGFR equation using creatinine, age, gender and ethnicity.
MDS: Myelodysplastic syndrome: a clonal marrow disorder with ineffective, dysplastic blood cell production.
MDT: Multidisciplinary team meeting that plans cancer treatment.
ME/CFS: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome; the name used in the NICE guideline.
MELD: Model for End-Stage Liver Disease: score from bilirubin, INR and creatinine to prioritise transplant.
MEN 1: Inherited syndrome of parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
MEN 2: Inherited syndrome of medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and (2A) hyperparathyroidism.
MEN1: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1: parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
MEN2: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2: inherited syndrome with phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma.
MEN2A: Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A: medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid disease.
METAVIR: Histological staging system for liver fibrosis, F0 (none) to F4 (cirrhosis).
MGUS: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance: a small paraprotein without CRAB that can progress.
MI: Myocardial infarction: death of heart muscle from prolonged ischaemia.
MLF: Medial longitudinal fasciculus: brainstem tract linking the CN VI and CN III nuclei for conjugate gaze.
MLH1: DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome.
MMF: Mycophenolate mofetil, an immunosuppressant used in lupus nephritis.
MMR: The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
MMSE: Mini-Mental State Examination, a longer cognitive test used in dementia.
MND: Motor neurone disease: progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons.
MODS: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome: failure of two or more organ systems, usually from systemic inflammation such as sepsis.
MODY: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young: single-gene diabetes before 25, often treated with sulfonylureas.
MONA: Old mnemonic for immediate ACS care: morphine, oxygen, nitrates, aspirin; oxygen now only if saturations below 94%.
MPN: Myeloproliferative neoplasm: a clonal marrow disorder overproducing one or more blood cell lines.
MPO: Myeloperoxidase: enzyme in myeloid granules; positive staining marks myeloid blasts.
MPT: Melphalan, prednisolone and thalidomide; a regimen for older patients.
MR angiography: MRI of the arteries with contrast, giving anatomical detail.
MRA: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone); blocks aldosterone.
MRC: Medical Research Council 0 to 5 scale for muscle power.
MRC grade: Muscle power scale from 0 (no movement) to 5 (normal power).
MRCP: MRI of the bile and pancreatic ducts; the most accurate non-invasive biliary imaging.
MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; used in atypical cases to exclude central or structural lesions.
MRI pelvis: Magnetic resonance imaging that maps abscesses and fistula tracts against the sphincters.
MRSA: Meticillin-resistant S. aureus; not killed by flucloxacillin.
MSCC: Metastatic spinal cord compression: an oncological emergency causing back pain and leg weakness.
MSH2: DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome.
MSM: Men who have sex with men.
MSSA: Meticillin-sensitive Staph. aureus; treated with flucloxacillin.
MSU: Mid-stream urine sample for microscopy and culture.
MTP: Metatarsophalangeal joint at the base of the toes.
MUDPILES: Mnemonic for raised anion gap acidosis: methanol, uraemia, DKA, paracetamol, iron, lactate, ethylene glycol, salicylates.
MUST: Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool: scores BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect; 2 or more is high risk.
MYC: Oncogene driving cell division; translocated in Burkitt's lymphoma.
Macroalbuminuria: Larger albumin leak (ACR 30 mg/mmol or more); overt proteinuria.
Macrocirculation: Flow in the large vessels, reflected by blood pressure and cardiac output.
Macrocytic: Red cells larger than normal (MCV above 100 fL).
Macrolide: Antibiotic class including azithromycin and clarithromycin; long-term use reduces exacerbations.
Macrolides: Antibiotics such as clarithromycin that can worsen myasthenia.
Macrophages: Immune cells that engulf particles; they fail to clear asbestos fibres and drive inflammation.
Macula: The sensory patch in the utricle or saccule where otoconia sit.
Macula densa: Sodium-sensing cells in the distal tubule that signal the afferent arteriole.
Maddrey's Discriminant Function: Severity score from prothrombin time and bilirubin; 32 or more means severe alcoholic hepatitis.
Magnesium sulphate: IV drug that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle by blocking calcium influx.
Major haemorrhage protocol: A hospital system to deliver large amounts of blood products quickly.
Malaise: A general feeling of being unwell.
Malar flush: Plum-red cheeks seen in mitral stenosis from low cardiac output.
Malar rash: Red butterfly-shaped rash over both cheeks and nose bridge, sparing the nasolabial folds, worse after sun.
Malignant hypertension: Very high BP with acute end-organ damage such as papilloedema, encephalopathy or AKI.
Malperfusion: Inadequate blood supply to an organ because its branch artery is compressed by the flap.
Mammogram: Low-dose breast X-ray, used for screening and first-line imaging in older women.
Mandibular: Relating to the lower jaw; the V3 division of the trigeminal nerve.
Mandibular advancement device: A mouthguard-like splint that holds the lower jaw forward to widen the airway.
Mannitol: An osmotic diuretic given IV that draws water out of the brain to lower ICP.
Mantoux: Tuberculin skin test; the induration is read at 48 to 72 hours, 5 mm or more is positive.
Marcus Gunn pupil: Another name for a relative afferent pupillary defect.
Marfan's: Inherited connective tissue disorder causing tall stature and a higher risk of pneumothorax.
Marfan's syndrome: Autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder from fibrillin-1 defects: tall, long limbs, lens dislocation, aortic root dilatation.
Masked hypertension: Normal BP in clinic but raised on ambulatory or home monitoring.
Mass effect: Pressure from a lesion pushing on and displacing nearby brain.
Mast cell: Tissue immune cell packed with histamine granules that releases them when IgE is cross-linked.
Mast cell stabiliser: Drug that prevents mast cells releasing histamine.
Mast cell tryptase: Enzyme released by mast cells; a raised level confirms anaphylaxis has occurred.
Mastectomy: Surgical removal of the whole breast.
Mastitis: Inflammation or infection of breast tissue, most often while breastfeeding.
Mastoiditis: Infection spreading from the middle ear into the mastoid air cells behind the ear.
Matrix metalloproteinases: Enzymes that break down elastin and collagen in the aortic wall.
Maxillary: Relating to the upper jaw; the V2 division of the trigeminal nerve.
Maxillary sinus: The largest sinus, in the cheekbone under the eye; the one most often infected.
McBurney's point: One-third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus; the classic point of appendix tenderness.
McDonald criteria: The clinical and MRI rules used to diagnose MS.
Mechanical thrombectomy: Removing a clot from a large artery with a catheter device.
Mechanical valve: A durable artificial valve that needs lifelong warfarin.
Mechanical ventilation: A machine breathes for the patient through an endotracheal tube.
Media: The middle, muscular and elastic layer of the artery wall.
Medial hypertrophy: Thickening of the muscle layer of an artery wall.
Medial longitudinal fasciculus: Brainstem tract coordinating horizontal eye movements between the two eyes.
Mediastinum: Central chest compartment between the lungs containing heart, great vessels and lymph nodes.
Medical expulsive therapy: Drugs, such as tamsulosin, used to help a stone pass on its own.
Medication overuse headache: Chronic daily headache caused by frequent use of acute headache treatments.
Megaloblastic: Anaemia with large, immature red cell precursors caused by impaired DNA synthesis (B12 or folate).
Megaloblasts: Large red cell precursors whose nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm.
Melanoma: Skin cancer of pigment cells that frequently spreads to the brain.
Memantine: An NMDA glutamate receptor antagonist for severe Alzheimer's or AChE inhibitor intolerance.
Membranous nephropathy: Commonest adult cause of nephrotic syndrome; anti-PLA2R antibodies form subepithelial immune deposits.
MenACWY: A vaccine against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y, offered to teenagers.
Menetrier's disease: Rare disease of giant gastric folds with protein loss and low acid.
Meninges: The three membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
Meningioma: A usually benign tumour of the meninges, attached to the dura, outside the brain tissue.
Meningism: Neck stiffness, photophobia and headache from irritated meninges.
Meningitis: Inflammation of the meninges, the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord.
Meningococcal septicaemia: Bloodstream infection with Neisseria meningitidis, often with a non-blanching rash.
Meniscus: C-shaped cartilage cushion in the knee; tears predispose to later OA.
Menopause: The end of menstruation, confirmed after 12 months without periods.
Mental Capacity Act: The 2005 law for England and Wales on assessing capacity and acting in best interests.
Mental Health Act: Law allowing detention and treatment of mental disorder; separate from the Mental Capacity Act.
Merocel: A compressed sponge nasal pack that expands with fluid.
Mesangial expansion: Increase in the supporting matrix between glomerular capillaries.
Mesentery: The fold of peritoneum that attaches bowel to the back of the abdomen and carries its blood vessels.
Mesial temporal sclerosis: Scarring of the hippocampus, a common cause of temporal lobe epilepsy.
Mesothelial cells: The cells lining the pleura and peritoneum, from which mesothelioma arises.
Mesothelioma: A malignant tumour of the pleura (or peritoneum), strongly linked to asbestos.
Metabolic acidosis: Low blood pH from excess acid or lost bicarbonate, shown by a low bicarbonate.
Metabolic encephalopathy: Brain dysfunction from a chemical disturbance such as high CO2, causing confusion and a flap.
Metabolic syndrome: Cluster of central obesity, high blood pressure, high glucose and abnormal lipids.
Metanephrines: Breakdown products of adrenaline and noradrenaline; measured in plasma or urine to detect phaeochromocytoma.
Metaphysis: The flared part of a long bone between the shaft and the growth plate.
Metastasis: Cancer that has spread from its original site to another organ, such as bone.
Methenamine silver: A silver stain that shows Pneumocystis organisms clearly under the microscope.
Methotrexate: Antifolate DMARD used in RA; can cause pneumonitis and fibrosis.
Methyldopa: Centrally acting antihypertensive safe in pregnancy.
Methylmalonic acid: A metabolite that rises in B12 deficiency and disrupts myelin synthesis.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase: A B12-dependent enzyme; its failure builds up methylmalonic acid and harms myelin.
Methylprednisolone: A high-dose IV corticosteroid used in autoimmune encephalitis.
Metoclopramide: A dopamine antagonist that speeds stomach emptying; used for gastroparesis.
Metronidazole: Antibiotic covering anaerobes; used with ciprofloxacin in penicillin allergy.
Meyer's loop: Lower optic radiation fibres looping through the temporal lobe, carrying the upper visual field.
Miconazole: Azole antifungal; oral gel is first line for oral thrush.
Micro-aspiration: Small-volume inhalation of secretions, e.g. leaking past an endotracheal tube cuff.
Microalbuminuria: Small amounts of albumin in the urine, an early sign of kidney damage, especially in diabetes.
Microaneurysms: Tiny outpouchings of weakened retinal capillaries; the earliest sign of retinopathy.
Microcalcification: Tiny calcium flecks on a mammogram, typical of DCIS.
Microcirculation: Blood flow through the smallest vessels (arterioles, capillaries, venules) where oxygen reaches cells.
Microcytic: Red cells smaller than normal (MCV below 80 fL).
Micrographia: Small handwriting that shrinks across the page.
Microtubule: Protein tubes inside cells needed for neutrophil movement; blocked by colchicine.
Microvascular decompression: Neurosurgery that moves the compressing artery off the trigeminal nerve root.
Mid-clavicular line: Vertical line through the midpoint of the clavicle; V4 sits on it in the 5th space.
Mid-diastolic murmur: A murmur in the middle of diastole, such as the rumble of mitral stenosis.
Midline shift: Displacement of the brain's midline structures to one side by a mass, a sign of dangerous pressure.
Migraine: A primary headache disorder with recurrent attacks of moderate to severe headache, often with nausea and light sensitivity.
Migratory: Moving from one joint to another over time.
Milk ladder: A stepwise plan to reintroduce milk, starting with well-baked forms, after 6 months.
Milk stasis: Milk staying in the ducts because the breast is not emptied well.
Miller Fisher syndrome: GBS variant with ataxia, areflexia and ophthalmoplegia.
Minimal change disease: Commonest childhood cause of nephrotic syndrome; normal on light microscopy, responds to steroids.
Minute ventilation: Volume of air breathed per minute: respiratory rate times tidal volume.
Mirabegron: Beta-3 agonist that relaxes the detrusor; second-line for urge, preferred in the elderly.
Mirels score: Score of site, pain, lesion type and size (each 1 to 3); 9 or more means prophylactic fixation.
Mitomycin C: Chemotherapy instilled into the bladder after TURBT to reduce recurrence.
Mitral regurgitation: Backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole.
Mitral stenosis: Narrowed mitral valve, usually rheumatic, which enlarges the left atrium and causes AF.
Mitral valve prolapse: Floppy mitral leaflets bulging back into the left atrium in systole.
Mitral valve repair: Surgery that fixes the patient's own mitral valve; preferred over replacement for MR.
Mixed cellularity: Hodgkin subtype with intermediate prognosis, more common in older adults.
Mixed delirium: Delirium alternating between hyperactive and hypoactive features.
Mixed urinary incontinence: Features of both stress and urge incontinence in the same person.
MoCA: Montreal Cognitive Assessment, a 30-point screen that is more sensitive for mild impairment.
Mobile: Moves freely under the skin and over deeper tissue.
Mobitz II: Second-degree block with constant PR and intermittent dropped QRS; risk of asystole.
Modafinil: A wakefulness-promoting drug; it does not treat the airway obstruction in OSA.
Modified Duke criteria: Updated Duke criteria: definite IE is 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.
Modified Glasgow: Severity score for acute pancreatitis using the PANCREAS criteria at 48 hours.
Modified New York criteria: Classification criteria for AS requiring radiographic sacroiliitis plus clinical features.
Molecular mimicry: When antibodies to a microbe cross-react with the body's own proteins.
Mometasone: An intranasal corticosteroid used for moderate to severe allergic rhinitis.
Monofilament: A 10 g nylon filament pressed on the foot to test protective sensation.
Monomorphic: All lesions look the same and are at the same stage.
Mononeuropathy: Damage to a single nerve, such as a cranial nerve palsy or carpal tunnel syndrome.
Monosodium urate: The salt of uric acid that forms the needle-shaped crystals of gout.
Monospot: Rapid test for heterophile antibodies in glandular fever (EBV).
Monotherapy: Using one drug at a time, stopping one before starting another.
Monro-Kellie doctrine: The skull is a fixed box of brain, blood and CSF, so a rise in one must be offset by another.
Montelukast: An oral leukotriene receptor antagonist used as an asthma add-on.
Motor neurone disease: Progressive degeneration of motor neurones that can weaken breathing muscles and cause type 2 failure.
Movicol: Brand of macrogol with electrolytes, taken as a drink.
Mu-opioid receptor: The main opioid receptor; activation in the brainstem slows breathing.
MuSK: Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase; antibodies against it cause a more severe, bulbar form of myasthenia.
Mucociliary clearance: The cilia-driven escalator that moves mucus and trapped particles out of the airways.
Mucocutaneous bleeding: Bleeding from skin and mucous membranes (gums, nose, periods), typical of platelet or vWF problems.
Mucosal oedema: Swelling of the lining of the nose and sinuses from inflammation.
Muddy brown casts: Granular casts of dead tubular cells seen on urine microscopy in ATN.
Muffled heart sounds: Quiet heart sounds because fluid around the heart dampens them.
Muller's sign: Pulsation of the uvula in aortic regurgitation.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia: Irregular tachycardia with three or more P wave shapes, linked to COPD.
Multinucleated giant cells: Fused infected cells with several nuclei, seen in herpes virus infections.
Multiparity: Having given birth to several children.
Multiple myeloma: A cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow causing lytic lesions, anaemia, high calcium and kidney damage.
Multiple sclerosis: Autoimmune demyelinating disease of the brain and spinal cord with relapsing neurological episodes.
Multiple system atrophy: Alpha-synuclein disease with parkinsonism and severe early autonomic failure.
Murphy's sign: Pain and a catch of breath on palpating the RUQ during inspiration; suggests cholecystitis.
Muscle-invasive: Bladder cancer that has grown into detrusor muscle (T2 or above).
Myasthenia gravis: Autoimmune disease where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness.
Myasthenic crisis: Life-threatening respiratory and bulbar weakness in myasthenia needing urgent respiratory support.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Slow-growing, aerobic, acid-fast bacillus that causes tuberculosis.
Mycophenolate mofetil: Immunosuppressant used for lupus nephritis and severe SLE; teratogenic.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Bacterium causing atypical pneumonia; associated with cold AIHA.
Myelin: The insulating sheath around nerve fibres.
Myeloblasts: Immature myeloid blasts, seen in AML.
Myelodysplastic syndrome: A clonal stem cell disorder of older people causing dysplastic cells, cytopenias and risk of AML.
Myelofibrosis: Marrow fibrosis causing a dry tap, teardrop cells and massive splenomegaly.
Myeloma: A cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow causing lytic bone lesions, anaemia and hypercalcaemia.
Myeloma screen: Tests for myeloma: serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains and urine Bence Jones protein.
Myocardial depression: Reduced pumping strength of the heart caused by inflammatory mediators.
Myocarditis: Inflammation of the heart muscle, usually viral, that can mimic a heart attack.
Myocardium: The muscular middle layer of the heart wall.
Myoclonic: Brief, shock-like muscle jerks without loss of consciousness.
Myoclonic jerks: Brief, shock-like muscle twitches; in faints caused by cerebral hypoperfusion.
Myofascial: Relating to muscles and the fascia that wraps them.
Myofibroblasts: Contractile, collagen-producing cells that drive scarring.
Myopathy: Muscle damage causing pain and weakness, a risk when statin levels rise.
Myopericarditis: Inflammation affecting both the myocardium and the pericardium.
Myxoedema: Thickened, puffy skin and tissues from glycosaminoglycan deposits in severe hypothyroidism.
Myxoedema coma: Life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension and reduced consciousness.
Ménière's disease: Endolymphatic hydrops causing attacks of vertigo for hours with tinnitus, fullness and hearing loss.
N-acetylcysteine: The antidote to paracetamol, given IV, that restores glutathione to detoxify NAPQI.
N. meningitidis: Neisseria meningitidis, a Gram-negative diplococcus and the commonest UK cause of bacterial meningitis.
NAAT: Nucleic acid amplification test: a very sensitive DNA test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.
NAC: N-acetylcysteine (acetylcysteine): the paracetamol antidote that replenishes liver glutathione.
NAD: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide: niacin-derived coenzyme for cellular energy production.
NADPH: Molecule that keeps glutathione in its active, protective form inside red cells.
NAFLD: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, linked to obesity and diabetes; can progress to cirrhosis.
NAPQI: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine: the toxic paracetamol metabolite that destroys liver cells when glutathione runs out.
NASCET: North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial criteria for measuring carotid stenosis percentage.
NBM: Nil by mouth: nothing to eat or drink.
NCS: Nerve conduction studies: measuring speed and size of nerve signals.
NEAD: Non-epileptic attack disorder: seizure-like events with a psychological, not electrical, cause.
NEWS2: National Early Warning Score 2; a score from vital signs that flags deterioration.
NF1: Neurofibromatosis type 1: café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, associated with phaeochromocytoma.
NG tube: Nasogastric tube passed through the nose into the stomach to drain it.
NG12: NICE guideline on recognising and referring suspected cancer.
NG120: NICE guideline on antimicrobial prescribing for acute cough.
NG145: NICE guideline on assessing and managing thyroid disease.
NG220: NICE guideline on multiple sclerosis in adults.
NG232: NICE guideline on head injury assessment and early management.
NG71: NICE guideline on Parkinson's disease in adults.
NG79: The NICE guideline on antibiotic prescribing for acute sinusitis.
NHS AAA screening programme: A one-off abdominal ultrasound offered to men in the year they turn 65.
NHS Health Check: Routine cardiovascular risk check for adults aged 40 to 74 in England.
NICE: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which publishes UK guidance.
NICE CG113: NICE guideline on generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults.
NICE CG150: NICE guideline on diagnosing and managing headaches in young people and adults.
NICE CG179: The NICE guideline on preventing and managing pressure ulcers.
NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: UK primary care guidance.
NICE NG12: NICE guideline on recognising and referring suspected cancer.
NICE NG123: NICE guideline on urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women.
NICE NG125: NICE guideline on preventing and treating surgical site infections.
NICE NG139: NICE guideline on preventing healthcare-associated infections.
NICE NG202: NICE guideline on obstructive sleep apnoea, obesity hypoventilation syndrome and COPD overlap.
NICE NG222: NICE guideline on depression in adults.
NICE NG50: NICE guideline on assessing and managing cirrhosis in people over 16.
NIHSS: NIH Stroke Scale: scores neurological severity (0 to 42) and guides reperfusion.
NIPPV: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, another name for NIV.
NIV: Non-invasive ventilation: mask ventilation that helps blow off CO2 in respiratory acidosis.
NLRP3 inflammasome: An immune protein complex that senses urate crystals and releases IL-1β.
NMDA: A glutamate receptor; overstimulation damages neurons, which memantine blocks.
NMJ: Neuromuscular junction: the synapse between a motor nerve and a muscle fibre.
NPDR: Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy: vessel damage without new vessel growth.
NPV: Negative predictive value: chance of no disease if the test is negative, TN/(TN+FN).
NR1 subunit: The part of the NMDA receptor targeted by the autoantibodies.
NRTI: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, e.g. tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir, lamivudine.
NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen, which constricts the afferent arteriole.
NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that inhibit COX enzymes, e.g. ibuprofen and naproxen.
NSCLC: Non-small cell lung cancer: adenocarcinoma, squamous cell and large cell carcinoma; the majority of cases.
NSTEMI: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction: raised troponin without ST elevation, usually from partial coronary occlusion.
NT-proBNP: A blood marker released by stretched ventricles; raised in heart failure.
NYHA: New York Heart Association classes I to IV, grading heart failure symptoms by activity limitation.
Na/K-ATPase: Cell membrane pump that moves potassium into cells; insulin increases its activity.
Nail pitting: Small dents in the nail surface, typical of psoriasis.
Naloxone: Short-acting competitive opioid receptor antagonist that reverses opioid overdose.
Naltrexone: Long-acting oral opioid antagonist used for relapse prevention, not for acute overdose.
Narrowband UVB: Phototherapy with a narrow band of ultraviolet B light for moderate-to-severe psoriasis.
Nasal polyps: Benign grey swellings of the nasal lining causing blockage and loss of smell.
Naseptin: Chlorhexidine and neomycin nasal cream to prevent recurrence; contains peanut (arachis) oil.
Nasolabial folds: The creases running from the sides of the nose to the corners of the mouth.
Natalizumab: Monoclonal antibody against α4-integrin that stops lymphocytes entering the CNS; used in highly active MS.
Natriuresis: Excretion of sodium in the urine.
Near-fatal asthma: Raised pCO2 or need for mechanical ventilation with raised inflation pressures.
Neck circumference: Collar size; above about 40 cm (16 inches) suggests a crowded airway and OSA risk.
Necrosis: Death of tissue, seen as dusky, grey or black skin.
Necrotising fasciitis: Rapidly spreading, life-threatening infection of the fascia; pain out of proportion, crepitus, needs surgery.
Necrotising soft tissue infection: Rapidly spreading, life-threatening infection that kills tissue; needs emergency surgical debridement.
Needle decompression: Wide-bore cannula into the 2nd intercostal space to release a tension pneumothorax.
Needle thoracocentesis: Needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax.
Negative feedback: When a hormone switches off the signal that made it; T4 normally suppresses TSH.
Negatively birefringent: Crystal optics on polarised light typical of urate crystals in gout.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae: Sexually transmitted bacterium that can infect a baby's eyes during birth.
Neisseria meningitidis: Encapsulated Gram-negative diplococcus causing meningitis and septicaemia.
Nelson's syndrome: Growth of a pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy, causing pigmentation and mass effect.
Neoadjuvant: Treatment given before surgery to shrink a tumour.
Neonatal haemolysis: Destruction of the newborn's red cells; risk with late-pregnancy nitrofurantoin.
Neonatal herpes: HSV infection of a newborn caught during delivery; can cause encephalitis and sepsis.
Neonatal lupus: Lupus features in a baby caused by maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies, most seriously congenital heart block.
Nephritic syndrome: Glomerular inflammation causing haematuria, red cell casts, hypertension and reduced renal function.
Nephrostomy: Tube placed through the skin into the kidney to drain urine.
Nephrotic syndrome: Heavy proteinuria, low albumin and oedema, with raised lipids.
Nephrotoxic: Harmful to the kidneys, as with NSAIDs, gentamicin and contrast agents.
Neprilysin: An enzyme that breaks down natriuretic peptides; blocking it boosts their beneficial effects.
Nerve conduction studies: Electrical tests of how fast and well nerves carry signals; used when the diagnosis is uncertain.
Neural tube defects: Birth defects of brain or spine such as spina bifida.
Neuro-observations: Regular checks of GCS, pupils, limb power and vital signs to detect neurological deterioration.
Neurocognitive: Relating to thinking, memory and concentration.
Neurofibrillary tangles: Clumps of hyperphosphorylated tau inside neurons in Alzheimer's.
Neurogenic inflammation: Inflammation caused by neuropeptides released from sensory nerve endings.
Neuropathic pain: Burning or shooting pain caused by damage to nerves themselves.
Neuropathic ulcer: A painless ulcer at a pressure point, such as under a metatarsal head, on a warm foot with pulses.
Neurovascular compression: A blood vessel pressing on a nerve, the commonest cause of trigeminal neuralgia.
Neutropenia: A low neutrophil count, which raises the risk of bacterial and fungal infection.
Neutropenic sepsis: Fever or sepsis with neutrophils at or below 0.5; needs IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
Neutrophil elastase: A protease from neutrophils that destroys alveolar elastin.
Neutrophilia: Raised neutrophil count, common in alcoholic hepatitis even without infection.
Neutrophilic inflammation: Smoking-driven airway inflammation typical of COPD, relatively steroid-resistant.
Next of kin: The patient's closest relative; has no legal power to consent for an adult.
Nicorandil: Potassium channel opener for angina; side effects include headache, flushing and anal ulceration.
Nicotinic: The acetylcholine receptor type at the neuromuscular junction.
Nidus: A place where bacteria can settle and multiply.
Nigrostriatal pathway: Dopamine pathway from the substantia nigra to the striatum.
Nintedanib: Oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor that slows IPF progression.
Nipple fissure: A crack or split in the nipple skin.
Nipple retraction: Nipple pulled inwards, often by tumour tethering the ducts.
Nissen fundoplication: Operation wrapping the gastric fundus 360 degrees around the lower oesophagus to stop reflux.
Nitrate tolerance: Loss of nitrate effect with continuous exposure; prevented by a nitrate-free interval.
Nitrites: Made when Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate; positive dipstick suggests infection.
Nitrofurantoin: Antibiotic for urinary infection; long-term use can cause pulmonary fibrosis.
Nocturia: Waking at night to pass urine.
Nodular glomerulosclerosis: Scarring of glomeruli into rounded nodules; same as Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.
Nodular sclerosis: Commonest Hodgkin subtype; young adults, often with mediastinal disease.
Nomogram: Graph of paracetamol level against time since ingestion with a treatment line; levels on or above it need NAC.
Non-HDL cholesterol: Total cholesterol minus HDL; the value NICE uses to judge statin response.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Lymphomas without Reed-Sternberg cells; older adults, random and extranodal spread.
Non-IgE-mediated: An allergy driven by T cells rather than IgE, with delayed symptoms and negative IgE tests.
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lungs from leaky capillaries rather than a failing heart.
Non-caseating: Without central cheese-like necrosis; typical of sarcoid granulomas.
Non-compressible: An artery the BP cuff cannot squeeze shut, giving a falsely high reading.
Non-epileptic attack disorder: Seizure-like attacks from psychological distress, with closed eyes and pelvic thrusting.
Non-erosive arthritis: Joint inflammation that does not destroy bone at the joint margins on X-ray, unlike rheumatoid arthritis.
Non-muscle-invasive: Bladder cancer confined to the mucosa or submucosa (Ta, T1, CIS).
Non-rebreathe mask: Oxygen mask with a reservoir bag delivering high-concentration oxygen at 15 L/min.
Non-rebreather mask: Mask with a reservoir bag giving high-concentration oxygen at 15 L/min.
Non-selective beta-blocker: Propranolol or carvedilol, which lower portal pressure to prevent variceal bleeding.
Non-visible haematuria: Blood found only on dipstick or microscopy.
Noonan syndrome: Genetic syndrome with short stature, webbed neck and pulmonary valve stenosis.
Noradrenaline: First-line vasopressor in septic shock; given by infusion in ICU.
Normal flora: Microbes that live harmlessly on the body and keep pathogens in check.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus: Enlarged ventricles causing incontinence, gait disturbance and dementia: wet, wobbly and wacky.
Normocytic: Red cells of normal size (MCV 80 to 100 fL).
Normocytic anaemia: Low haemoglobin with normal-sized red cells.
Notifiable disease: An infection doctors must legally report to public health, such as TB, measles or meningitis.
NovoRapid: Rapid-acting mealtime insulin (aspart), stopped while the IV insulin infusion runs.
Nucleation: The first step of crystal formation.
Nucleus basalis of Meynert: A group of cholinergic neurons whose loss underlies memory deficits in Alzheimer's.
Nystagmus: Involuntary rhythmic eye movements, with a slow drift and a fast corrective beat.
Nystatin: Polyene antifungal suspension used for oral thrush; not absorbed from the gut.
OAB: Overactive bladder: urgency, frequency and nocturia from detrusor overactivity.
OCP: Oral contraceptive pill, a risk factor for vaginal thrush.
OCT: Optical coherence tomography: a cross-sectional scan of the retina that measures macular thickness.
OGD: Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy: camera test of the upper gut used to take duodenal biopsies.
OGTT: Oral glucose tolerance test: glucose measured 2 hours after a 75 g glucose drink.
ONTT: Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial: showed steroids speed recovery but do not change final vision.
OPSI: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection: fulminant sepsis, usually pneumococcal, in an asplenic patient.
ORBIT: Score estimating bleeding risk on anticoagulation.
ORS: Oral rehydration solution: water with set amounts of salt and glucose to aid absorption.
OSA: Obstructive sleep apnoea: repeated airway collapse in sleep, a cause of secondary hypertension.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome: Obesity with daytime hypercapnia from under-breathing; often coexists with OSA.
Obstructive pattern: Spirometry with FEV1/FVC below 0.7, from narrowed or collapsing airways.
Obstructive uropathy: Kidney damage from blocked urine flow.
Occupational asthma: Adult-onset asthma caused by a workplace agent; better away from work.
Ocrelizumab: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B cells; a disease-modifying therapy for MS.
Oculomotor nerve palsy: Third nerve palsy: a 'down and out' eye, ptosis and a dilated pupil, a warning sign of herniation.
Oedema: Swelling from excess fluid in the tissues.
Oesophageal candidiasis: Candida infection of the oesophagus causing painful swallowing; AIDS-defining.
Oesophageal intubation: A tracheal tube wrongly placed in the oesophagus, so the stomach, not the lungs, is ventilated.
Oesophageal stricture: Narrowing of the oesophagus; a contraindication to oral bisphosphonates.
Oestrogen: Main female sex hormone; stimulates breast glandular tissue.
Olfactory hallucination: Smelling something that is not there, a sign of temporal lobe involvement.
Oligoarthritis: Arthritis affecting two to four joints.
Oligoclonal bands: Distinct IgG bands in CSF but not serum, showing antibody made inside the CNS.
Oligodendrocytes: Cells that make myelin in the central nervous system.
Oliguria: Low urine output, defined in AKI as less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
Oliguric: Passing less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour of urine.
Omalizumab: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used for refractory chronic urticaria.
Omental patch: Surgical repair of a perforated ulcer by plugging the hole with a piece of omentum.
Omentum: A fatty apron of peritoneum that can wall off local inflammation.
On-off phenomenon: Swings between good mobility (on) and immobility (off) on long-term levodopa.
Oncotic pressure: Pulling pressure of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, that keeps fluid inside vessels.
One-stop clinic: Breast clinic where examination, imaging and biopsy happen in one visit.
Onion-skin: Layered periosteal new bone on X-ray, typical of Ewing's sarcoma.
Onycholysis: Painless separation of the nail from its nail bed.
Open aortic repair: Replacing the aneurysmal aorta with a synthetic graft through a laparotomy.
Open fracture: A fracture where the bone communicates with the outside through a wound.
Opening pressure: CSF pressure measured at the start of an LP; raised in bacterial meningitis.
Opening snap: A sharp early-diastolic sound as stiff mitral leaflets snap open in mitral stenosis.
Ophthalmia neonatorum: Conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life.
Opioid: A drug acting on opioid receptors, such as codeine or morphine; not recommended for tension-type headache.
Opioids: Strong painkillers such as morphine and codeine; cause constipation and confusion.
Opsonic activity: The ability of fluid proteins such as complement to coat bacteria for killing by phagocytes.
Opsonisation: Coating of bacteria with antibody or complement so phagocytes can engulf them.
Optic atrophy: A pale optic disc from lost optic nerve fibres after damage.
Optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve: painful eye movement, reduced acuity and colour vision.
Oral candida: Thrush: white plaques in the mouth that scrape off.
Oral candidiasis: Oral thrush, a side effect of inhaled steroids; prevented by rinsing the mouth.
Oral hairy leucoplakia: White corrugated patches on the side of the tongue from EBV, a sign of immunosuppression.
Oral hairy leukoplakia: EBV-related white ridges on the side of the tongue in HIV; does not scrape off.
Orbit: The bony socket that holds the eye, its muscles and fat.
Orbital apex: The back of the orbit where muscles converge around the optic nerve.
Orbital cellulitis: Infection of the tissues behind the orbital septum, causing painful, reduced eye movements; an emergency.
Orbital decompression: Surgery removing orbital bone or fat to relieve pressure on the eye and optic nerve.
Orbital fibroblasts: Connective tissue cells in the orbit that carry the TSH receptor and drive swelling in TED.
Organ/space SSI: Infection of the organ or anatomical space entered during the operation, such as an intra-abdominal abscess.
Organophosphates: Insecticides that inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing a cholinergic toxidrome.
Orlistat: Lipase inhibitor that reduces fat absorption; causes oily stools.
Oropharyngeal airway: A curved plastic (Guedel) tube placed in the mouth to stop the tongue blocking the airway.
Orphan Annie eye: Clear, empty-looking nuclei typical of papillary carcinoma.
Orthopnoea: Breathlessness when lying flat, relieved by sitting up; counted by the number of pillows needed.
Orthostatic hypotension: A fall in BP of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.
Ortner's syndrome: Hoarse voice from an enlarged left atrium compressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Osborn wave: Another name for the J wave seen on the ECG in hypothermia.
Osler's nodes: Painful raised nodules on finger or toe pulps caused by immune complex deposition.
Osler-Weber-Rendu disease: Another name for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
Osmolality: Concentration of dissolved particles in blood; very high in HHS, and rapid changes can cause cerebral oedema.
Osmotic diuresis: Excess urine output because glucose in the urine pulls water with it, causing dehydration.
Osmotic diuretic: A drug that stays in the blood and draws water out of tissues by osmosis, then is passed in urine.
Osteoarthritis: Degenerative joint disease with cartilage loss, bony overgrowth and low-grade inflammation.
Osteoblast: Bone cell that lays down new bone.
Osteoblastic: Causing new bone formation, as in prostate cancer metastases.
Osteoclast: Bone cell that dissolves and resorbs bone.
Osteoid: The unmineralised protein matrix of bone, laid down by osteoblasts.
Osteolytic: Causing bone destruction, as in breast cancer metastases.
Osteomalacia: Soft bones from poor mineralisation, causing bone pain, proximal myopathy and a waddling gait.
Osteomyelitis: Infection of bone and bone marrow.
Osteonecrosis of the jaw: Rare death of jaw bone linked to bisphosphonates and denosumab, often after dental work.
Osteopenia: Bone density below normal but not osteoporotic: T score between -1 and -2.5.
Osteophytes: Bony spurs at the edges of a joint, formed as the bone tries to repair itself.
Osteoporosis: Low bone mass and weak bone structure raising fracture risk.
Ostia: Plural of ostium: the drainage openings of the sinuses.
Ostium: The small opening through which a sinus drains into the nose.
Otoconia: Tiny calcium carbonate crystals in the utricle that sense gravity and linear movement.
Ovarian teratoma: A germ cell tumour of the ovary that can contain neural tissue.
Overactive bladder: Urgency with frequency and nocturia, with or without urge incontinence.
Overdose: Taking more of a drug or substance than the body can safely handle, causing toxic effects.
Overflow incontinence: Dribbling leakage from a chronically over-full bladder due to retention.
Oxcarbazepine: A carbamazepine relative; a second-line option that can also lower sodium.
Oxidative stress: Cell damage from reactive oxygen species, which free iron helps generate.
Oxybutynin: Antimuscarinic for urge incontinence; can cause confusion, dry mouth and constipation in older people.
Oxymetazoline: An alpha-agonist decongestant nasal spray; long-term use causes rebound congestion.
P mitrale: Broad, notched P waves from left atrial enlargement, as in mitral stenosis.
P pulmonale: Tall peaked P waves (above 2.5 mm) in inferior leads from right atrial enlargement.
P. falciparum: The most common and most dangerous malaria species; causes cerebral malaria.
P. malariae: Less common malaria species causing milder disease.
P. ovale: Malaria species that, like vivax, forms hypnozoites and can relapse.
P. vivax: Malaria species that forms liver hypnozoites and can relapse.
P2: The pulmonary component of the second heart sound; loud in pulmonary hypertension.
P2Y12: A platelet ADP receptor; blocking it with clopidogrel, prasugrel or ticagrelor stops platelets clumping.
P450 inducers: Drugs such as rifampicin, phenytoin and carbamazepine that increase liver enzyme activity and NAPQI production.
PACI: Partial anterior circulation infarct: two of the three TACI features.
PAD: Peripheral arterial disease, another name for PVD.
PAH: Pulmonary arterial hypertension: disease of the small lung arteries themselves, such as idiopathic PAH.
PAN: Polyarteritis nodosa, a medium-vessel vasculitis linked with hepatitis B.
PANCREAS: Mnemonic: PaO2, Age, Neutrophils, Calcium, Raised urea, Enzymes, Albumin, Sugar.
PASI: Psoriasis Area and Severity Index; above 10 means moderate-to-severe disease.
PBC: Primary biliary cholangitis: autoimmune destruction of small bile ducts; AMA positive.
PBMV: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty: a catheter balloon splits the fused commissures.
PBP2a: Altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams, so the cell wall keeps being built.
PCA: Patient-controlled analgesia: a pump that lets the patient give themselves opioid doses.
PCC: Prothrombin complex concentrate: ready-made clotting factors for rapid warfarin reversal.
PCI: Percutaneous coronary intervention: a catheter through the wrist or groin opens the blocked artery with a balloon and stent.
PCNL: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy: keyhole removal of a large stone through the back into the kidney.
PCP: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: dry cough and exertional desaturation when CD4 is below 200.
PCR: Polymerase chain reaction: detects viral genetic material; gold standard for Covid-19.
PCSK9: Liver protein that destroys LDL receptors; gain-of-function mutations cause rare FH.
PCSK9 inhibitor: Injectable antibody that stops LDL receptor breakdown; reserved for escalation.
PComm: Posterior communicating artery; an aneurysm here compresses the third nerve.
PDE-5 inhibitor: Drug such as sildenafil that boosts nitric oxide signalling to relax pulmonary arteries.
PDGF: Platelet-derived growth factor, which stimulates fibroblasts in myelofibrosis.
PDR: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy: new vessels growing on the retina or disc.
PE: Pulmonary embolism: a clot blocking a lung artery.
PEA: Pulseless electrical activity: organised rhythm on the monitor but no pulse.
PEF: Peak expiratory flow: the fastest rate a person can blow out, in L/min.
PEFR: Peak expiratory flow rate; the same as PEF.
PEG: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy: a tube through the abdominal wall into the stomach for long-term feeding.
PEGylated interferon: A long-acting injected interferon, the historic treatment for hepatitis B and C.
PEP: Post-exposure prophylaxis: 28 days of antiretrovirals after a significant exposure.
PERC: Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria; if all eight are met, PE can be excluded without testing.
PESI: Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index; classes 1 to 2 can be treated as outpatients.
PET: Positron emission tomography; shows metabolically active tumour for staging.
PET-CT: Scan combining metabolic activity with anatomy; used to stage lymphoma and assess response.
PFO: Patent foramen ovale: a small persistent opening between the atria.
PHQ-9: Nine-item questionnaire scoring depressive symptoms over 2 weeks from 0 to 27 to grade severity.
PI-RADS: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System: scores MRI lesions 1 to 5; 3 or above means biopsy.
PICA: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery: its occlusion causes lateral medullary syndrome.
PIP: Proximal interphalangeal joint, the middle finger joint.
PITS: Mnemonic: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior quadrantanopias.
PKD1: The gene, on chromosome 16, mutated in most cases of ADPKD.
PML: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: JC virus brain demyelination in severe immunosuppression.
PML-RARA: Fusion gene from t(15;17) that blocks promyelocyte maturation in APML.
PMP22: Peripheral myelin protein 22; its duplication causes CMT1A.
PMR: Polymyalgia rheumatica: inflammatory pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles in people over 50.
PND: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea: waking from sleep suddenly breathless, needing to sit up.
POCI: Posterior circulation infarct: brainstem, cerebellar or occipital stroke.
POMC: Pro-opiomelanocortin: the precursor protein cut into ACTH and MSH.
PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, given with high-dose steroids to protect the stomach.
PPIs: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole; they raise C. difficile risk.
PPV: Positive predictive value: chance of disease if the test is positive, TP/(TP+FP).
PR: Per rectum; a digital rectal examination.
PR depression: Downward shift of the PR segment on ECG, a typical sign of pericarditis.
PR interval: Time from start of P wave to start of QRS.
PSA: Prostate specific antigen: a protein from prostate cells; normal below 4 µg/L.
PSC: Primary sclerosing cholangitis: stricturing of bile ducts, linked to ulcerative colitis.
PSP: Progressive supranuclear palsy: parkinsonism with vertical gaze palsy and early falls.
PT: Prothrombin time: clotting test used, with bilirubin, in Maddrey's discriminant function.
PTBD: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage: a drain through the liver into the ducts when ERCP is not possible.
PTH: Parathyroid hormone: raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and gut.
PTHrP: Parathyroid hormone-related protein: made by some tumours, acts on the PTH receptor to raise calcium.
PUD: Peptic ulcer disease: ulcers of the stomach or duodenum.
PUVA: Psoralen plus UVA photochemotherapy for severe psoriasis; raises squamous cell carcinoma risk.
PVD: Peripheral vascular disease: narrowing of the limb arteries by atherosclerosis.
PVR: Post-void residual volume: urine left after voiding; a high value means retention.
PYY: Peptide YY: gut hormone that reduces appetite; rises after bariatric surgery.
PaCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood; normal 4.7–6.0 kPa.
PaO2: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood; normal 11–13 kPa on air.
Pabrinex: Brand of intravenous high-dose B vitamins including thiamine, used in alcohol-dependent patients.
Pack-years: Packs of 20 cigarettes smoked per day multiplied by years smoked.
Paget's disease: Disordered bone remodelling with very high ALP but normal calcium and phosphate.
Palatine tonsils: The two lymphoid lumps either side of the back of the throat.
Palliative care: Care focused on comfort and quality of life rather than cure.
Pallor: Abnormal paleness of the skin from lack of blood flow.
Palmar creases: The lines on the palms; they darken in Addison's disease.
Palmar erythema: Reddening of the palms, a sign of chronic liver disease.
Pancoast tumour: Lung cancer at the apex that invades the sympathetic chain, brachial plexus or recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas with severe upper abdominal pain; a GLP-1 mimetic side effect.
Pancytopenia: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together.
Pannus: Thickened, invasive inflamed synovium that erodes cartilage and bone in RA.
Pansystolic murmur: A murmur lasting the whole of systole, as in mitral or tricuspid regurgitation.
Papillary muscle: Muscle in the ventricle that anchors the mitral leaflets via chordae.
Papillary muscle rupture: Tear of a papillary muscle after MI, causing sudden severe mitral regurgitation.
Papilloedema: Swelling of the optic disc caused by raised intracranial pressure.
Pappenheimer bodies: Iron-containing granules in red cells, seen in sideroblastic anaemia.
Paracentesis: Putting a needle or drain into the peritoneal cavity to sample or remove ascitic fluid.
Paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunc: Circulatory collapse and renal impairment after large-volume drainage without albumin cover.
Paracetamol: A simple analgesic; first line for tension-type headache.
Paradoxical embolus: A venous clot that crosses to the arterial side through a hole in the heart, such as a PFO.
Paraesthesia: Pins and needles or numbness, here from ischaemic nerves.
Parakeratosis: Retained nuclei in the outer skin layer from incomplete maturation; gives psoriatic scale.
Paralysis: Loss of movement; in limb ischaemia it means muscle is dying.
Paranasal sinuses: Air-filled spaces in the facial bones (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid) that drain into the nose.
Paraneoplastic: Caused by the immune response to a tumour rather than by the tumour itself.
Paraparesis: Weakness of both legs, here from spinal cord ischaemia.
Paraplegia: Paralysis of both legs, usually from a spinal cord lesion.
Parapneumonic effusion: A collection of fluid in the pleural space next to a pneumonia.
Paraprotein: An abnormal antibody made by a single clone of plasma cells, seen in myeloma.
Parasternal heave: Lifting felt at the left sternal edge from an enlarged right ventricle.
Parasympathetic: The rest-and-digest part of the autonomic nervous system, carried largely by the vagus nerve.
Parenchyma: The functional tissue of an organ; in the brain, the neurons and glia rather than the coverings.
Parietal cells: Stomach lining cells that make acid and intrinsic factor.
Parietal peritoneum: The peritoneal layer lining the abdominal wall; it has somatic nerves, so pain is sharp and well localised.
Parkinson's disease: Degenerative dopamine-deficient disorder causing tremor, rigidity and slow movement.
Parkinsonism: Slowness, rigidity and tremor, as seen in Parkinson's disease.
Parotid: The large salivary gland in front of the ear.
Parous: Having given birth at least once.
Partial reversibility: FEV1 improves significantly after a bronchodilator, but obstruction remains.
Parvovirus B19: Virus causing 'slapped cheek' rash that can temporarily stop red cell production.
Pasteurella multocida: Bacterium from cat and dog mouths that infects bite wounds; covered by co-amoxiclav.
Patch test: Allergens taped on the back for 48 hours to detect delayed contact allergy.
Pathological fracture: A fracture through bone weakened by disease, caused by trauma that would not break normal bone.
Paxlovid: Oral nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir for early Covid-19 in high-risk patients.
Peak flow: Peak expiratory flow: the fastest rate of breathing out, in L/min.
Peak gradient: The maximum pressure difference across the valve on echo; above 40 mmHg is severe AS.
Pear drops: Sweet, fruity breath smell caused by exhaled acetone in ketoacidosis.
Peau d'orange: Orange-peel pitting of breast skin from blocked dermal lymphatics.
Pelger-Huët: Neutrophils with hyposegmented or bilobed nuclei; a classic film finding in MDS.
Pelvic floor: Sheet of muscles supporting the bladder, uterus and bowel and helping close the urethra.
Pelvic floor muscle training: Supervised exercises for at least 3 months; first-line for stress incontinence.
Pelvic lymph node dissection: Removal of pelvic nodes during cystectomy for staging and control.
Pemberton's test: Raising both arms over the head; facial plethora or stridor suggests thoracic inlet obstruction.
Penicillamine: Copper chelator used in Wilson's disease, not haemochromatosis.
Penicillin V: Phenoxymethylpenicillin: the oral daily prophylaxis after splenectomy.
Penicillin allergy: True immune reaction to penicillin: rash, angioedema or anaphylaxis, not diarrhoea or nausea.
Penicillin-binding protein: Bacterial enzyme that builds the cell wall; the target of beta-lactam antibiotics.
Peptic ulcer: A break in the stomach or duodenal lining, often from NSAIDs or H. pylori.
Percutaneous colostomy tube: A tube placed through the abdominal wall into the colon to decompress and anchor it.
Percutaneous transhepatic biliary draina: Draining the bile ducts through the skin and liver under imaging guidance.
Perforation: A hole through the full thickness of the wall of a hollow organ.
Performance status: A score of how well a patient functions day to day, used to decide if they can tolerate treatment.
Perfusion scan: Nuclear scan showing areas of reduced blood flow to the myocardium under stress.
Perianal abscess: An acute collection of pus in the tissues around the anus.
Periarticular: Around a joint rather than inside it.
Periarticular osteopenia: Reduced bone density around a joint; the earliest X-ray sign of RA.
Pericardial effusion: Fluid collecting in the pericardial sac.
Pericardial friction rub: Scratching sound heard when inflamed pericardial layers rub together.
Pericardial knock: An early diastolic sound in constrictive pericarditis as filling stops abruptly.
Pericardiectomy: Surgical removal of the pericardium for constrictive pericarditis.
Pericardiocentesis: Draining pericardial fluid with a needle, ideally sub-xiphoid under ultrasound.
Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium causing pleuritic chest pain and saddle ST elevation.
Pericardium: The fibrous two-layered sac around the heart.
Pericranial: Around the skull: the scalp, temple, neck and shoulder muscles.
Perihilar: Around the hila, where the main bronchi and vessels enter each lung.
Perimenopause: The years around the menopause when hormone levels swing most.
Periorbital cellulitis: Infection of the eyelid skin in front of the orbital septum, with normal eye movements.
Periosteal elevation: Lifting of the periosteum by pus or oedema, seen early on MRI.
Periosteal reaction: New bone laid down by lifted periosteum, seen on X-ray as a later sign.
Periosteum: The tough membrane covering the outer surface of bone.
Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, causing numbness, pain or weakness.
Peripheral vertigo: Vertigo from the inner ear or vestibular nerve rather than the brain.
Peristalsis: Waves of muscle contraction that push urine down the ureter.
Peritoneal carcinomatosis: Cancer spread across the peritoneum, causing low-SAAG malignant ascites.
Peritoneal cavity: The space between the two layers of peritoneum lining the abdomen and covering the gut.
Peritoneal dialysis: Dialysis using the lining of the abdomen as the filter, with fluid exchanged through a catheter.
Peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound tenderness and rigidity.
Peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the organs.
Peritonsillar abscess: Pus between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles, causing trismus and a hot potato voice.
Periureteric fat stranding: Hazy fat around the ureter on CT, showing recent stone passage or inflammation.
Perivalvular abscess: An abscess in the tissue around an infected valve.
Periventricular: Next to the brain's ventricles; the classic site of MS plaques.
Permissive hypotension: Accepting a lower blood pressure in bleeding patients to avoid worsening the haemorrhage.
Pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune B12 deficiency from antibodies against intrinsic factor or gastric parietal cells.
Pessary: A medicated tablet inserted into the vagina.
Petechiae: Pinpoint red spots from capillary bleeding, typical of low platelets.
Petechial: Tiny pinpoint bleeding spots in the skin that do not blanch.
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Autosomal dominant hamartomatous GI polyps with dark freckles on lips, palms and soles.
Peyer's patches: Clusters of lymphoid tissue in the distal ileum, targeted by typhoid.
Phaeochromocytoma: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla causing episodic headache, sweating and palpitations.
Phagocytosis: Engulfing and destroying microbes by white cells such as macrophages.
Phalen's: Holding the wrists flexed for a minute reproduces carpal tunnel symptoms.
Pharyngeal dilator muscles: Throat muscles, such as genioglossus, that hold the pharynx open; their tone falls during sleep.
Pharyngitis: Sore throat from inflammation of the pharynx.
Pharynx: The throat behind the nose and mouth, the part of the airway that collapses in OSA.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin: Penicillin V, oral daily antibiotic prophylaxis against pneumococcus.
Phenylephrine: Alpha-agonist eye drop that constricts superficial vessels; blanches episcleritis but not scleritis.
Phenytoin: A sodium channel blocking AED given IV as second line in status epilepticus.
Philadelphia chromosome: Shortened chromosome 22 from t(9;22), carrying the BCR-ABL fusion gene.
Phlebotomy: Drawing blood from a vein; therapeutic phlebotomy is venesection.
Phosphate binder: A drug taken with meals to bind dietary phosphate in the gut.
Photophobia: Pain or discomfort on exposure to light.
Photosensitive: Made worse by sunlight or ultraviolet light exposure.
Phototherapy: Treatment of skin disease with ultraviolet light.
Phyllodes tumour: A rare, fast-growing fibroepithelial tumour that can be benign or malignant.
Pill-rolling: Resting tremor where thumb and fingers rub as if rolling a pill.
Pilonidal abscess: An abscess in the natal cleft from infected hair follicles, not related to the anus.
Pimecrolimus: A topical calcineurin inhibitor, like tacrolimus, used in eczema.
Pinnae: The visible outer parts of the ears.
Pinpoint pupils: Very small, constricted pupils, typical of opioid or cholinergic toxicity.
Piperacillin with tazobactam: A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic used first-line in neutropenic sepsis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam: Broad-spectrum anti-Pseudomonal penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, for severe HAP.
Pirfenidone: Oral antifibrotic drug that slows IPF progression.
Pitting: The spleen's removal of inclusions such as nuclear remnants from red cells.
Pitting oedema: Swelling that keeps a dent after pressing, from fluid in the tissues.
Pivmecillinam: Penicillin-type antibiotic used second-line for lower UTI.
Plantar fasciitis: Inflammation of the plantar fascia insertion at the heel, causing heel pain.
Plaque: A focal area of demyelination seen on MRI as a bright T2 lesion.
Plaque psoriasis: The commonest type: well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on extensors.
Plaque rupture: Breakdown of a plaque's cap, exposing material that triggers clotting.
Plasma exchange: Removing the patient's plasma and replacing it with donor plasma; treatment for TTP.
Plasmapheresis: Removing plasma from the blood to clear harmful antibodies.
Plasmodium: The protozoan parasite that causes malaria.
Pleura: The thin membranes lining the lungs and inner chest wall.
Pleural aspirate: Fluid drawn from the pleural space with a needle so it can be tested for pH, glucose and organisms.
Pleural effusion: Fluid collecting between the two layers of the pleura.
Pleural plaques: Benign, often calcified patches of pleural thickening that mark past asbestos exposure.
Pleural rub: Creaking sound on auscultation as inflamed pleural layers rub together.
Pleural thickening: Fibrous thickening of the pleura; diffuse or nodular thickening may suggest mesothelioma.
Pleuritic: Sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in or coughing, from inflamed pleura.
Pleuritis: Inflammation of the pleura, causing sharp chest pain on breathing in and sometimes an effusion or rub.
Pleurodesis: Sealing the pleural space (e.g. with talc) to stop an effusion recurring.
Plummer's disease: Another name for toxic multinodular goitre.
Plummer-Vinson syndrome: Iron deficiency anaemia with a post-cricoid web causing dysphagia.
Pneumococcal vaccine: Vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae, given 2 weeks before elective splenectomy and boosted every 5 years.
Pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from inhaled mineral dust (coal, silica, asbestos).
Pneumocystis jirovecii: Fungus causing pneumonia in people with CD4 below 200.
Pneumoperitoneum: Free gas in the peritoneal cavity, usually from a perforated hollow organ.
Podiatry: Specialist foot care, including nail and callus care and footwear advice.
Podocyte: Specialised cell wrapping glomerular capillaries whose foot processes stop protein leaking.
Point-of-care test: Rapid finger-prick antibody test giving a result in minutes; 90-day window period.
Polarised light microscopy: Microscopy with polarised light, used on joint fluid to identify crystals by shape and birefringence.
Polyarthralgia: Pain in many joints without obvious swelling.
Polyarthritis: Arthritis affecting five or more joints.
Polychromasia: Bluish-tinged young red cells on a film, reflecting high reticulocyte output.
Polycythaemia: Raised haemoglobin and red cell mass, here from chronic hypoxia.
Polymicrobial: Caused by more than one species of organism together.
Polymorphonuclear: Neutrophils; the white cells that dominate CSF in bacterial meningitis.
Polymyalgia rheumatica: Inflammatory condition of older adults causing proximal pain and morning stiffness with a raised ESR.
Polymyositis: Inflammatory myopathy with proximal weakness and a markedly raised CK.
Polyol pathway: Route by which excess glucose is turned into sorbitol and fructose, stressing nerve cells.
Polysomnography: Overnight sleep study recording airflow, chest effort, oxygen saturation, EEG and heart rate; the gold standard for OSA.
Pons: Part of the brainstem where the trigeminal nerve enters.
Poorly demarcated: With a blurred edge that merges into normal skin.
Popliteal fossa: The hollow at the back of the knee.
Portal hypertension: Raised pressure in the portal vein, usually from a scarred cirrhotic liver resisting blood flow.
Portal of entry: The route by which organisms get into the body.
Portosystemic collaterals: Veins linking portal and systemic circulations that open up in portal hypertension.
Positive energy balance: Energy intake persistently exceeding energy expenditure, so fat stores grow.
Post-ROSC care: Oxygen, treating the cause and ICU support after circulation returns.
Post-coital prophylaxis: A single antibiotic dose after sex to prevent UTI.
Post-herpetic neuralgia: Persistent burning nerve pain after shingles.
Post-ictal: The period of confusion, drowsiness and headache after a seizure; absent after a faint.
Post-renal: AKI caused by obstruction to urine flow after the kidneys, such as BPH or stones.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Kidney inflammation 1-3 weeks after strep infection, causing haematuria, oedema and hypertension.
Post-void residual: Urine left in the bladder after voiding, measured by ultrasound.
Posterior acoustic enhancement: Bright area behind a fluid-filled lesion on ultrasound.
Posterior canal: The most dependent semicircular canal; affected in most BPPV.
Posteromedial papillary muscle: Mitral papillary muscle usually supplied only by the RCA, so it ruptures after inferior MI.
Postictal: The recovery period after a seizure, often with confusion and drowsiness.
Postpartum thyroiditis: Thyroid inflammation after childbirth, often with a thyrotoxic then hypothyroid phase.
Postural drainage: Positioning so gravity drains sputum from affected lung segments.
Postural hypotension: A fall in blood pressure on standing, causing dizziness.
Potassium chloride: Potassium salt added to IV fluids to replace potassium lost and driven into cells during treatment.
Potassium citrate: Urine alkaliniser used to prevent calcium stones.
Potassium iodide: Iodine given in thyroid storm to block release of thyroid hormone.
Pott's disease: Tuberculosis of the spine, causing back pain and vertebral collapse.
Prader-Willi syndrome: Genetic syndrome with neonatal hypotonia, then hyperphagia, obesity and learning difficulty.
Pre-auricular lymph node: Lymph node just in front of the ear; enlarged in viral conjunctivitis.
Pre-diabetes: Glucose above normal but below the diabetes cut-off (HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol).
Pre-renal: AKI caused by reduced blood flow to otherwise healthy kidneys.
Precipitant: A trigger that brings on a condition.
Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid used in severe alcoholic hepatitis when Maddrey's DF is 32 or more.
Pregabalin: An anticonvulsant related to gabapentin, used for neuropathic pain.
Prehn's sign: Pain relieved by lifting the testis; supports epididymitis rather than torsion.
Preload: The stretch on the ventricle at the end of filling, set by venous return.
Premenopausal: Still having periods, before the menopause.
Pretibial myxoedema: Raised, waxy plaques on the shins in Graves' disease.
Priapism: Prolonged painful erection; can occur from leukostasis in leukaemia.
Primaquine: Antimalarial drug that can trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Primary: The original tumour from which secondary deposits spread.
Primary CNS lymphoma: EBV-driven brain lymphoma in advanced HIV, usually a single lesion.
Primary PCI: Emergency PCI as the first reperfusion treatment for STEMI, within 120 minutes.
Primary adrenal insufficiency: Adrenal failure from disease of the adrenal gland itself; ACTH is high.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia: Inherited defect of cilia causing poor mucus clearance, sinusitis, subfertility and sometimes dextrocardia.
Primary headache: A headache disorder that is not caused by another condition, such as migraine or cluster headache.
Primary hyperaldosteronism: The adrenal glands make too much aldosterone on their own, causing hypertension and low potassium.
Primary infection: The first-ever infection with HSV, with no existing antibodies; usually the most severe.
Primary open-angle glaucoma: Chronic raised eye pressure damaging the optic nerve; listed in the notes as a contraindication to amitriptyline.
Primary prevention: Treatment to prevent a first cardiovascular event in someone without CVD.
Primary progressive: MS that worsens steadily from onset with no discrete relapses.
Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum infection causing a single painless genital ulcer (chancre).
Probe to bone: Bedside test: a sterile probe touching bone through an ulcer strongly suggests osteomyelitis.
Prochlorperazine: A dopamine antagonist used short-term for nausea and vertigo; it does not treat BPPV.
Prodrome: Early warning symptoms, such as tingling or burning, before lesions appear.
Progesterone: Hormone of the luteal phase that also acts on breast tissue.
Progestogen-only: Contraception without oestrogen, such as the progestogen-only pill, implant or hormonal coil.
Prognostic benefit: A drug effect that improves survival rather than just symptoms.
Promethazine: Sedating antihistamine with strong anticholinergic effects.
Promyelocyte: Myeloid precursor between myeloblast and myelocyte; accumulates in APML.
Pronator drift: When an arm held out palm-up drifts down and turns inwards, a sign of subtle upper motor neurone weakness.
Prophylactic antibiotics: Antibiotics given before infection occurs, usually at induction of anaesthesia, to reduce SSI risk.
Prophylactic factor replacement: Regular scheduled factor infusions to prevent bleeds, mainly in severe haemophilia.
Prophylaxis: Treatment given to prevent disease in someone exposed.
Propranolol: Non-selective beta-blocker used to prevent variceal bleeding in cirrhosis.
Proprioception: The sense of where the joints are in space, without looking.
Proptosis: Forward bulging of the eye out of the orbit.
Propylthiouracil: Antithyroid drug inhibiting thyroperoxidase; first-line in the first trimester and in storm.
Prostacyclin analogue: Drug mimicking prostacyclin, a natural vasodilator, used in PAH (e.g. epoprostenol).
Prostaglandins: Lipid mediators released in anaphylaxis that add to vasodilation and bronchospasm.
Protease inhibitor: Drug such as atazanavir that stops viral proteins maturing.
Proteases: Enzymes, for example neutrophil elastase, that break down proteins in tissue.
Protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins; detects the paraprotein of myeloma, a PMR mimic.
Proteinuria: Protein in the urine; a marker of kidney damage and worse prognosis.
Proteus: Gram-negative urease-producing bacterium linked to UTIs and struvite stones.
Proteus mirabilis: Urease-producing Gram-negative bacterium that causes struvite stones.
Prothrombin time: Time for blood to clot via the extrinsic pathway; prolonged in liver synthetic failure.
Proximal: Nearer the trunk; for muscles, the shoulder and hip girdles.
Pseudo-obstruction: Massive colonic dilatation without a mechanical blockage, also seen in frail elderly patients.
Pseudodementia: Depression that looks like dementia; the MMSE is typically normal.
