Pseudogout: Acute arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, usually in the knee or wrist of older people.
Pseudohyphae: Chains of elongated yeast cells, typical of Candida on microscopy.
Pseudomembranous colitis: Severe C. difficile colitis with yellow plaques on the colon lining.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Gram-negative rod that chronically colonises damaged airways; marks more severe disease.
Psittacosis: Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia psittaci, caught from infected birds such as parrots.
Psoriasis: Chronic immune-mediated skin disease with thick, scaly plaques from fast keratinocyte turnover.
Psoriatic arthritis: Inflammatory, usually seronegative arthritis linked to psoriasis, classically affecting DIP joints.
Pterygoid muscles: Jaw muscles near the tonsil; their spasm causes trismus in quinsy.
Public Health England: The former name of the national public health agency, replaced by UKHSA in 2021.
Public interest: Disclosure to protect others from serious harm, which can outweigh confidentiality.
Puerperal: Occurring in the weeks after childbirth.
Pulmonary hypertension: Raised pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lung air spaces from high pulmonary venous pressure.
Pulmonary regurgitation: Backflow through the pulmonary valve, often because the dilated artery stretches the valve ring.
Pulmonary rehabilitation: A supervised exercise and education programme that improves breathlessness and exercise tolerance.
Pulmonary stenosis: Narrowed pulmonary valve obstructing right ventricular outflow; usually congenital.
Pulmonary vascular resistance: How hard it is for blood to flow through the lung vessels.
Pulmonary vasodilators: Drugs that relax lung artery smooth muscle to lower pulmonary pressure, used in PAH.
Pulsatile hepatomegaly: An enlarged liver that pulses with each heartbeat, typical of severe TR.
Pulsatile mass: A swelling that throbs with each heartbeat.
Pulse deficit: A pulse that is weaker, delayed or absent compared with the same pulse on the other side.
Pulse pressure: Systolic minus diastolic blood pressure: narrow in AS, wide in AR.
Pulseless VT: Ventricular tachycardia without a pulse; shockable.
Pulsus alternans: A regular pulse that alternates between strong and weak beats; a sign of severe LV impairment.
Pulsus paradoxus: An exaggerated fall in systolic BP on inspiration, seen in cardiac tamponade and severe asthma.
Pulsus parvus et tardus: A small-volume, slow-rising pulse typical of severe aortic stenosis.
Punched-out erosions: Sharply defined bone erosions near joints on X-ray, seen in recurrent gout.
Purpuric: Larger non-blanching purple patches from bleeding into the skin.
Purulent: Containing pus; green or yellow sputum.
Pyelonephritis: Infection of the kidney, causing fever, loin pain and rigors.
Pyrazinamide: An anti-tuberculosis drug that raises serum urate.
Pyridostigmine: Long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; first-line symptomatic treatment for myasthenia.
Pyridoxal-5-phosphate: Active vitamin B6; needed more for ALT than AST synthesis, so its deficiency lowers ALT.
Pyrimethamine: Antiparasitic used with sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis.
Q fever: Infection with Coxiella burnetii from farm animals.
QFracture: UK fracture risk calculator, an alternative to FRAX.
QRISK3: NICE-recommended score estimating 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke.
QRS: ECG complex showing ventricular depolarisation; widens in severe hyperkalaemia.
QRisk: Score estimating 10-year cardiovascular risk; above 10% means offer a statin.
QT: The ECG interval from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave; prolonged in hypothermia.
QT interval: ECG time from start of QRS to end of T wave; short in hypercalcaemia.
QTc: QT interval corrected for heart rate.
Quantiferon: Interferon-gamma release blood test for latent tuberculosis.
Queen Anne's sign: Another name for Hertoghe sign: loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows.
Quetiapine: Atypical antipsychotic used first line for hallucinations in Parkinson's.
Quincke's sign: Visible pulsation of the nail bed capillaries in aortic regurgitation.
Quinsy: Peritonsillar abscess: a collection of pus beside the tonsil.
R0: Complete resection with microscopically clear margins.
R3A: Active proliferative retinopathy on screening; needs urgent referral.
RA: Rheumatoid arthritis: chronic autoimmune symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints.
RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: hormones that retain salt and water when kidney perfusion falls.
RANKL: Signal molecule that drives osteoclast formation and activation.
RAPD: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the pupil dilates when light swings to the eye with the damaged optic nerve.
RBBB: Right bundle branch block: RSR' in V1–3 and slurred S in lateral leads.
RCA: Right coronary artery, supplying the inferior wall and usually the SA and AV nodes.
RDW: Red cell distribution width: a high value means red cells vary widely in size.
REM sleep behaviour disorder: Acting out dreams (shouting, kicking) because normal REM paralysis is lost.
REM sleep disorder: Acting out dreams (shouting, kicking) because normal REM sleep paralysis is lost.
RIF: Right iliac fossa: the lower right area of the abdomen.
RIPE: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol: the first-line TB regimen.
RNA virus: Virus whose genetic material is RNA, such as norovirus and rotavirus.
ROSC: Return of spontaneous circulation: a pulse returns.
ROSIER: Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room scale, separating stroke from mimics.
RSV: Respiratory syncytial virus; a common respiratory virus, worst in infants and the elderly.
RUQ: Right upper quadrant of the abdomen, where the liver and gallbladder lie.
RV: Right ventricle, which pumps blood into the pulmonary arteries.
RV afterload: The resistance the right ventricle pumps against, set mainly by pulmonary vascular resistance.
RV strain: ECG pattern of ST depression and T inversion in V1-V3 from right ventricular overload.
Radical cystectomy: Surgical removal of the whole bladder, with urinary diversion.
Radicular pain: Pain shooting along the territory of a nerve root.
Radio-femoral delay: The femoral pulse arriving after the radial; seen in type B dissection and coarctation.
Radio-radial delay: One radial pulse arriving later than the other; points to type A dissection.
Radioactive iodine: Radioiodine treatment that destroys thyroid tissue; can worsen eye disease.
Radiofrequency ablation: Catheter heat destroys the tissue causing an arrhythmia.
Radioiodine: Radioactive iodine treatment that destroys thyroid tissue; often leads to hypothyroidism.
Radiotherapy: Treatment with ionising radiation to kill cancer cells, used for painful bone metastases.
Ramipril: ACE inhibitor used first-line for diabetic nephropathy with ACR 3 mg/mmol or more.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: Facial nerve palsy from VZV reactivation, with severe ear pain and vesicles in or around the ear.
Ranolazine: Antianginal add-on drug used when other agents are insufficient.
Ranson's criteria: An older pancreatitis severity score using admission and 48-hour values.
Rapid Rhino: An inflatable anterior nasal pack for bleeds not stopped by simple pressure.
Rapid tranquillisation: Urgent use of medication to calm a dangerously agitated patient.
Rasburicase: Recombinant urate oxidase that breaks down uric acid; prevents and treats tumour lysis.
Rate-limiting CCB: Calcium channel blocker that slows the heart (verapamil, diltiazem).
Raynaud's phenomenon: Fingers turning white, blue then red in the cold from blood vessel spasm.
Re-entry: An impulse circling a loop of tissue and repeatedly re-exciting it.
Re-orientation: Helping a patient know where they are and what time it is, using clocks, calendars and family.
Re-sedation: Return of opioid toxicity once short-acting naloxone wears off.
Reactivation: Latent virus becoming active again and causing a recurrence.
Reactive arthritis: Sterile inflammatory arthritis starting 1 to 4 weeks after a GU or GI infection.
Reactive oxygen species: Unstable oxygen molecules that damage cell membranes, proteins and DNA.
Rebound: A worsening of symptoms caused by the treatment itself, here headache from frequent painkillers.
Rebound tenderness: Pain felt when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released, from parietal peritoneal irritation.
Reciprocal change: ST depression in leads facing the opposite wall to an ST elevation.
Recombinant factor VIII: Factor VIII made by genetic engineering, given IV to treat or prevent bleeds.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Branch of the vagus nerve that supplies the vocal cords.
Red flags: Features suggesting cancer: skin changes, hard irregular mass, lymphadenopathy.
Redcurrant jelly: Thick, dark red, blood-stained sputum typical of Klebsiella pneumonia.
Redeployment: Moving a worker to a different role away from the harmful exposure.
Redundant: Describes bowel that is longer than normal and forms extra floppy loops.
Reed-Sternberg cells: Large cells with bilobed nuclei and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli; diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.
Reflex syncope: Fainting caused by an inappropriate autonomic reflex; vasovagal is the commonest type.
Reflex tachycardia: A rise in heart rate when a vasodilator lowers BP; why beta-blockade comes first.
Refractory anaphylaxis: Breathing or circulation problems that persist despite two doses of IM adrenaline.
Refractory period: Time after depolarisation when a cell cannot fire again.
Regenerative nodules: Clumps of regrowing liver cells surrounded by scar tissue in cirrhosis.
Regional wall motion abnormality: A segment of heart muscle that moves poorly, showing ischaemia or scar.
Reiter's syndrome: Older name for reactive arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis.
Relapsing-remitting: MS course with attacks followed by partial or full recovery; the commonest form.
Relative afferent pupillary defect: Abnormal swinging light test showing reduced signal from one optic nerve.
Remodelling: Permanent structural airway change: thickened walls, fibrosis, muscle hypertrophy.
Renal angle: Same as the costovertebral angle; tender in pyelonephritis.
Renal artery stenosis: Narrowing of the artery to a kidney; creatinine jumps when an ACE inhibitor is started.
Renal biopsy: Taking a core of kidney tissue to examine the glomeruli; gold standard.
Renal colic: Severe loin-to-groin pain from a kidney stone; a classic misdiagnosis for ruptured AAA.
Renal replacement therapy: Dialysis or haemofiltration used to take over kidney function.
Renal screen: Blood tests for glomerular causes: ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, dsDNA, C3, C4, immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis.
Renal vein thrombosis: Clot in the renal vein causing flank pain and haematuria; classic in membranous nephropathy.
Renin: Kidney enzyme that drives the angiotensin-aldosterone system; high when aldosterone is low.
Renin:aldosterone ratio: Blood test screening for primary hyperaldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin.
Reperfusion: Restoring blood flow, which can release potassium and acid from damaged muscle.
Reperfusion injury: Tissue damage caused when blood returns to ischaemic tissue, releasing oxidative and inflammatory products.
Repetitive nerve stimulation: EMG test firing a nerve repeatedly; myasthenia shows a falling (decremental) response.
Rescue antibiotic: An antibiotic used only if symptoms do not improve after a set time.
Rescue pack: Prednisolone and antibiotics kept at home to start at the onset of an exacerbation.
Residual mass: A lump still present after a cyst has been drained; needs biopsy.
Resistant hypertension: Blood pressure not controlled despite three drugs, including a diuretic.
Respiratory acidosis: Low pH caused by CO2 retention from inadequate ventilation.
Respiratory alkalosis: High blood pH from blowing off too much CO2 by overbreathing.
Respiratory arrest: Breathing has stopped or is ineffective while the heart may still be beating.
Respiratory failure: Failure of the lungs to keep blood oxygen up and/or carbon dioxide down, defined by PaO2 below 8 kPa.
Rest pain: Ischaemic pain in the foot at rest, often at night, when flow is inadequate even without exercise.
Restrictive myopathy: Stiff, swollen muscle that cannot stretch, so the eye cannot move fully.
Restrictive pattern: Low FEV1 and FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio, as in fibrosis.
Resuscitation Council UK: UK body that publishes the anaphylaxis treatment algorithm.
Reticular activating system: Brainstem network that keeps us awake; CO2 retention depresses it, causing drowsiness.
Reticular shadowing: A net-like pattern of lines on X-ray from thickened interstitium.
Reticulocyte: A young red cell; a low count means the marrow is not responding.
Reticulocytes: Young red cells released from the marrow; raised when the marrow is compensating.
Reticulocytosis: Raised reticulocyte count, showing the marrow is making red cells faster.
Retinal detachment: Separation of the retina from the underlying layer; an emergency.
Retinopathy: Diabetic damage to retinal vessels; its presence supports diabetic nephropathy as the cause of proteinuria.
Retrobulbar neuritis: Optic neuritis behind the eye, so the disc looks normal at first.
Retroperitoneal: Behind the peritoneum; most AAA ruptures bleed here at first.
Retrovirus: RNA virus that copies itself into DNA and inserts it into the host genome.
Revascularisation: Restoring blood flow to an ischaemic limb.
Reverse cholesterol transport: HDL carrying cholesterol from tissues back to the liver for removal.
Reverse tick: Downsloping ST depression typical of digoxin effect.
Reverse transcriptase: Viral enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.
Reversibility: Improvement in FEV1 after a bronchodilator; 12% or more supports asthma.
Revision: A repeat operation to replace or fix a failed joint replacement.
Reye's syndrome: Rare, serious liver and brain injury in children linked to aspirin.
Reynold's pentad: Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion: severe cholangitis with sepsis.
Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin and CK, which can cause AKI; seen after long lies or crush injury.
Rheumatic fever: Autoimmune illness after group A streptococcal throat infection that can scar heart valves.
Rheumatic heart disease: Valve scarring years after rheumatic fever; a common cause of AR worldwide.
Rheumatoid arthritis: Autoimmune inflammatory arthritis of small joints; the commonest cause of scleritis.
Rheumatoid factor: Autoantibody against IgG Fc, positive in many with RA and negative in spondyloarthropathies.
Rhinitis medicamentosa: Rebound nasal congestion caused by overuse of decongestant sprays.
Rhinosinusitis: Inflammation of the nasal lining and the paranasal sinuses together.
Rhinovirus: The commonest cause of the common cold.
Rhonchi: Low-pitched, snoring sounds from secretions in larger airways.
Richter's hernia: Only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so it can strangulate without causing obstruction.
Richter's transformation: CLL turning into an aggressive high-grade lymphoma.
Rifampicin: Antibiotic added for prosthetic valves because it penetrates biofilm.
Rifaximin: Poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria in hepatic encephalopathy.
Right axis deviation: QRS axis beyond +90 degrees, often from right ventricular hypertrophy.
Right heart catheterisation: A catheter passed into the right heart and pulmonary artery to measure pressures directly; the gold standard.
Right heart failure: Failure of the right ventricle causing raised JVP, oedema, ascites and hepatomegaly.
Right hemicolectomy: Removal of the caecum, ascending colon and terminal ileum, joining ileum to colon.
Right-to-left shunt: Blood passing from the right heart to the left without going through the lungs.
Rigid sigmoidoscopy: Examination of the rectum and sigmoid with a straight rigid scope; used to untwist sigmoid volvulus.
Rigidity: Constant, involuntary board-like tension of the abdominal wall, typical of generalised peritonitis.
Rigler sign: Gas seen on both sides of the bowel wall on X-ray; a sign of perforation.
Rigler's sign: Gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall on abdominal X-ray, indicating perforation.
Rigors: Uncontrollable shaking with fever, suggesting bacteraemia.
Rimegepant: An oral CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) for acute treatment or prevention of migraine.
Ring sideroblasts: Red cell precursors with iron trapped in a ring around the nucleus; diagnostic of sideroblastic anaemia.
Ring-enhancing lesion: A lesion whose rim lights up with contrast on CT or MRI while the centre stays dark.
Ringed sideroblasts: Red cell precursors with iron-loaded mitochondria ringing the nucleus, seen on marrow iron stain in MDS.
Ringer's lactate: A balanced crystalloid fluid, very similar to Hartmann's solution.
Rinne: Tuning fork test comparing air and bone conduction.
Rinne's test: Tuning fork test comparing air and bone conduction in one ear; positive (air louder) is normal or sensorineural.
Risedronate: Oral bisphosphonate, an alternative first-line option.
Rituximab: Antibody drug that depletes B cells; used in warm AIHA.
Rivastigmine: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, available as a patch, used in Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia.
Romberg: A test where the patient sways or falls with eyes shut, showing loss of position sense.
Romberg test: Standing with eyes shut to test position sense and balance.
Romberg's: Unsteadiness with eyes closed, showing loss of position sense.
Rome criteria: Symptom-based diagnostic criteria for IBS centred on pain linked to defecation.
Root entry zone: The point where a cranial nerve enters the brainstem; vulnerable to compression and demyelination.
Ropinirole: Oral dopamine agonist for Parkinson's and restless legs.
Roth spots: Retinal haemorrhages with pale centres, seen on fundoscopy in endocarditis.
Rotigotine: Dopamine agonist given as a skin patch; used when patients are nil by mouth.
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: Bariatric operation creating a small stomach pouch joined directly to the small bowel.
Rovsing's sign: Pain in the right iliac fossa when the left iliac fossa is pressed.
Rupture: Bursting of the aneurysm wall, causing massive internal bleeding.
Ruptured AAA: Burst abdominal aortic aneurysm: abdominal or back pain, pulsatile mass and shock.
Rust-coloured sputum: Brownish blood-tinged sputum typical of Streptococcus pneumoniae lobar pneumonia.
Ryles tube: A wide-bore nasogastric tube used to decompress the stomach.
S. haematobium: Schistosoma haematobium, the fluke that infects the bladder and causes squamous cell carcinoma.
S. pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae, a Gram-positive diplococcus and the commonest adult cause.
S. pyogenes: Group A streptococcus: a common cause of cellulitis.
S1Q3T3: Deep S wave in lead I, Q wave and inverted T in lead III; a sign of RV strain.
S2: The second heart sound, from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.
S3: Third heart sound, heard in volume overload and heart failure.
S3 gallop: Third heart sound in early diastole, a sign of a failing, overfilled ventricle.
S4: An extra heart sound before S1 from the atrium pushing blood into a stiff ventricle.
SA node: The heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium.
SAAG: Serum-ascites albumin gradient: serum minus ascitic albumin; 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertension.
SABA: Short-acting beta-2 agonist, such as salbutamol; a reliever.
SAH: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: bleeding into the CSF-filled space between arachnoid and pia mater.
SALT: Speech and language therapy, assessing speech and swallow.
SAMA: Short-acting muscarinic antagonist, such as ipratropium.
SBP: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: infected ascites, a medical emergency.
SCLC: Small cell lung cancer: aggressive neuroendocrine tumour that spreads early and secretes hormones.
SERM: Selective oestrogen receptor modulator, such as tamoxifen.
SFJ: Saphenofemoral junction: where the great saphenous vein meets the femoral vein.
SGLT-2: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 in the proximal tubule; its inhibitors cause glycosuria.
SGLT-2 inhibitor: A drug such as dapagliflozin that makes the kidney excrete glucose and protects against CKD progression.
SGLT-2 inhibitors: Diabetes drugs (gliflozins) that make the kidney pass glucose in urine.
SGLT2: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2; inhibitor drugs (e.g. dapagliflozin) lower glucose via the urine but can trigger euglycaemic DKA.
SGLT2 inhibitor: A gliflozin drug (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) that makes the kidney excrete glucose and sodium.
SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia with normal potassium.
SIGN criteria: Scottish (SIGN) tonsillectomy criteria: 7+ episodes in 1 year, 5+ in each of 2 years, or 3+ in each of 3 years.
SIRS: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome: whole-body inflammation with fever, tachycardia and raised WCC.
SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease that can cause membranous nephropathy.
SMA: Superior mesenteric artery: supplies the midgut from the duodenum to the distal transverse colon.
SNRI: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, such as venlafaxine or duloxetine.
SOAR: Score predicting short-term mortality after ischaemic stroke.
SOD1: Superoxide dismutase gene; mutations cause a subset of familial ALS.
SOL: Space-occupying lesion: a mass such as a tumour, abscess or haematoma that takes up room in the skull.
SPECT: Single-photon emission CT, a nuclear medicine scan of function or blood flow.
SPEP: Serum protein electrophoresis; separates blood proteins to reveal a monoclonal band.
SRS: Stereotactic radiosurgery: a single precise, high-dose beam aimed at a small target, sparing surrounding brain.
SSI: Surgical site infection: infection of the wound or operated site after surgery.
SSRI: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, such as sertraline.
SSRIs: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine; raise GI bleeding risk.
ST depression: Downward shift of the ST segment on ECG, a sign of subendocardial ischaemia.
STEMI: ST-elevation myocardial infarction: full-thickness infarction from complete occlusion, needing urgent reperfusion.
STOP-BANG: Screening questionnaire: Snoring, Tired, Observed apnoea, Pressure, BMI, Age, Neck size, Gender.
SVC: Superior vena cava: carries blood from the head, neck and arms to the heart.
SVC obstruction: Blocked superior vena cava: facial swelling, plethora, distended neck veins, raised JVP.
SVR: Systemic vascular resistance: the resistance to flow across the body's circulation.
SVT: Supraventricular tachycardia: a fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm from above the ventricles.
Sacral ganglia: Sensory nerve clusters at the base of the spine; site of HSV-2 latency.
Sacroiliac joint: Joint between the sacrum and the iliac bone of the pelvis; inflamed early in AS.
Sacroiliitis: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, the most specific X-ray finding in AS.
Sacubitril-valsartan: An ARNI: a neprilysin inhibitor combined with an ARB, replacing the ACE inhibitor in resistant HFrEF.
Saddle anaesthesia: Numbness of the perineum, buttocks and inner thighs, as in cauda equina syndrome.
Saddle-shaped ST elevation: Concave ST elevation across many leads, typical of pericarditis.
Safeguarding: Protecting children and vulnerable adults from abuse or neglect; a reason to share information.
Safety-netting: Telling a patient which symptoms should make them seek help again, and when.
Salicylate: The active compound in aspirin; also the name of the blood level measured in overdose.
Saline irrigation: Rinsing the nose with salt water to wash out mucus.
Salmonella: A Gram-negative bacterium spread by eggs and poultry, causing diarrhoea and fever.
Salmonella typhi: The Salmonella serotype causing typhoid fever, a systemic illness spread faeco-orally.
Saltatory conduction: Fast nerve conduction where impulses jump between nodes of Ranvier on myelinated axons.
Samter's triad: Asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity.
Sandblasting: Blasting surfaces with sand or grit; a classic silica exposure.
Sarcoidosis: Multisystem disease of non-caseating granulomas, mainly in the lungs and lymph nodes.
Satellite lesions: Small separate red spots beyond the main edge of a rash; classic for cutaneous candidiasis.
Saturday night palsy: Radial nerve compression in the upper arm from sleeping on it while intoxicated.
Scadding: Chest X-ray staging of sarcoidosis from 0 (normal) to 4 (fibrosis).
Scarlet fever: Group A strep infection with a sandpaper rash, flushed cheeks and strawberry tongue.
Schilling test: An old test of B12 absorption, no longer used.
Schistocytes: Fragmented red cells from mechanical shearing in damaged vessels.
Schistosomiasis: Parasitic fluke infection from fresh water; S. haematobium lives in bladder veins.
Schober's test: Bedside test of lumbar forward flexion; marks should separate by at least 5 cm.
Sciatica: Pain radiating down the back of the leg from irritation of the L5 or S1 roots.
Scintigraphy: Isotope uptake scan showing which parts of the thyroid take up tracer.
Scleral icterus: Yellowing of the whites of the eyes from raised bilirubin.
Scleritis: Painful, deep inflammation of the sclera that can threaten sight.
Scleromalacia: Thinning and softening of the sclera, which can progress to perforation.
Sclerotic lesion: An area of abnormally dense new bone, appearing whiter on X-ray.
Scotoma: A patch of lost or altered vision.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency: Adrenal failure from low pituitary ACTH; no pigmentation and aldosterone is preserved.
Secondary headache: A headache caused by another condition, such as haemorrhage, infection or raised pressure.
Secondary hyperaldosteronism: High aldosterone driven by low effective circulating volume, as in cirrhosis.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism: High PTH in response to low calcium, as in CKD.
Secondary hypertension: High blood pressure due to an identifiable, often treatable, underlying cause.
Secondary hyperthyroidism: Thyrotoxicosis driven by the pituitary, so TSH is raised or not suppressed.
Secondary hypothyroidism: Thyroid underactivity caused by pituitary failure, so TSH is low or inappropriately normal.
Secondary peritonitis: Peritonitis from a surgical source such as perforation; usually polymicrobial with free air.
Secondary polycythaemia: A raised red cell count driven by a cause outside the marrow, such as hypoxia raising erythropoietin.
Secondary prevention: Treatment to prevent further events in someone with established CVD.
Secondary progressive: MS that becomes steadily progressive after a relapsing-remitting phase.
Secukinumab: Monoclonal antibody against IL-17A, used when TNF inhibitors are unsuitable.
Seddon classification: Grades nerve injury as neurapraxia, axonotmesis or neurotmesis.
See-saw breathing: Inspiratory stridor with expiratory wheeze, from upper airway swelling plus bronchospasm.
Seizure: A burst of abnormal, hypersynchronous electrical activity in the brain causing symptoms.
Self-limiting: An illness that gets better on its own without treatment.
Semaglutide: Weekly GLP-1 mimetic for weight loss; stop if under 5% loss at 12 weeks on maximum dose.
Semicircular canal: One of three fluid-filled loops in the inner ear that sense head rotation.
Sengstaken-Blakemore tube: Balloon tube inflated in the stomach and oesophagus to compress bleeding varices as a bridge.
Sensitisation: Making IgE to an allergen after first exposure, so later exposure triggers a reaction.
Sensorineural hearing loss: Hearing loss from inner ear or nerve damage; the commonest complication of meningitis.
Sensory level: A horizontal line on the trunk below which sensation is reduced; points to a spinal cord lesion.
Sentinel node biopsy: Removal of the first node(s) draining the tumour to stage the axilla.
Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by the body's response to infection.
Sepsis 6: Six steps within an hour for sepsis: oxygen, cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, lactate and urine output.
Sepsis Six: Oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate and urine output within one hour.
Septic arthritis: Bacterial infection inside a joint; an emergency to exclude first.
Septic emboli: Clumps of infected material carried in the bloodstream that lodge in distant vessels.
Septic screen: Set of tests to find the infection source: urine and sputum cultures, chest X-ray, imaging.
Septic shock: Sepsis with hypotension needing vasopressors and a high lactate.
Septicaemia: Bacteria multiplying in the blood with a systemic response.
Sequestrum: A fragment of dead, infected bone in chronic osteomyelitis.
Serial peak flow: Repeated peak expiratory flow readings over weeks, at and away from work.
Seroconversion: When antibodies to HIV first appear, 3 to 12 weeks after infection.
Serology: Blood tests that detect antibodies against an organism, used to confirm Mycoplasma.
Seronegative: Rheumatoid factor negative; used for the spondyloarthropathies.
Serositis: Inflammation of a serous lining such as the pleura (pleuritis) or pericardium (pericarditis).
Serum precipitins: Blood antibodies against specific inhaled antigens; support hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Seton: A thread or band passed through a fistula tract to keep it draining and protect the sphincter.
Sevelamer: A non-calcium phosphate binder used for hyperphosphataemia in CKD.
Shear stress: The dragging force of flowing blood on the vessel wall.
Shifting dullness: Flank dullness that moves to the uppermost side becoming resonant when the patient rolls: proves free fluid.
Shigella: A Gram-negative bacillus causing bloody dysentery; very few organisms are infective.
Shockable: Rhythms that respond to defibrillation: VF and pulseless VT.
Short Synacthen test: Synthetic ACTH given, then cortisol measured at 30 minutes; confirms adrenal insufficiency.
Sick day rules: Doubling hydrocortisone during febrile illness to copy the normal stress cortisol surge.
Sick euthyroid syndrome: Abnormal thyroid tests in acutely ill patients whose thyroid gland is actually normal.
Sick sinus syndrome: Sinus node dysfunction causing bradycardia, pauses or alternating brady-tachy.
Sick-day rules: Advice for diabetics when unwell: never stop insulin, check ketones and glucose often, and seek help early.
Sickle cell disease: Inherited haemoglobin disorder; transfusions cause iron overload and venesection is unsuitable.
Sideroblastic anaemia: Anaemia where iron is present but cannot be used to make haem.
Siderocytes: Red cells containing iron granules, seen when splenic function is lost.
Sigmoid volvulus: Volvulus of the sigmoid colon; the commonest type in adults, typically elderly and constipated.
Signet ring sign: On HRCT, a dilated bronchus next to its smaller artery, like a ring with a stone.
Sildenafil: A PDE-5 inhibitor used as a pulmonary vasodilator in PAH.
Silent chest: Almost no breath sounds because so little air moves; a life-threatening sign.
Silica: Crystalline mineral dust from quarrying, mining, sandblasting and stonework.
Silicosis: Fibrosis from silica dust, mainly upper zone, with eggshell calcification of hilar nodes.
Simple analgesia: Non-opioid painkillers such as paracetamol, aspirin and NSAIDs.
Simple cyst: Thin-walled, fluid-only cyst with no solid part on ultrasound; benign.
Sinus tract: A channel from infected tissue to the skin surface that discharges pus.
Sinusitis: Infection or inflammation of the paranasal sinuses.
Sister Mary Joseph nodule: Hard nodule at the umbilicus from metastatic abdominal or pelvic cancer.
Sitz bath: Sitting in warm shallow water to soothe the perianal area.
Skin patch testing: Allergens taped to the back and read after 2 to 3 days to diagnose contact dermatitis.
Skin prick testing: Allergen drops pricked into forearm skin; a wheal at 15 minutes shows IgE sensitisation.
Skin tethering: Skin dimpling as tumour pulls on the supporting ligaments.
Slamming: Injecting recreational drugs during sex; a risk for HIV through shared needles.
Sleep architecture: The normal pattern of sleep stages through the night, broken up by repeated arousals in OSA.
Sleep hygiene: Habits that support good sleep: regular hours, no alcohol or screens before bed, a dark quiet room.
Sliding scale: Variable-rate insulin adjusted to glucose; not used in DKA, where a fixed rate is needed.
Slow-rising pulse: A pulse that takes longer than normal to reach its peak, typical of aortic stenosis.
Smudge cells: Ruptured fragile lymphocytes on a blood film; typical of CLL.
SnNout: A highly Sensitive test, if Negative, rules OUT disease.
Snellen: Letter chart acuity, e.g. 6/6 normal, 6/36 reduced.
Soap bubble: A multi-chambered lytic X-ray appearance, typical of giant cell tumour.
Sodium bicarbonate: An alkali used to correct metabolic acidosis in CKD.
Sodium channel blockade: Blocking of fast sodium channels in heart muscle, slowing conduction and widening the QRS.
Sodium cromoglicate: Mast cell stabiliser eye drop for recurrent or persistent allergic conjunctivitis.
Sodium valproate: A broad-spectrum AED that is highly teratogenic and avoided in women of childbearing age.
Somatic mutation: Gene change arising in one body cell, not inherited, that can make a nodule autonomous.
Sorbitol: A sugar alcohol made from glucose that builds up in cells and causes osmotic stress.
Source control: Removing the source of infection, such as an infected line, or draining an abscess.
SpIn: A highly Specific test, if Positive, rules IN disease.
Spacer: A chamber attached to an inhaler that reduces drug deposited in the mouth.
Spasticity: Velocity-dependent increased tone from an upper motor neurone lesion.
Specific IgE: IgE directed against one named allergen, measured in blood (RAST).
Sphenoid sinus: Deep sinus behind the nose, near the pituitary and cavernous sinus.
Spherocytes: Small round red cells without central pallor; seen in warm AIHA and hereditary spherocytosis.
Sphincterotomy: Cutting the sphincter of Oddi at ERCP to let stones out.
Spider naevi: Small red spots with radiating vessels on the upper body, a sign of chronic liver disease.
Spigelian hernia: A hernia through the linea semilunaris at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath.
Spinal cord compression: Emergency compression of the cord, often by bone metastases, causing back pain and leg weakness.
Spinal stenosis: Narrowing of the spinal canal causing leg pain on walking, relieved by sitting or bending forward.
Spirometry: Breathing test measuring FEV1 and FVC to detect obstruction or restriction.
Spironolactone: Aldosterone antagonist diuretic, first-line for cirrhotic ascites.
Splanchnic vasodilation: Widening of gut blood vessels in cirrhosis, which leaves the rest of the circulation underfilled.
Splenomegaly: Enlarged spleen, in cirrhosis from portal hypertension.
Splinter haemorrhages: Thin red-brown streaks under the nails from tiny emboli or capillary bleeds.
Split S2: Second heart sound heard as two parts, aortic then pulmonary closure.
Spodick's sign: A downsloping TP segment on the ECG in acute pericarditis.
Spondyloarthropathy: Family of HLA-B27 linked arthritides affecting the spine and entheses: AS, psoriatic, reactive and enteropathic arthritis.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, diagnosed by ascitic neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³.
Squamous cell carcinoma: Cancer of squamous cells; in the bladder linked to schistosomiasis and long-term catheters.
Squamous metaplasia: Replacement of normal lining by squamous epithelium after chronic irritation.
Squaring: Loss of the normal concave front of vertebral bodies from inflammation at the corners.
Squaring of the thumb: Square-looking thumb base caused by osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint.
St John's Wort: Herbal antidepressant that induces liver P450 enzymes.
Stable angina: Predictable chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest or GTN, from a fixed plaque.
Staggered overdose: Tablets taken over more than 1 hour, so the paracetamol nomogram cannot be used and NAC starts immediately.
Staghorn calculus: Large branching stone filling the renal pelvis and calyces, usually struvite.
Stanford type A: Dissection involving the ascending aorta or arch; a surgical emergency.
Stanford type B: Dissection limited to the descending aorta, distal to the left subclavian; usually managed medically.
Staph aureus: Staphylococcus aureus; its preformed toxin in food causes vomiting within 1 to 6 hours.
Staph epidermidis: Skin commensal that can contaminate room-temperature platelet units.
Staph. aureus: Coagulase-positive gram-positive coccus; the commonest cause of endocarditis, especially in IVDU.
Staph. epidermidis: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus causing early prosthetic valve and line infections.
Staphylococcus aureus: Gram-positive coccus in clusters living on skin; the commonest cause of mastitis and abscess.
Starry sky: Biopsy appearance of Burkitt's: pale macrophages scattered among dark tumour cells.
Stat: Immediately, given as a single dose now.
Statin: A cholesterol-lowering drug that stabilises atherosclerotic plaques.
Status epilepticus: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery in between.
Status migrainosus: A migraine attack lasting more than 72 hours.
Steatorrhoea: Pale, oily, foul-smelling stools from unabsorbed fat.
Stenosing tenosynovitis: Narrowing and inflammation of a tendon sheath, as in trigger finger.
Stent: A mesh tube left in an artery to keep it open.
Stereotactic radiosurgery: Highly focused high-dose radiotherapy to a small target such as a single metastasis.
Sterile pyuria: White cells in the urine with no growth on standard culture; think chlamydia.
Steroid emergency card: Card carried by steroid-dependent patients telling clinicians to give hydrocortisone in emergencies.
Steroid-resistant: Disease that does not remit after an adequate course of steroids.
Steroid-sparing agent: A drug added so the steroid dose can be reduced, limiting steroid side effects.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome: A severe, life-threatening blistering reaction of skin and mucous membranes, usually drug-induced.
Stoma: An opening of bowel onto the abdominal wall, making open repair harder.
Stony dull: A very dull percussion note over fluid, classic of a pleural effusion.
Stool chart: Record of bowel movements, used to spot constipation.
Stratum corneum: The outermost dead-cell layer of the epidermis that forms the skin barrier.
Strep. bovis: Streptococcus (gallolyticus) linked with colorectal carcinoma; needs a colonoscopy.
Strep. pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae: the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
Strep. viridans: Alpha-haemolytic mouth streptococci causing subacute endocarditis after dental disease.
Streptococcus milleri: A group of streptococci (anginosus group) that classically form abscesses in the brain, liver and chest.
Streptococcus pneumoniae: Encapsulated Gram-positive diplococcus; the commonest cause of OPSI.
Streptococcus pyogenes: Group A Strep; the most common cause of cellulitis.
Streptolysin O: A Group A strep toxin that damages cells; antibodies to it (ASO titre) show recent infection.
Stress echo: Ultrasound of the heart during exercise or drug stress, looking for wall motion abnormalities.
Stress incontinence: Leakage of urine when intra-abdominal pressure rises (cough, sneeze, exercise) because the pelvic floor or sphincter is weak.
Striatum: Caudate and putamen; receives dopamine from the substantia nigra.
Stridor: High-pitched noise on breathing in caused by upper airway narrowing.
String of pearls: Beaded, varicose dilatation of bronchi on HRCT.
Stroma: The supporting connective tissue of an organ.
Struvite: Magnesium ammonium phosphate stone formed in alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria.
Sub-xiphoid: Just below the xiphisternum; the preferred route for pericardiocentesis.
Subacute combined degeneration: Spinal cord damage from B12 deficiency, causing neuropathy with upper motor neurone signs.
Subacute thyroiditis: Another name for De Quervain's thyroiditis.
Subarticular sclerosis: Increased bone density beneath the joint surface, seen as a whiter band on X-ray.
Subchondral cysts: Fluid-filled holes in the bone just beneath damaged cartilage, seen on X-ray.
Subchondral sclerosis: Increased bone density just beneath the joint surface, seen on X-ray.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism: Low TSH with normal free T4.
Subclinical hypothyroidism: Raised TSH with normal free T4 and usually no symptoms.
Subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer beneath the dermis.
Subendocardial: The inner layer of the heart muscle, most vulnerable to ischaemia.
Subendothelial collagen: Collagen under the vessel lining; when exposed it makes platelets stick.
Subepicardial: The outer layer of the myocardium, just under the epicardium.
Subepithelial: Between the GBM and the podocytes, where membranous immune deposits sit.
Subglottic: The part of the airway just below the vocal cords, the narrowest point in a small child.
Subperiosteal collection: Fluid or pus trapped beneath the periosteum, visible on ultrasound.
Substantia nigra: A midbrain area of dopamine neurons; its loss causes parkinsonism.
Sudden cardiac death: Unexpected death from a cardiac cause, usually an arrhythmia.
Sulfadiazine: Sulfonamide used with pyrimethamine to treat toxoplasmosis.
Sulfasalazine: DMARD used for severe or chronic reactive arthritis.
Sumatriptan: The commonest triptan, taken orally, nasally or by subcutaneous injection.
Superficial SSI: Infection limited to the skin and subcutaneous tissue around the incision.
Superficial femoral artery: The main artery of the thigh; a common site of atherosclerotic occlusion.
Superior cerebellar artery: Artery from the basilar artery whose loop most often compresses the trigeminal root.
Superior limbus: The upper edge where the cornea meets the white sclera.
Supersaturated: Holding more dissolved salt than it can keep in solution, so crystals form.
Supervised exercise: Structured walking programme, 2 hours a week for 3 months, first-line for claudication.
Supralevator: The space above the levator ani muscles; abscesses here are deep and hard to see.
Suprapubic: Just above the pubic bone, over the bladder.
Surgical decompression: An operation to remove tumour, bone or disc pressing on the cord or roots.
Surgical site infection: Infection of an operation wound causing redness, pain and discharge.
Surveillance: Repeat ultrasound scans at set intervals to watch an aneurysm's growth.
Suxamethonium: Depolarising muscle relaxant used in anaesthesia; myasthenic patients are resistant to it.
Swan neck deformity: Finger with hyperextended PIP and flexed DIP.
Sweat test: Measures sweat chloride; raised in cystic fibrosis.
Swinging fever: A temperature that repeatedly spikes and falls, suggesting a collection of pus such as an empyema or abscess.
Swinging light test: Moving a torch between the eyes to detect a relative afferent pupillary defect.
Sympathetic withdrawal: Sudden loss of sympathetic tone to vessels, letting them dilate.
Sympathomimetic: Mimicking adrenaline: agitated, sweaty, fast heart, high blood pressure, dilated pupils.
Synacthen: Tetracosactide, a synthetic ACTH used in stimulation tests.
Synchronised DC cardioversion: An electric shock timed to the R wave to restore normal rhythm.
Synchronised cardioversion: A shock timed to the R wave, used for tachycardias with a pulse.
Syncope: A brief loss of consciousness from reduced brain blood flow, with rapid recovery.
Syndesmophytes: Vertical bony bridges growing from vertebral body margins in AS.
Synergistic: Two factors combining to give an effect greater than their sum.
Synovial fluid: The lubricating fluid inside a joint, sampled by aspiration.
Synovitis: Inflammation of the synovial lining of a joint.
Synovium: The lining membrane of a joint that produces synovial fluid.
Systemic anti-cancer treatment: Drugs that act throughout the body, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy or immunotherapy.
Systemic candidiasis: Candida in the blood or organs, in severely immunocompromised patients.
T score: Bone density compared with a young adult reference, in standard deviations; below -2.5 is osteoporosis.
T-cell mediated: Inflammation driven by T lymphocytes rather than antibodies.
T-wave inversion: Upside-down T waves on ECG, which can indicate ischaemia.
T2 hyperintensity: A bright area on a T2-weighted MRI, as seen with MS plaques.
T3: Triiodothyronine, the most active thyroid hormone, mostly made by converting T4 in tissues.
TA-GvHD: Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease: donor lymphocytes attack the recipient, causing rash, jaundice and pancytopenia.
TACI: Total anterior circulation infarct: hemiparesis, homonymous hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction together.
TACO: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload: pulmonary oedema from too much volume, with raised JVP and hypertension.
TAVI: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a new valve placed via a catheter, usually from the femoral artery.
TB: Tuberculosis, a Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection; routinely notifiable.
TCC: Transitional cell carcinoma, the most common bladder cancer.
TDP-43: A protein that aggregates in many cases of frontotemporal dementia and ALS.
TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4.
TGF-beta: Transforming growth factor beta, a cytokine that drives marrow fibrosis.
TIA: Transient ischaemic attack: sudden, brief, negative focal neurological symptoms from ischaemia.
TIA clinic: Specialist rapid-access clinic where suspected TIA is assessed within 24 hours.
TIBC: Total iron-binding capacity; rises in iron deficiency as the body makes more transferrin.
TIMI: A simpler risk score for unstable angina and NSTEMI, predicting death, reinfarction or urgent revascularisation.
TIPS: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt: a stent linking portal and hepatic veins to lower portal pressure.
TLC: Total lung capacity; reduced in restrictive lung disease.
TLCO: Transfer factor for carbon monoxide: how well gas crosses into the blood; low in fibrosis.
TLoC: Transient loss of consciousness: the umbrella term NICE uses for blackouts.
TNF inhibitor: Biologic blocking TNF-alpha, e.g. adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab.
TNF-alpha: Pro-inflammatory cytokine central to AS and RA inflammation.
TNF-alpha inhibitor: Biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, e.g. adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab.
TNM: Staging system: tumour depth, nodes and metastases.
TOE: Transoesophageal echocardiography: ultrasound probe in the oesophagus, used when the patient is too unstable for CT.
TOXBASE: The UK National Poisons Information Service online database for managing poisoning.
TP: True positive: test positive and disease present.
TPMT: Thiopurine methyltransferase, the enzyme that breaks down azathioprine; low activity causes marrow toxicity.
TPN: Total parenteral nutrition: all nutritional needs given intravenously.
TPO antibodies: Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase; positive in Hashimoto's and predict progression of subclinical disease.
TRALI: Transfusion-related acute lung injury: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6 hours, often after FFP.
TRAP: Tremor, rigidity, akinesia and postural instability: the cardinal features of Parkinson's.
TRAb: TSH receptor antibodies, which cause Graves' disease and drive thyroid eye disease.
TRH: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus that tells the pituitary to release TSH.
TRUS: Transrectal ultrasound, used to guide prostate biopsy.
TSH: Thyroid stimulating hormone; low in hyperthyroidism.
TSH receptor antibodies: Autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor; diagnostic of Graves' disease.
TTP: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: microthrombi causing MAHA, low platelets, fever, AKI and neurology.
TURBT: Transurethral resection of bladder tumour: removing it through a scope to treat and stage.
TURP: Transurethral resection of the prostate: cutting away obstructing tissue through a cystoscope.
Tachyarrhythmia: An abnormal heart rhythm with a rate above 100 bpm.
Tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 bpm, here a sign of dehydration.
Tachyphylaxis: A rapidly falling response to a drug with repeated doses.
Tacrolimus: A topical calcineurin inhibitor used as a steroid-sparing treatment in severe eczema.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: Stress-induced apical ballooning of the left ventricle, mimicking MI.
Tamoxifen: Selective oestrogen receptor modulator used for ER-positive premenopausal breast cancer.
Tamponade: Fluid or blood in the pericardium compressing the heart.
Tamsulosin: An alpha-1 blocker for BPH that eases outflow obstruction.
Taper: Gradual dose reduction to avoid relapse and adrenal insufficiency.
Target lesion: Round skin lesion with three concentric rings: dark centre, pale ring, red outer ring.
Tarsal conjunctiva: Conjunctiva lining the inside of the eyelid.
Tau: A protein that becomes hyperphosphorylated and forms tangles inside neurons.
Tc-99m: Technetium-99m, a radioactive tracer used in nuclear medicine scans.
Temporal arteritis: Another name for giant cell arteritis affecting the temporal arteries.
Temporal artery biopsy: Removal of a segment of temporal artery to confirm giant cell arteritis.
Temporal lobe: The brain lobe for memory, smell and language; HSV's favourite target.
Tendon xanthomas: Cholesterol deposits in tendons such as the Achilles or knuckles; a hallmark of FH.
Tenecteplase: A modified tissue plasminogen activator given as a single IV bolus.
Tenosynovitis: Inflammation of the sheath around a tendon.
Tensilon test: Historic test giving IV edrophonium to see if weakness briefly improves; rarely used due to cardiac risk.
Tension pneumothorax: Air trapped in the pleural space under pressure, shifting the mediastinum.
Tension-type headache: A bilateral, pressing, band-like headache without vomiting or aura.
Tented T waves: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves on ECG, an early sign of hyperkalaemia.
Teratogenic: Able to cause birth defects when taken in pregnancy.
Teriparatide: Daily injected PTH analogue that builds new bone; specialist use.
Terlipressin: Vasopressin analogue that constricts splanchnic vessels, lowering portal pressure in variceal bleeding.
Terminal ductal-lobular unit: The milk-producing lobule and its small duct, where cysts form.
Terminal ileum: The last part of the small bowel, where B12 is absorbed.
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism: Autonomous high PTH with high calcium after years of secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Test-of-cure: Repeat culture after treatment to confirm the infection has gone.
Testicular atrophy: Shrunken testes; a sign of hypogonadism.
Tetrahydrofolate: The active form of folate needed to make DNA bases.
Tetralogy of Fallot: Congenital heart defect with a ventricular septal defect and right-to-left shunting, causing cyanosis.
Th1: T helper 1 cells driving cell-mediated inflammation and granulomas.
Th17: T-helper 17 cells, which release IL-17 and drive psoriatic inflammation.
Th2: T helper 2 cells, which drive allergic, eosinophilic inflammation.
Thalassaemia: Reduced or absent synthesis of alpha or beta globin chains, giving microcytic anaemia.
Therapeutic misadventure: Accidental toxicity from a prescribed medicine, for example morphine accumulating in kidney failure.
Thiamine: Vitamin B1, a cofactor for glucose metabolism; deficiency causes Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Thiazide: Diuretic that reduces urinary calcium; used to prevent calcium stones.
Third heart sound: Low-pitched extra sound in early diastole, a sign of heart failure.
Third nerve palsy: Oculomotor nerve palsy: ptosis and a 'down and out' eye; diabetic ones usually spare the pupil.
Third-spacing: Fluid shifting out of the blood into tissues or body cavities, causing hypovolaemia.
Thoracic aortic aneurysm: An aneurysm of the aorta in the chest, causing chest pain and compression symptoms.
Thoracoscopy: A camera passed into the pleural space to inspect and biopsy the pleura.
Three-vessel disease: Significant narrowing in all three main coronary arteries (LAD, circumflex, RCA).
Three-way catheter: Catheter with an extra channel so fluid can run in to irrigate the bladder.
Thrill: A palpable vibration over the heart from a loud murmur.
Throat swab: A swab of the tonsils sent for culture to identify Group A strep.
Thrombectomy: Removal of a clot from an artery, surgically or with a catheter.
Thrombin: Enzyme that turns fibrinogen into fibrin to form a stable clot.
Thrombocytopenia: Low platelet count, the most sensitive lab sign of cirrhosis.
Thrombocytosis: Raised platelet count; often reactive in iron deficiency or bleeding.
Thrombolysis: Clot-busting drug treatment such as alteplase; contraindicated in aortic dissection.
Thrombophlebitis: Inflamed, clotted superficial vein felt as a tender cord.
Thrombosed haemorrhoid: A haemorrhoid containing clot: a painful purple lump at the anal margin, without fever.
Thrombosis: A clot forming in place, here on a narrowed atherosclerotic artery.
Thrombus: A blood clot formed within a vessel.
Thrush: Common name for oral or vaginal candidiasis.
Thudichum speculum: Small metal speculum used to open the nostril for examination.
Thunderclap: A sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute; suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Thunderclap headache: A sudden, severe headache reaching maximum intensity within about a minute; a red flag for subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Thymectomy: Surgical removal of the thymus; definitive treatment in myasthenia, especially with thymoma.
Thymidine: A DNA building block whose synthesis needs folate (and B12 to recycle folate).
Thymoma: A tumour of the thymus in the anterior mediastinum, linked to myasthenia.
Thymus: Gland in the anterior mediastinum where T cells mature; drives antibody production in myasthenia.
Thyroglobulin: Protein stored in thyroid follicles from which T4 and T3 are made; antibodies to it occur in Hashimoto's.
Thyroid acropachy: Finger clubbing with soft-tissue swelling in Graves' disease.
Thyroid eye disease: Autoimmune inflammation of the tissues around the eye, usually with Graves' disease.
Thyroid storm: Life-threatening decompensated thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachycardia and delirium.
Thyroid-binding globulin: Protein carrying thyroid hormone; lost in urine, lowering total T4.
Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins: IgG antibodies in Graves' that bind and activate the TSH receptor.
Thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
Thyroperoxidase: Thyroid enzyme that makes T4 and T3; blocked by antithyroid drugs.
Thyrotoxicosis: Too much circulating thyroid hormone from any cause.
Ticagrelor: P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet, an alternative second antiplatelet to clopidogrel.
Tidal volume: Volume of air moved in or out in one normal breath.
Tilt-table test: A test tilting the patient upright to provoke reflex syncope; reserved for unclear recurrent cases.
Time-critical: Medicines that must be given within a set time of the scheduled dose to avoid harm.
Time-specific: Capacity is judged at the time of the decision and can change, for example as delirium clears.
Tinea pedis: Athlete's foot: fungal infection between the toes, a common entry point for cellulitis.
Tinel's: Tapping over a nerve reproduces tingling in its territory.
Tinel's sign: Tapping over a nerve reproduces tingling in its distribution; positive at the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Tinkling bowel sounds: High-pitched bowel sounds heard in mechanical bowel obstruction.
Tinnitus: Ringing or buzzing in the ears.
Tirzepatide: Dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist injection used for weight loss.
Tissue factor: A protein exposed in damaged vessel walls that starts the coagulation cascade.
Todd's paresis: Temporary weakness of a limb after a focal motor seizure.
Tokyo Guidelines: International criteria for diagnosing and grading acute cholangitis and cholecystitis.
Tolvaptan: A vasopressin receptor blocker that slows cyst growth in ADPKD.
Tonic: The stiffening phase of a seizure, with sustained muscle contraction.
Tonic-clonic seizure: A generalised seizure with stiffening then rhythmic jerking of the limbs.
Tonsillectomy: Surgical removal of the palatine tonsils.
Tonsillitis: Infection and inflammation of the palatine tonsils.
Tophi: Chalky lumps of urate crystals under the skin, on the ears or over joints, in long-standing gout.
Topical NSAID: An anti-inflammatory gel or cream, such as diclofenac, applied over the joint.
Topiramate: An AED that causes weight loss, kidney stones and cognitive slowing.
Torsades de pointes: Polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline, triggered by a long QT.
Torsional nystagmus: Nystagmus that rotates the eye around its front-to-back axis; typical of posterior canal BPPV.
Toxic adenoma: Single autonomous thyroid nodule making excess hormone.
Toxic multinodular goitre: Enlarged thyroid with several autonomous nodules making excess hormone; usually over 50.
Toxicology screen: Blood or urine tests for drugs taken in overdose.
Toxidrome: A recognisable group of signs caused by a class of toxin acting on one receptor system.
Toxins A and B: C. difficile toxins that damage the colon lining and cause colitis.
Toxoplasmosis: Toxoplasma gondii infection causing ring-enhancing brain lesions when CD4 is below 100.
Trabecular: The spongy inner bone made of struts, lost early in osteoporosis.
Tracheal tube: A cuffed tube passed through the vocal cords into the trachea; seals and protects the airway.
Track marks: Scars along veins from repeated injection drug use.
Tram-track sign: Parallel thickened bronchial walls seen lengthways on imaging.
Tranexamic acid: Antifibrinolytic drug that stops clots breaking down; useful for dental and mucosal bleeding.
Transbronchial biopsy: Lung tissue sample taken through a bronchoscope.
Transepidermal water loss: Water evaporating through the skin; increased when the barrier is faulty.
Transferrin saturation: Percentage of the iron-carrying protein transferrin that is loaded with iron.
Transient elastography: Non-invasive ultrasound technique measuring liver stiffness in kPa (FibroScan).
Transient synovitis: Self-limiting, non-infective hip inflammation in children, often after a viral illness.
Transitional cell carcinoma: Cancer of the urothelium; the most common bladder cancer.
Translocation: Movement of bacteria or toxins from one compartment (bile) into the blood.
Transmural: Through the full thickness of the heart wall.
Transthoracic echocardiogram: Ultrasound of the heart through the chest wall; the gold standard for valve disease.
Transudate: Low-protein fluid pushed out by pressure, as in portal hypertension.
Transverse myelitis: Inflammation across a segment of spinal cord, giving a sensory level, weakness and bladder problems.
Trastuzumab: Antibody treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer, which crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly.
Trendelenburg test: Bedside tourniquet test of where venous reflux occurs, now replaced by duplex.
Trephine: A core of bone marrow tissue taken with a biopsy needle to show marrow architecture.
Trichomonas vaginalis: Sexually transmitted protozoan causing frothy, offensive yellow-green discharge.
Tricuspid regurgitation: Backflow from right ventricle to right atrium; pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge.
Tricuspid stenosis: Narrowed tricuspid valve, usually rheumatic, giving a mid-diastolic murmur.
Trigeminal ganglion: Sensory nerve cluster of cranial nerve V; site of HSV-1 latency.
Trigeminal nerve: Cranial nerve V; carries sensation from the face and supplies the chewing muscles.
Trigeminal neuralgia: Brief, severe, electric-shock facial pain in the territory of the trigeminal nerve.
Trigeminal-autonomic: Reflex pathway linking the trigeminal nerve with autonomic features such as tearing; involved in cluster headache.
Trigeminovascular system: Trigeminal nerve fibres supplying meningeal blood vessels; their activation drives migraine pain.
Triglycerides: Blood fats from diet and the liver; very high levels risk pancreatitis.
Trimester: One of three roughly 13-week periods of pregnancy.
Trimethoprim: An antibiotic that raises creatinine and potassium by blocking tubular secretion.
Triple assessment: Clinical examination, imaging and core needle biopsy of a breast lump.
Triple therapy: ICS + LABA + LAMA, usually in one inhaler.
Triple-negative: Tumour negative for ER, PR and HER2, so no targeted hormone or HER2 drug works.
Triptan: A 5-HT1B/1D agonist used to treat acute migraine attacks.
Triptans: Serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists, such as sumatriptan, used to treat acute migraine.
Trismus: Difficulty opening the mouth because of jaw muscle spasm.
Troisier's sign: Finding a palpable Virchow's node on examination.
Trophic changes: Shiny skin, hair loss and thick nails from long-term poor blood supply.
Troponin: Heart muscle protein released into blood when myocytes die; raised in MI.
Trousseau's sign: Carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated above systolic pressure.
Trousseau's syndrome: Migratory thrombophlebitis linked to pancreatic cancer, not myeloma.
Truelove and Witts: Criteria grading UC flare severity by stool count and systemic markers.
Tryptase: Mast cell enzyme measured in blood to confirm anaphylaxis.
Tubuloglomerular feedback: The kidney's reflex in which sodium delivery to the distal tubule adjusts afferent arteriole tone.
Tumour lysis syndrome: Rapid tumour cell death releasing potassium, phosphate and urate, with low calcium, risking AKI and arrhythmia.
Tunnel vision: Loss of peripheral vision so only the centre remains, a common pre-faint symptom.
Turbid: Cloudy, as CSF looks when full of white cells.
Turner syndrome: Chromosomal condition (45,X) in girls with one X, so an X-linked recessive gene can be expressed.
Tympanic: Drum-like, hollow note on percussion, caused by gas-filled bowel.
Tympanic membrane: The eardrum; red and bulging in acute otitis media.
Type 1: Respiratory failure with low oxygen but normal or low carbon dioxide: an oxygenation problem.
Type 2: Respiratory failure with low oxygen and carbon dioxide above 6 kPa: a ventilation problem.
Type 2 respiratory failure: Low pO2 with a raised pCO2 (above 6.0 kPa).
Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction within minutes, e.g. hay fever, urticaria, anaphylaxis.
Type II hypersensitivity: Antibodies binding a fixed cell-surface antigen, causing damage or blocking function.
Type II respiratory failure: Low oxygen with a raised carbon dioxide from inadequate ventilation.
Type III hypersensitivity: Immune-complex-mediated reaction, causing inflammation where complexes deposit.
Type IV hypersensitivity: Delayed, T-cell-mediated reaction taking 2 to 3 days, e.g. allergic contact dermatitis.
Tyrosine kinase: Enzyme that switches on cell signalling; overactive in CML.
U score: British Thyroid Association ultrasound grade from U1 (benign) to U5 (malignant).
U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: the routine kidney blood test (sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine).
UAS7: Urticaria activity score over 7 days (0 to 42), tracking wheals and itch.
UC: Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon starting at the rectum.
UIP: Usual interstitial pneumonia: the basal, peripheral honeycombing CT pattern typical of IPF.
UKHCDO: UK Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation, which writes UK haemophilia guidelines.
UKHSA: UK Health Security Agency, the public health body that receives notifications and runs contact tracing.
UKMEC: UK criteria grading how safe each contraceptive is for a given condition; 4 means unacceptable risk.
ULN: Upper limit of normal for a lab test.
UMN: Upper motor neurone: from cortex to brainstem; a facial UMN lesion spares the forehead.
URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, such as a cold or sore throat.
USS KUB: Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, used to look for obstruction.
Uhthoff's phenomenon: Temporary worsening of MS symptoms with heat, such as a hot bath or exercise.
Ulcerative colitis: Inflammatory bowel disease with continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, rarely causing fistulas.
Ulnar deviation: Drift of the fingers towards the little finger side at the MCP joints.
Ultrasound-guided: Using ultrasound to place the needle accurately.
Ultrasound-guided aspiration: Drawing pus out through a needle while watching on ultrasound.
Unconjugated bilirubin: Bilirubin not yet processed by the liver; rises when red cells break down.
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation: Mitochondria burn fuel without making ATP, producing heat and lactic acid.
Unfractionated heparin: An IV anticoagulant that stops clots growing and can be quickly reversed.
Universal donor: Group O red cells, which lack A and B antigens.
Unmyelinated fibres: Small nerve fibres without a myelin sheath, including autonomic fibres; vulnerable in diabetes.
Unopposed oestrogen: Oestrogen action without the balancing effect of progesterone.
Unstable angina: Chest pain at rest or worsening, from plaque rupture without infarction; troponin normal.
Unwise decision: A choice others disagree with; under the MCA it is not evidence of lacking capacity.
Upper airway surgery: Operations to widen the throat, such as removing tonsils or palate tissue; third-line and rarely used.
Upper lobe diversion: Prominent upper lobe vessels on CXR from raised pulmonary venous pressure.
Upper outer quadrant: The part of the breast towards the armpit; holds most breast tissue.
Uraemia: Build-up of waste products in the blood, causing nausea, confusion, pericarditis and a grey-brown skin tinge.
Uraemic pericarditis: Pericardial inflammation from uraemia; chest pain relieved by sitting forward and a dialysis indication.
Urate-lowering therapy: Long-term drugs (allopurinol, febuxostat) that lower serum urate to prevent gout attacks.
Urea: A waste product of protein breakdown cleared by the kidneys; rises disproportionately in pre-renal AKI.
Urease: Bacterial enzyme that splits urea into ammonia, making urine alkaline.
Ureteric: Relating to the ureter, the tube from kidney to bladder.
Ureteroscopy: Camera passed up the ureter to remove or fragment a stone.
Urethral closure pressure: The pressure the urethra and pelvic floor hold against to keep urine in.
Urethritis: Inflammation of the urethra causing dysuria and discharge.
Urge incontinence: Leakage after a sudden strong urge to pass urine, caused by detrusor overactivity.
Urgency: Sudden strong need to pass urine.
Urinary alkalinisation: IV sodium bicarbonate to make urine alkaline, trapping salicylate in the urine to speed excretion.
Urinary antigen: A urine test detecting bacterial proteins, used for Legionella and Strep pneumoniae.
Urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder fully.
Urine culture: Growing bacteria from urine to identify them and their antibiotic sensitivities.
Urine cytology: Microscopy of urine for cancer cells; insensitive for low-grade tumours.
Urine osmolality: How concentrated the urine is; above 500 mOsm/kg suggests pre-renal AKI.
Urodynamic studies: Bladder pressure tests that show detrusor overactivity or stress leakage.
Urodynamics: Pressure studies of bladder filling and voiding, used when the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery.
Uropathogen: An organism that commonly causes urinary infection.
Urothelial carcinoma: Another name for transitional cell carcinoma.
Urothelium: Transitional epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and urethra.
Urticaria: Itchy, raised red wheals (hives) caused by histamine release in the skin.
Urticarial vasculitis: Inflamed vessels causing wheal-like lesions that last over 24 hours and leave bruising.
Ustekinumab: Monoclonal antibody against the p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23.
Utricle: An inner ear sac whose macula holds the otoconia.
Uveitis: Inflammation of the uvea, causing pain, photophobia and blurred vision.
Uvula: The small fleshy tag hanging from the soft palate; pushed away from a quinsy.
V wave: JVP wave from right atrial filling in systole; giant in tricuspid regurgitation.
V/Q mismatch: Air reaching lung units that get no blood flow, so oxygen is not picked up.
V/Q ratio: Ventilation to perfusion ratio; falls when collapsed lung is still perfused.
V/Q scan: Ventilation/perfusion scan; shows lung areas that are ventilated but not perfused.
V1: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve: forehead, eye and upper nose.
V2: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve: cheek, upper lip and upper teeth.
V2 receptor: ADH receptor in the collecting duct that triggers aquaporin-2 insertion.
V3: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve: jaw, lower lip, chin and chewing muscles.
VAP: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: pneumonia arising 48 hours or more after intubation.
VBG: Venous blood gas: gives pH and bicarbonate reliably, but not oxygen.
VCA IgM: Antibody to the EBV viral capsid antigen showing recent infection.
VEGF: Vascular endothelial growth factor: signal released by ischaemic tissue that drives new vessel growth.
VEP: Visual evoked potentials: measures conduction time along the visual pathway; delayed in demyelination.
VF: Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic ventricular activity with no cardiac output.
VFR: Visiting friends and relatives: travellers at high risk because they often skip prophylaxis.
VGCC: Voltage-gated calcium channel at the nerve terminal; targeted by antibodies in LEMS.
VOC: Vaso-occlusive crisis: painful sickling episode from blocked small vessels.
VP shunt: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt: a tube draining CSF from the brain's ventricles to the abdomen.
VSD: Ventricular septal defect: a hole in the septum; after MI it is septal rupture.
VT: Ventricular tachycardia: a fast, broad-complex rhythm from the ventricles.
VZV: Varicella zoster virus, the chickenpox and shingles virus; it causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
Vagal manoeuvres: Valsalva or carotid sinus massage, which slow AV node conduction.
Vaginal candidiasis: Thrush; a common side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors due to glucose in the urine.
Valaciclovir: Prodrug of aciclovir with better absorption, so fewer daily doses.
Valgus: Deformity with the knee pointing inwards, giving a knock-kneed look.
Valid consent: Consent given voluntarily by an informed person with capacity.
Valsalva: Forced expiration against a closed airway to increase vagal tone.
Valve area: The opening area of the aortic valve; normal is 3-4 cm².
Vancomycin: IV glycopeptide antibiotic used for MRSA.
Varenicline: A partial nicotinic agonist used to help people stop smoking.
Varices: Dilated collateral veins, usually in the oesophagus, that can bleed catastrophically.
Varus: Deformity with the knee pointing outwards, giving a bow-legged look.
Vasa nervorum: The tiny blood vessels supplying peripheral nerves.
Vascular calcification: Calcium deposits in artery walls, raising cardiovascular risk in CKD.
Vascular dementia: Dementia from cumulative ischaemic brain damage, causing stepwise decline.
Vaso-occlusion: Blockage of small vessels by sickled red cells, causing infarction and pain.
Vaso-occlusive crisis: Painful episode where sickled cells block small vessels, causing ischaemia, often in bone.
Vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, lowering blood pressure.
Vasogenic oedema: Brain swelling from fluid leaking out of damaged blood vessels into the surrounding tissue.
Vasopressin: Hormone used as a second vasopressor when noradrenaline alone is not enough.
Vasopressor: Drug that constricts blood vessels to raise blood pressure, e.g. noradrenaline.
Vasovagal: Involving the vagus nerve and blood vessels: slowing of the heart plus vessel dilation.
Vasovagal syncope: A faint from a reflex drop in heart rate and BP, with pallor and no rash.
Vastus lateralis: Muscle of the outer thigh, the site for IM adrenaline.
Vegetation: An infected clump of platelets, fibrin and bacteria stuck to a heart valve.
Velcro crackles: Fine, end-inspiratory crackles like pulling apart velcro; typical of pulmonary fibrosis.
Venepuncture: Taking blood from a vein, a classic vasovagal trigger.
Venesection: Therapeutic removal of blood (usually 450 to 500 mL) to remove iron.
Venodilation: Widening of veins, which pools blood and reduces preload.
Venography: Imaging of veins; MR or CT venography shows the cerebral venous sinuses.
Venous eczema: Itchy, scaly skin on the lower legs from chronic venous hypertension, often bilateral.
Venous pooling: Blood collecting in the leg veins on standing, reducing return to the heart.
Venous return: Blood flow back to the heart; raising the legs increases it.
Venous sinus thrombosis: A clot in the brain's draining venous sinuses, which can raise ICP and mimic IIH.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia: Pneumonia arising in a patient on a ventilator, often from Pseudomonas.
Ventricular tachycardia: Fast broad-complex rhythm from the ventricles; can cause collapse or sudden death.
Venturi mask: A mask that delivers a fixed, controlled oxygen percentage.
Verapamil: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows the AV node.
Verbal de-escalation: Calm, non-confrontational talking to reduce agitation without drugs.
Vertebral collapse: Compression fracture of a vertebral body, causing back pain and height loss.
Vertebral wedge fracture: Collapse of the front of a vertebral body, typical of osteoporosis.
Vertical transmission: Passing an infection from mother to baby during pregnancy or birth.
Vertigo: A false sense that you or the room is spinning.
Vesicovaginal fistula: An abnormal opening between bladder and vagina causing constant leakage, often after obstructed labour.
Vestibular neuritis: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve: continuous vertigo for days, hearing normal.
Vestibular rehabilitation: Exercise therapy that helps the brain compensate for vestibular problems.
Vestibular sedatives: Drugs such as prochlorperazine and cinnarizine that dampen vertigo but slow recovery if used long-term.
Vibration sense: Feeling a vibrating 128 Hz tuning fork on a bony point; lost early in neuropathy.
Viral load: Amount of HIV RNA in blood, measured by PCR, showing disease activity.
Viral prodrome: The early flu-like symptoms of a viral infection before the main illness.
Virchow's node: Enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node from abdominal cancer spread.
Virchow's triad: The three causes of thrombosis: venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability.
Visceral adiposity: Fat stored around the abdominal organs, the most metabolically harmful type.
Visceral peritoneum: The peritoneal layer covering the organs; autonomic nerves make its pain dull and poorly localised.
Viscus: A hollow internal organ such as the stomach, duodenum or colon.
Visible haematuria: Blood that can be seen in the urine; also called macroscopic or frank haematuria.
Visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart (6/6 is normal).
Visual field deficit: Loss of part of the field of vision, such as a homonymous hemianopia.
Vitamin D analogue: Topical drug like calcipotriol that reduces keratinocyte proliferation.
Vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment in patches; associated with Addison's.
Vitrectomy: Surgery to remove the vitreous gel, blood or scar tissue.
Vitreous haemorrhage: Bleeding into the vitreous gel, causing floaters or sudden vision loss.
Vmax: Peak velocity of blood through the aortic valve on echo.
Volvulus: Twisting of a segment of bowel around its own mesentery, causing obstruction and possible ischaemia.
Von Graefe's sign: The upper eyelid lags behind the eye when looking down.
Von Hippel-Lindau: Inherited tumour syndrome associated with phaeochromocytoma and renal cancers.
WBRT: Whole-brain radiotherapy: radiation to the entire brain for multiple metastases.
WPW: Wolff-Parkinson-White: an accessory pathway causing delta waves and re-entrant tachycardias.
Waist circumference: Measure of central fat; above 94 cm in men or 80 cm in women means raised CV risk.
Waldenström macroglobulinaemia: A lymphoma producing an IgM paraprotein.
Waldeyer's ring: The ring of lymphoid tissue (adenoids, palatine and lingual tonsils) guarding the throat.
Walking pneumonia: A mild atypical pneumonia, usually Mycoplasma, where the patient feels unwell but stays up and about.
Wallenberg's: Lateral medullary syndrome from a PICA infarct, with crossed sensory loss and Horner's.
Warfarin: A vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant; the only oral anticoagulant for mechanical valves.
Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: Antibodies against red cells active at body temperature; associated with CLL.
Washout: Surgical flushing of an infected joint to remove pus and bacteria.
Watch and wait: Monitoring without treatment until disease causes symptoms; used in early CLL.
Water bottle sign: A large, globular heart shadow on chest X-ray from a big pericardial effusion.
Water hammer pulse: Another name for the collapsing pulse of aortic regurgitation.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal septicaemia, causing acute adrenal failure.
Waterlow: Pressure ulcer risk score: 10 at risk, 15 high risk, 20 very high risk.
Waterlow score: Tool that scores pressure-sore risk, not malnutrition.
Wearing-off: Return of Parkinson's symptoms before the next levodopa dose is due.
Weber: Tuning fork test placed on the forehead to lateralise hearing loss.
Weber's syndrome: Midbrain stroke: ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.
Weber's test: Tuning fork on the forehead; it lateralises to the good ear in sensorineural loss and the bad ear in conductive loss.
Weibel-Palade bodies: Storage granules in endothelial cells that hold von Willebrand factor.
Well-demarcated: With a sharp, clear edge between affected and normal skin.
Wellens syndrome: Rest chest pain with deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3, signalling critical proximal LAD stenosis.
Wells score: A clinical score of DVT probability; 2 or more means DVT likely.
Wenckebach: Mobitz I block: PR lengthens until a beat is dropped.
Wernicke's: Receptive aphasia from a superior temporal gyrus lesion: fluent speech with poor comprehension.
Wernicke's encephalopathy: Acute brain dysfunction from thiamine deficiency: confusion, ataxia and eye movement problems.
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Wernicke's encephalopathy progressing to Korsakoff's permanent memory loss with confabulation.
Wet wrapping: Damp bandages over emollient or steroid to boost absorption in severe childhood eczema.
Wheal: A raised, pale or red, itchy swelling of the skin that fades within 24 hours.
Wheal-and-flare: A raised swelling with surrounding redness, the immediate IgE skin reaction.
Wheeze: Whistling expiratory sound from narrowed lower airways (bronchospasm).
Whipple procedure: Pancreaticoduodenectomy: removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, bile duct and gallbladder.
Whipple's triad: Hypoglycaemic symptoms, a low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is given.
Whole blood PCR: A blood test that detects meningococcal DNA when LP cannot be done.
Whole-brain radiotherapy: Radiation to the whole brain, used for numerous metastases, at a cost to memory and cognition.
Widened mediastinum: A broadened central shadow on chest X-ray, here from a dilated dissected aorta.
Wilson and Jungner: The WHO criteria a disease and test must meet to justify population screening.
Wilson's disease: Autosomal recessive copper overload with liver and neuropsychiatric disease.
Window period: Time after infection when a test can still be negative.
Witnessed apnoeas: Pauses in breathing during sleep seen by a bed partner, often ending in a snort or gasp.
Wolff-Chaikoff effect: Iodine excess temporarily shutting down thyroid hormone synthesis, causing hypothyroidism.
Wound dehiscence: Separation of the edges of a closed surgical wound.
Wound swab: Sample of wound discharge sent for culture and antibiotic sensitivities.
