X-linked recessive: Inheritance via a faulty gene on the X chromosome: males affected, females usually carriers.
Xanthelasma: Soft yellow cholesterol plaques on the eyelids.
Xanthine: Purine breakdown product that can form radiolucent stones.
Xanthine oxidase: Enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid.
Xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from broken-down blood, typical of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Xylometazoline: A decongestant nasal spray; causes rebound congestion if used for more than a week.
Y descent: The fall in the JVP waveform as the tricuspid valve opens; absent in tamponade.
Yersinia: A genus of Gram-negative bacteria; Yersinia enterocolitica is the classic trigger of mesenteric adenitis.
Yersinia enterocolitica: A Gram-negative bacterium spread by contaminated food that can cause mesenteric adenitis and 'pseudoappendicitis'.
Z score: Bone density compared with people of the same age and sex.
Z-thumb: Thumb deformity with flexed MCP and hyperextended IP joint.
Ziehl-Neelsen: A stain that shows acid-fast bacilli as red rods on a blue background.
Zoledronic acid: Yearly intravenous bisphosphonate used by specialists.
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome: Severe peptic ulcers, reflux and diarrhoea from a gastrinoma.
Zona fasciculata: Middle cortical layer that makes cortisol.
Zona glomerulosa: Outer cortical layer that makes aldosterone.
aTIV: Adjuvanted trivalent influenza vaccine, offered to people aged 65 and over.
abdominal angina: Pain after eating caused by gut arteries too narrow to meet digestive demand.
abdomino-perineal resection: Removal of rectum, anal canal and anus, leaving a permanent end colostomy.
achalasia: Failure of the LOS to relax with loss of peristalsis, causing dysphagia to solids and liquids.
acid-fast: Retains stain after acid washing because of a waxy mycolic acid cell wall.
acidosis: A process lowering blood pH below 7.35.
acinar cells: The pancreatic cells that make digestive enzymes.
acoustic neuroma: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve causing hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance.
acromegaly: Excess growth hormone in adults, causing soft tissue and bone overgrowth.
action potential: The electrical cycle of a heart cell; hypercalcaemia shortens it.
action tremor: Tremor during voluntary movement, such as pouring or writing.
activated charcoal: Oral adsorbent that binds drugs in the gut; best within an hour of ingestion.
active rewarming: Adding heat with warmed IV fluids, forced-air blankets or internal methods.
active surveillance: Monitoring low-risk cancer with PSA, MRI and biopsy, treating only if it progresses.
acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden rise in eye pressure causing a red, painful eye, haloes and vomiting.
acute bronchitis: Short-lived, usually viral, inflammation of the bronchi causing cough, without lung consolidation.
acute chest syndrome: Fever, chest pain, hypoxia and a new lung infiltrate in sickle cell disease; a medical emergency.
acute cholangitis: Infection of an obstructed bile duct: fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
acute fatty liver of pregnancy: Third-trimester fat infiltration of the liver causing acute liver failure.
acute mesenteric ischaemia: Sudden loss of bowel blood supply, usually from an embolus or thrombosis.
acute pancreatitis: Sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by its own enzymes being switched on too early.
acute promyelocytic leukaemia: A subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia classically complicated by DIC.
acute urinary retention: Sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a distended bladder.
acute-on-chronic: Sudden decompensation of an already cirrhotic liver after an acute insult.
adenocarcinoma: Cancer arising from glandular epithelium, here of the small bowel.
adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence: Stepwise mutations turning a benign adenomatous polyp into invasive cancer over years.
adenomatous polyp: A benign, pre-malignant growth of colonic glandular tissue.
adenovirus: Virus family; serotypes 40 and 41 cause mild childhood gastroenteritis.
adhesions: Bands of scar tissue inside the abdomen, usually after surgery, that can kink or trap bowel.
adjusted calcium: Total calcium corrected for the albumin level; the value used to make decisions.
adjuvant chemotherapy: Chemotherapy given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence.
adrenal adenoma: Benign tumour of the adrenal cortex; the commonest endogenous cause of Cushing's.
adrenal crisis: Life-threatening cortisol deficiency with shock, vomiting and low sodium.
adrenalectomy: Surgical removal of an adrenal gland.
aerosols: Tiny airborne particles that can carry virus over longer distances than droplets.
affect: The outward expression of emotion seen by the examiner.
afterload: The resistance a ventricle must pump against.
aganglionic: Lacking the nerve cell bodies (ganglia) that let the bowel wall relax.
air leak: Continued escape of air from the lung into the pleural space.
air-bone gap: Difference between air and bone thresholds; a gap means conductive loss.
air-fluid level: A flat line on X-ray where gas sits above fluid inside a cavity.
albumin: Main blood protein; low in malnutrition and malabsorption.
alcoholic hepatitis: Acute inflammation of the liver from heavy drinking, often after a binge.
alcoholic ketoacidosis: Ketoacidosis after heavy drinking and starvation, with a normal or low glucose.
aldosterone: Adrenal hormone that makes the kidney retain sodium and water and lose potassium.
alfacalcidol: Active vitamin D analogue that works without PTH or renal activation.
alfuzosin: An alpha-1 antagonist used like tamsulosin in BPH.
alkalosis: A process raising blood pH above 7.45.
alpha-1 antagonist: Drug that blocks alpha-1 receptors, relaxing smooth muscle; first-line in BPH.
alpha-toxin: Lecithinase made by Clostridium perfringens that destroys cell membranes.
alteplase: A recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve clot.
alveoli: Tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens.
amaurosis fugax: Painless, temporary, curtain-like loss of vision in one eye from retinal artery ischaemia.
aminosalicylates: 5-ASA drugs such as mesalazine and sulfasalazine.
amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for sleep and pain.
amlodipine: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for hypertension; a drug cause of constipation.
ammonia: A toxic by-product of protein breakdown normally cleared by the liver's urea cycle.
amoxicillin: A penicillin antibiotic; causes a rash in EBV infection.
ampicillin: A penicillin antibiotic closely related to amoxicillin.
ampulla of Vater: Where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct open into the duodenum.
amputation: Surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb.
amygdala: Brain region that detects threat and drives fear responses.
amylase: A pancreatic enzyme that digests starch; 3x the upper limit supports pancreatitis.
anabolic steroids: Testosterone-like drugs used in bodybuilding; they raise red cell production.
anaerobes: Bacteria that grow without oxygen, common in the mouth and dental plaque.
anaerobic glycolysis: Breaking down glucose without oxygen, producing lactate.
anal cancer: Usually squamous cell carcinoma of the anus; can mimic a fissure off the midline.
anal fissure: A linear tear in the lining of the anal canal.
anal tone: Resting tightness of the anal sphincter, checked on rectal examination.
anal verge: The outer edge of the anal canal where it meets perianal skin.
anaplastic carcinoma: Rare, very aggressive thyroid cancer in the elderly.
anastomosis: A surgical join between two ends of bowel.
anastomotic leak: Leakage of bowel contents from a surgical join, typically days 5 to 7.
andexanet alfa: Decoy factor Xa protein that reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
androgen deprivation therapy: Treatment that removes or blocks testosterone to slow prostate cancer.
angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery from inside with a balloon, sometimes with a stent.
anhedonia: Loss of interest or pleasure in activities that used to be enjoyable.
anhidrosis: Loss of sweating on one side of the face.
anion gap: (Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl); a raised value means unmeasured acid such as ketones or lactate.
ankle-brachial pressure index: Ratio of ankle to arm systolic blood pressure; low values mean arterial disease.
annulus fibrosus: The tough outer ring of an intervertebral disc.
anoderm: The thin, sensitive skin lining the lower anal canal.
anorectal manometry: A test that measures pressures in the anal sphincters and rectum.
anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder with deliberate restriction of intake and very low body weight.
anosmia: Loss of the sense of smell; a distinctive Covid-19 symptom.
antacids: Alkaline medicines that neutralise stomach acid for quick relief.
anterior axillary line: A vertical line down from the front fold of the armpit.
anterior chamber: Fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.
anterior epistaxis: Bleeding from the front of the nose, usually Little's area; typically mild.
anterior ethmoidal artery: Branch of the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid) supplying the upper anterior nose.
anterior horn cells: Lower motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal cord.
anterior resection: Removal of the upper rectum with anastomosis, often protected by a loop ileostomy.
anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of the front of the nasal cavity with a headlight and speculum.
anterior uveitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body: photophobia, small pupil, ciliary flush.
anterograde amnesia: Inability to form new memories after the brain injury.
anti-GAD: Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase; positive in autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
anti-HBc: Antibody to hepatitis B core antigen; shows natural infection (IgM recent, IgG past or chronic).
anti-HBs: Antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen; means immunity from vaccine or recovery.
anti-HCV: Antibody to hepatitis C; shows exposure but not whether infection is still active.
anti-LKM: Anti-liver/kidney microsomal antibody, the marker of type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.
anti-TNF: Biologic drugs neutralising tumour necrosis factor alpha.
anti-TTG: Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody; blood test for coeliac disease.
anti-VEGF: Drugs injected into the eye that block VEGF, reducing leakage and new vessels.
anti-androgen: Drug that blocks androgen receptors, e.g. bicalutamide, flutamide, cyproterone.
anti-endomysial antibodies: IgA antibodies against the connective tissue around smooth muscle; highly specific for coeliac disease.
anti-factor Xa: Blood test measuring LMWH activity, used when monitoring is needed.
anti-tTG: Antibodies against tissue transglutaminase; IgA anti-tTG is the first-line coeliac test.
anti-tTG IgA: Antibody blood test used to screen for coeliac disease.
anticholinergics: Drugs blocking acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, slowing the gut.
anticoagulant: Drug that reduces the blood's ability to form clots.
anticoagulants: Drugs that reduce clotting, such as warfarin or apixaban.
anticonvulsants: Anti-seizure drugs; some speed up vitamin D breakdown.
antiemetics: Drugs that reduce vomiting, such as ondansetron.
antigenic drift: Gradual point mutations in H and N causing seasonal epidemics and annual vaccine updates.
antigenic shift: Reassortment between strains creating a novel subtype with pandemic potential.
antimicrobial stewardship: Using antibiotics only when needed to limit resistance and side effects.
antimuscarinic: Drug that blocks muscarinic receptors, calming an overactive bladder; can cause retention.
antiphospholipid syndrome: An autoimmune thrombophilia causing venous and arterial clots and miscarriages.
antiplatelet: Drug that stops platelets clumping, reducing arterial clots.
antispasmodic: A drug that relaxes gut smooth muscle to relieve cramps.
antithrombin: A natural anticoagulant protein that heparins enhance.
antithrombin III: Natural anticoagulant protein; heparin boosts its action.
antrum: The lower part of the stomach before the pylorus.
aphasia: Loss of language ability from a brain lesion.
apical node: The highest lymph node at the vascular tie; its involvement makes Duke's C2.
apixaban: DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa.
aplastic crisis: Sudden stop in red cell production, usually from parvovirus B19, with a low reticulocyte count.
appendicitis: Inflammation of the appendix, usually from blockage of its lumen.
appendicular abscess: A pus collection around the appendix, often after perforation, causing swinging fever.
appendix mass: An inflamed appendix walled off by omentum and bowel, felt as a tender RIF lump.
aquagenic pruritus: Itching after contact with water, especially a hot bath; characteristic of PV.
aquaporin-2: Water channel inserted into collecting duct cells by ADH.
aquaporin-4: Water channel on astrocytes; antibodies against it cause neuromyelitis optica.
aquaporins: Water channels inserted into collecting duct cells by ADH.
aqueous humour: Clear fluid that fills the front of the eye.
arabinogalactan: A cell wall polysaccharide in mycobacteria, target of ethambutol.
arachnoid granulations: Protrusions of arachnoid into the venous sinuses where CSF is reabsorbed.
arachnoid mater: The thin middle meningeal layer, beneath the dura.
arcuate fasciculus: White matter tract linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas.
argatroban: A direct thrombin inhibitor used instead of heparin in HIT.
artemisinin: Fast-acting antimalarial drug class from sweet wormwood.
arterial ulcer: A skin ulcer caused by poor arterial blood supply, usually from peripheral arterial disease.
artesunate: Artemisinin drug given IV as first-line treatment for severe falciparum malaria.
arthralgia: Joint pain without swelling or inflammation.
asbestos: Fibrous mineral once used in insulation; causes mesothelioma and raises lung cancer risk.
ascending cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts from obstruction, with fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
aspart: A rapid-acting insulin given with meals.
aspiration: Inhaling blood or fluid into the airway.
aspiration pneumonia: Lung infection from inhaling food, fluid or stomach contents.
aspirin: Antiplatelet that irreversibly blocks COX-1, stopping thromboxane A2 production.
aspirin-sensitive asthma: Asthma worsened by aspirin and NSAIDs, often with nasal polyps.
asterixis: A coarse flapping tremor of outstretched, dorsiflexed hands; sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
astrocytes: Brain support cells that take up ammonia and swell when it accumulates.
ataxia: Lack of coordination, here a broad-based unsteady gait.
atheroma: The fatty plaque inside an artery wall in atherosclerosis.
atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty plaque in artery walls, narrowing them.
atherosclerotic: Describing fatty, fibrous plaques that build up in artery walls and narrow them.
atorvastatin: A statin given at 80mg after ACS to lower cholesterol and stabilise plaques.
atrial fibrillation: An irregularly irregular heart rhythm; a major source of emboli.
atrial septal defect: A hole between the two atria that can allow right-to-left passage of clot.
atrophic gastritis: Chronic inflammation that thins the stomach lining and loses acid-producing glands.
atrophy: Shrinking of an organ, here a testis after ischaemic damage.
atropine: Long-acting cycloplegic and mydriatic eye drop.
atypical cover: Antibiotics, such as a macrolide, that also treat Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Legionella.
atypical lymphocytes: Large reactive CD8+ T cells seen on the blood film in EBV.
atypical organisms: Bacteria such as Mycoplasma and Legionella not covered by penicillins; covered by macrolides.
audiogram: The chart produced by pure tone audiometry.
audiometry: Hearing test plotting the quietest sounds heard at each frequency.
aural fullness: A feeling of pressure or blockage in the ear.
auramine: A fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli; the fastest smear method.
autodigestion: The pancreas being digested by its own activated enzymes.
autoimmune screen: Blood tests for autoantibodies such as RF, anti-CCP, ANA and ANCA.
autologous stem cell transplant: High-dose chemotherapy then return of the patient's own stored stem cells.
autonomic: Symptoms from the sympathetic nervous system: sweating, tremor, palpitations and anxiety.
autonomic dysfunction: Faulty control of automatic functions such as heart rate and blood pressure.
autonomic nervous system: Nerves controlling involuntary functions such as heart rate, blood pressure and sweating.
autonomic neuropathy: Damage to autonomic nerves, which can blunt the warning response to hypoglycaemia.
autosomal dominant: Inheritance where one copy of the gene causes the condition; each child has a 50% risk.
autosomal recessive: Inheritance needing two faulty copies of a gene; two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child.
autosplenectomy: Shrinking and loss of the spleen through repeated infarction in sickle cell disease.
avascular necrosis: Bone death from lost blood supply, often of the femoral head; MRI finds it early.
axillary nerve: Supplies deltoid and skin over the lower lateral deltoid.
axonotmesis: Axon disrupted but its connective tissue sheath intact, so it can regrow.
azathioprine: A thiopurine immunosuppressant used as a steroid-sparing drug.
barium swallow: X-ray after swallowing barium contrast; most sensitive test for hiatus hernia.
basal cisterns: CSF spaces around the base of the brain, where SAH blood collects on CT.
basal ganglia: Deep brain nuclei controlling movement initiation, damaged in Parkinson's disease.
basal plasmacytosis: Plasma cells crowded at the base of the mucosa; a sign of chronic colitis.
basal-bolus: Insulin regimen of a long-acting daily dose plus rapid-acting doses with meals.
bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic that increases salt and water loss.
benzodiazepines: Sedative drugs such as diazepam that enhance GABA; avoided long-term because of dependence.
berry aneurysm: A small saccular outpouching at an arterial bifurcation, usually on the Circle of Willis.
beryllium: Metal whose dust can cause lung disease and raises lung cancer risk.
beta cells: Insulin-producing cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans.
beta-adrenergic: Relating to beta receptors stimulated by adrenaline and noradrenaline.
beta-blockers: Drugs such as propranolol that block adrenaline's effect on the heart and muscles.
beta-hCG: Pregnancy hormone; measured to exclude ectopic pregnancy.
betahistine: Histamine analogue used to reduce the frequency of Ménière's attacks.
bicalutamide: An anti-androgen that blocks androgen receptors.
bicarbonate buffer: The CO2, carbonic acid and bicarbonate system that resists changes in pH.
biconvex: Bulging outwards on both sides, like a lens or lemon.
bilateral cortical innervation: Both hemispheres supply the upper face, so a one-sided cortical lesion spares the forehead.
bilateral infiltrates: Shadowing in both lungs on imaging, typical of Covid-19 pneumonia.
bile acid malabsorption: Unabsorbed bile acids reach the colon and cause watery diarrhoea.
bile acids: Detergent-like molecules from the liver that form micelles to absorb fat.
bile leak: Bile escaping after gallbladder surgery, e.g. from a slipped cystic duct clip.
bile salts: Detergent molecules in bile that keep cholesterol dissolved; reabsorbed in the terminal ileum.
biliary colic: Pain from a stone temporarily blocking the cystic duct, without infection.
biliary stent: A tube placed in the bile duct, usually at ERCP, to relieve obstruction.
bilious vomiting: Green vomit containing bile, suggesting obstruction beyond the ampulla.
biopsy: Taking a tissue sample for histology.
bipolar disorder: Mood disorder with episodes of depression and mania or hypomania.
bisacodyl: Stimulant laxative available as tablets or suppository.
bisoprolol: A cardioselective beta-blocker that slows the heart and lowers oxygen demand after MI.
bisphosphonate: Drug that binds bone and kills osteoclasts, reducing bone resorption.
bisphosphonates: Drugs that inhibit osteoclasts, used for bone metastases (e.g. zoledronic acid).
bitemporal hemianopia: Loss of both outer visual fields, from a chiasm lesion such as a pituitary tumour.
bladder outlet obstruction: Blockage at the bladder neck or urethra that stops the bladder emptying.
blanch: To turn pale when pressed, as normal skin does.
blanching: Whitening of a red area when its vessels constrict or are pressed.
blasts: Immature blood cells; many in the blood suggest acute leukaemia.
bleb: A small air-filled blister under the visceral pleura, usually at the lung apex.
bleomycin: A chemotherapy drug in BEP; can cause lung fibrosis.
bloating: A feeling of abdominal fullness or swelling.
blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to grow bacteria and identify the organism and its sensitivities.
blood-aqueous barrier: Tight junctions in iris and ciliary vessels that keep protein and cells out of the aqueous.
blood-retinal barrier: Tight junctions in retinal vessels that stop fluid and protein leaking into the retina.
board-like: Describes a rigid abdomen with involuntary muscle spasm from peritonitis.
bolus: A set volume of fluid given quickly through a drip.
bone marrow biopsy: Sample of marrow, usually from the pelvis, to count plasma cells.
bone profile: Blood panel of calcium, phosphate, albumin and ALP.
bone resorption: Breakdown of bone by osteoclasts, releasing calcium into the blood.
bone scan: Isotope scan showing areas of high bone turnover, such as metastases.
bony prominence: An area where bone lies close under the skin, such as the sacrum or heel.
boom-bust: Doing too much on good days and then crashing for days afterwards.
bortezomib: A proteasome inhibitor used to treat myeloma.
botulinum toxin: A nerve toxin injected to temporarily paralyse the internal anal sphincter.
brachioradialis reflex: Supinator reflex at the wrist, C5/C6.
brachytherapy: Radiotherapy given by implanting radioactive seeds in the prostate.
bradykinesia: Slowness of movement with decreasing amplitude on repetition.
brain atrophy: Shrinkage of brain tissue with age or alcohol, stretching bridging veins.
brain fog: Difficulty thinking, concentrating and finding words.
bridging veins: Veins crossing from the brain surface to the dural sinuses; tear in subdural haemorrhage.
broad-spectrum antibiotics: Antibiotics that kill a wide range of bacteria, including normal gut flora.
bromocriptine: Older dopamine agonist used for prolactinoma.
bronchi: The large airways branching from the trachea into each lung.
bronchial breath sounds: Harsh, hollow breath sounds with a gap between inspiration and expiration, heard over consolidated lung.
bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds heard over consolidated lung.
bronchoalveolar lavage: Washing a lung segment with saline at bronchoscopy to collect a sample.
bronchodilator: A drug that widens the airways, such as salbutamol.
bronchoscopy: Camera passed into the airways to see and biopsy a tumour; the confirmatory test.
bronchospasm: Narrowing of the airways; a risk of non-selective beta-blockers in asthma.
brush border: Microvilli on enterocytes, carrying digestive enzymes.
bubble echocardiogram: Echo with agitated saline to show right-to-left shunting across a PFO.
bubbling: Air bubbles in the water seal, showing an ongoing air leak.
buccal: Given inside the cheek, absorbed through the lining of the mouth.
buccal mucosa: The lining of the inside of the cheeks.
budesonide: Steroid with high first-pass liver metabolism, used for Crohn's induction.
buffalo hump: Fat pad over the upper back and base of the neck.
bulbar: Relating to the brainstem cranial nerves controlling speech and swallowing.
bulbar injection: Redness of the conjunctiva over the eyeball itself, rather than inside the lids.
bulk-forming: Laxatives that absorb water to increase stool mass, such as ispaghula husk.
bulla: An air space larger than 1 cm within the lung, common in emphysema.
burr hole: A small hole drilled in the skull to drain a clot in an emergency.
burr hole craniostomy: Drilling a small hole in the skull to drain liquefied chronic subdural blood.
bypass: Surgery that routes blood around a blocked artery using a vein or graft.
cAMP: Cyclic AMP: a second messenger that relaxes smooth muscle when raised by beta-2 agonists.
cART: Combination antiretroviral therapy: usually three drugs from at least two classes.
cabergoline: Long-acting dopamine agonist; first-line for prolactinoma.
cachexia: Wasting of muscle and fat from chronic disease such as cancer.
caecum: The first pouch of the large bowel, where the appendix attaches.
calamine lotion: Soothing pink lotion used to ease chickenpox itch.
calcified vessels: Arteries stiffened by calcium, common in diabetes and CKD, giving falsely high ABPI.
calcimimetic: A drug that mimics calcium at its sensing receptor, switching off PTH release.
calcineurin inhibitors: Ciclosporin and tacrolimus; block T-cell activation.
calcitonin: Hormone that rapidly but briefly lowers calcium; used with steroids in severe cases.
calcitriol: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active form; increases gut calcium absorption.
calcium channel blockers: Drugs that block calcium entry into smooth muscle, causing relaxation.
calcium gluconate: IV calcium preparation used for acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia.
calcium-sensing receptor: Receptor on parathyroid cells that detects calcium and reduces PTH when calcium is high.
calf muscle pump: Calf muscles squeezing deep veins during walking to push blood back to the heart.
canalicular: Spread along natural channels such as bile ducts, airways or the urinary tract.
cannonball metastases: Multiple large round lung metastases, classically from renal cell carcinoma.
capillary blood glucose: Finger-prick glucose reading at the bedside.
capillary closing pressure: The external pressure that collapses capillaries and stops blood flow (about 32 mmHg).
capillary leak: Inflamed capillaries letting fluid escape into tissues and body spaces.
capillary refill: Time for colour to return after pressing the skin; over 2 seconds suggests poor perfusion.
capillary refill time: Seconds for skin colour to return after pressing; over 2 to 3 seconds suggests shock.
capsular invasion: Tumour breaking through its capsule; defines follicular carcinoma.
carbon-13 urea breath test: Breath test detecting H. pylori, which splits labelled urea into labelled CO2.
carboplatin: A platinum chemotherapy drug used for seminoma.
carcinoid: Neuroendocrine tumour that can secrete hormones including ACTH.
cardiogenic shock: Low blood pressure and poor organ perfusion because the heart is failing as a pump.
carotid Doppler: Ultrasound measuring carotid narrowing and blood flow.
carotid bruit: A whooshing sound over the carotid from turbulent flow through a stenosis.
carotid endarterectomy: Surgery to remove atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery.
carotid stenosis: Narrowing of the carotid artery, usually by atherosclerosis.
carpal tunnel: Median nerve compression at the wrist, causing tingling in the fingers.
carpal tunnel syndrome: Median nerve compression at the wrist under the flexor retinaculum.
carpopedal spasm: Spasm of the hands and feet, fingers flexed at the knuckles.
caseating necrosis: Cheese-like dead tissue at the centre of a TB granuloma.
cast nephropathy: Tubular blockage by protein casts made of light chains.
catabolic: Breaking down tissue, for example muscle protein.
catabolism: Breaking down body tissues (fat, muscle) for energy.
cataracts: Clouding of the eye's lens; a chronic hypocalcaemia complication.
catheterisation: Passing a tube into the bladder to drain urine.
cauda equina: Bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord.
cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the cauda equina causing saddle anaesthesia, sphincter disturbance and bilateral leg signs.
cautery: Sealing a bleeding vessel with heat or chemicals.
cavernous sinus: Venous channel beside the pituitary containing CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI and the carotid artery.
cavernous sinus thrombosis: Infected clot in the venous sinus beside the pituitary, causing bilateral eye signs and cranial nerve palsies.
cavitating: Forming air-filled holes within lung consolidation.
cavitation: Formation of an air-filled hole in the lung where necrotic tissue has drained away.
cefotaxime: IV third-generation cephalosporin used for orbital cellulitis.
ceftriaxone: A third-generation cephalosporin given IM to treat gonorrhoea.
cefuroxime: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used with metronidazole in penicillin allergy.
cell-mediated immunity: T cell immunity; when it falls, VZV can reactivate.
cells and flare: Slit-lamp signs of inflammatory cells and protein in the anterior chamber.
cellulitis: Bacterial skin infection with fever and spreading, well-demarcated redness.
central obesity: Fat gain around the abdomen and trunk with relatively thin limbs.
central retinal artery: Branch of the ophthalmic artery supplying the inner retina.
central scotoma: A blind or dim spot in the centre of the visual field.
central sulcus: The groove between the two prostate lobes; lost when cancer spreads across the gland.
centrilobular: Around the central vein of the liver lobule (zone 3), where paracetamol damage is worst.
cephalosporins: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as ceftriaxone; a major C. difficile risk.
cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit: Loop from cerebellum through thalamus to motor cortex, thought to generate essential tremor.
cerebral amyloid angiopathy: Amyloid deposits in cortical vessel walls causing lobar haemorrhages in the elderly.
cerebral malaria: Severe falciparum malaria with reduced consciousness, confusion or seizures.
cerebral oedema: Swelling of the brain from excess water, causing drowsiness and seizures.
cervical lymph nodes: Lymph nodes in the neck; often enlarged after a sore throat.
cervical myelopathy: Spinal cord compression in the neck causing UMN signs and sensory loss.
chest drain: A tube inserted into the pleural space, connected to an underwater seal, to let air or fluid out.
chickenpox: Itchy, feverish childhood illness with spots at different stages at once.
chlordiazepoxide: Long-acting benzodiazepine used to manage alcohol withdrawal.
chloroquine: Antimalarial for non-resistant vivax and ovale; falciparum is often resistant.
chlorphenamine: Sedating oral antihistamine used for itch.
chlortalidone: A thiazide-like diuretic that can cause metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia.
cholangiocarcinoma: Cancer of the bile ducts; tumour marker CA 19-9.
cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, usually from a blocked duct; fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from a gallstone blocking the cystic duct.
cholecystostomy: A drain into the gallbladder through the skin, for patients unfit for surgery.
choledocholithiasis: A stone in the common bile duct.
cholelithiasis: The presence of stones in the gallbladder.
cholera: Vibrio cholerae infection causing profuse rice-water diarrhoea; urgently notifiable.
cholestatic: An LFT pattern where ALP and GGT rise most, meaning impaired bile flow.
cholesterol stones: The commonest gallstones, formed when bile carries too much cholesterol.
cholestyramine: Bile acid sequestrant that binds bile acids in the gut.
chorda tympani: Branch of CN VII carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
choriocarcinoma: A germ cell tumour of trophoblast cells that produces very high hCG.
choroid: Vascular layer between the retina and sclera.
chronic cholecystitis: Longstanding low-grade gallbladder inflammation causing flatulent dyspepsia.
chronic fatigue syndrome: Long-term disabling fatigue worsened by exertion, often after a viral illness.
chronic mesenteric ischaemia: Gradual narrowing of gut arteries causing pain after meals and weight loss.
chronic pancreatitis: Long-term pancreatic inflammation destroying exocrine and endocrine tissue.
chronic urinary retention: Slow, painless bladder distension with incomplete emptying.
chronic venous insufficiency: Long-term failure of leg veins to return blood, causing swelling and skin changes.
ciclosporin: Calcineurin inhibitor used IV as rescue in steroid-refractory UC.
ciliary body: Ring of muscle behind the iris that focuses the lens and makes aqueous humour.
ciliary flush: Redness concentrated in a ring around the cornea, typical of intraocular inflammation.
cinacalcet: A calcimimetic drug that activates the calcium-sensing receptor and lowers PTH.
ciprofloxacin: A quinolone antibiotic given as a single dose to close contacts of meningococcal disease.
circumflex: The left circumflex artery, supplying the lateral wall of the left ventricle.
circumstantiality: Speech that takes long detours with unnecessary detail before reaching the point.
cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with regenerative nodules and loss of function.
cisplatin: Platinum chemotherapy drug, used with gemcitabine for stage III/IV NSCLC.
citalopram: An SSRI alternative to sertraline; can be switched directly.
clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic that inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises the INR.
claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking caused by ischaemia, relieved by rest.
claw hand: Hyperextended knuckles with flexed fingers from weak hand intrinsics, typically ulnar.
clindamycin: A broad-spectrum antibiotic strongly associated with C. difficile.
clonal: Arising from one abnormal cell that has multiplied.
clonus: Rhythmic involuntary muscle jerks on stretching, a sign of hyperexcitable reflexes.
clopidogrel: A P2Y12 antiplatelet used with aspirin when bleeding risk is high or the patient is already anticoagulated.
closed settings: Places where people live close together, such as cruise ships, care homes and hospitals.
closed-loop obstruction: A bowel segment blocked at both ends, so pressure builds rapidly inside it.
clostridial myonecrosis: Another name for gas gangrene: muscle death caused by clostridial toxins.
clot retention: Inability to pass urine because blood clots block the urethra.
clubbing: Loss of the nail bed angle and bulbous fingertips; seen in squamous cell lung cancer.
co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; first-line for cholecystitis, avoid in penicillin allergy.
co-codamol: Paracetamol combined with codeine; codeine causes constipation.
co-trimoxazole: A sulfonamide-containing antibiotic linked to pancreatitis.
coagulation: The process of blood clotting through the clotting factor cascade.
coagulation cascade: Chain of clotting factor reactions that makes fibrin; untouched by antiplatelets.
coagulation screen: Blood clotting tests: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and often D-dimer.
cobblestone: Mucosa broken into raised islands by deep fissuring ulcers, typical of Crohn's.
cochlea: Spiral inner ear organ for hearing.
coeliac disease: Autoimmune small bowel disease triggered by gluten, causing villous atrophy and malabsorption.
coffee-ground: Vomit containing altered, dark blood from the upper GI tract.
cogwheel rigidity: Rigidity with superimposed tremor giving a ratchety feel, typical of Parkinson's.
cold nodule: Nodule taking up little isotope; higher malignancy risk.
colecalciferol: Plain vitamin D3; needs liver and kidney activation.
colectomy: Surgical removal of the colon; curative in UC.
collecting duct: Final part of the nephron, where ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed.
colloid nodule: Benign nodule made of colloid-filled follicles.
colonic flora: The normal bacteria of the colon that keep pathogens like C. difficile in check.
colonisation: Carrying an organism without it causing disease.
colonoscopy: Camera examination of the whole colon allowing biopsy and polyp removal.
colovesical fistula: An abnormal connection between the colon and the bladder.
colposcopy: Magnified examination of the cervix, with biopsy of abnormal areas.
columnar epithelium: Tall, column-shaped lining cells, like those of the stomach and intestine.
common bile duct: The duct carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
common peroneal nerve: Branch of the sciatic nerve wrapping round the fibular neck; supplies dorsiflexors and evertors.
common peroneal palsy: Injury to the nerve at the fibular head, giving foot drop with inversion spared.
comorbidity: Another long-term condition the patient has, such as diabetes or heart failure.
compensation: A change in the other system (lungs or kidneys) that pushes pH back towards normal.
complete heart block: No atrial impulses reach the ventricles, causing a slow independent ventricular rhythm; a risk after inferior MI.
compression bandaging: Firm layered bandaging for venous ulcers; unsafe if arterial supply is poor.
compression stockings: Graduated elastic stockings that squeeze the leg to help venous return.
compression ultrasound: Ultrasound where the probe presses on the vein; a vein that will not compress contains clot.
compressive optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from pressure, causing reduced acuity, colour loss and RAPD.
conductive hearing loss: Hearing loss from the outer or middle ear, such as wax or fluid.
confabulation: Unintentionally making up false memories to fill gaps in memory.
confrontation testing: Bedside comparison of the patient's visual field with the examiner's.
congenital rubella syndrome: Fetal damage from first-trimester rubella: deafness, cataracts and heart defects.
congenital varicella syndrome: Fetal damage from first-trimester chickenpox: low birth weight, limb hypoplasia and skin scarring.
conjunctiva: Thin membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelids.
conjunctivitis: Red, watery, inflamed eyes; part of the measles prodrome.
consensual reflex: Constriction of one pupil when light is shone into the other eye.
consolidation: Alveoli filled with fluid or pus, as in pneumonia; gives focal signs and CXR shadowing.
constitutive: Switched on all the time, without needing a signal.
consumptive coagulopathy: Bleeding disorder caused by using up platelets and clotting factors faster than they are made.
contact tracing: Finding and advising everyone who was exposed to a case so they can be tested or protected.
conus medullaris: The tapering end of the spinal cord, around L1/L2.
core temperature: Temperature deep in the body, measured with an oesophageal or other internal probe.
corneal ulceration: A break in the corneal surface that can threaten vision.
coronary angiography: X-ray imaging of the coronary arteries with injected contrast to find blockages, often followed by PCI.
corrective saccade: A quick catch-up eye movement showing the vestibulo-ocular reflex has failed.
corticospinal tract: The main descending UMN pathway from cortex to spinal cord.
corticosteroids: Anti-inflammatory steroid drugs such as prednisolone.
corticotroph: The pituitary cell type that makes ACTH.
cortisol: The main glucocorticoid hormone made by the adrenal cortex; raises glucose and BP.
coryza: Runny, blocked nose from inflammation of the nasal lining.
costochondritis: Inflammation of the rib cartilage causing chest pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall.
cotton wool spots: Fluffy white patches from small retinal infarcts (nerve fibre layer ischaemia).
cough impulse: A palpable expansion of a lump when the patient coughs, typical of a hernia.
counter-regulatory: Hormone responses (adrenaline, glucagon, cortisol) that raise glucose when it falls.
crackles: Clicking sounds on inspiration as fluid-filled small airways and alveoli pop open.
cranial DI: DI from too little ADH made or released by the hypothalamus or pituitary.
craniopharyngioma: Suprasellar tumour, often in children, compressing the chiasm from above.
craniotomy: Surgery removing a piece of skull to reach the brain or a clot.
creatine kinase: Enzyme released from damaged muscle; checked in hyperthermia.
creatinine: Waste product from muscle, filtered by the kidney and used to estimate kidney function.
cremaster: Thin muscle around the spermatic cord that raises the testis.
cremasteric reflex: Stroking the inner thigh makes the testis rise; usually absent in torsion.
crepitations: Another name for crackles heard with the stethoscope.
crepitus: A crackling feeling under the fingers, here from gas in soft tissue.
crescendo: Angina that becomes more frequent, longer or triggered by less effort over days to weeks.
crescendo TIA: Repeated TIAs increasing in frequency, needing emergency admission.
crescendo angina: Angina becoming more frequent or severe over a short period, a form of unstable angina.
crescent-shaped: Curved like a new moon, hugging the brain surface: the subdural CT shape.
critical ischaemia: Blood supply so poor that the limb is threatened, with rest pain or tissue loss.
critical limb ischaemia: Severe PAD with rest pain, ulcers or gangrene, often ABPI below 0.5.
cryoprecipitate: A concentrated blood product rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
crypt abscesses: Neutrophils collecting in colonic crypts; a UC biopsy hallmark.
crypt hyperplasia: Lengthening of intestinal crypts as the lining tries to regenerate.
cryptorchidism: Undescended testis; the main testicular cancer risk factor.
crystalloid: Clear IV fluid such as Hartmann's, Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline.
cyanotic heart disease: Congenital heart defects that mix deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation.
cyclizine: An anticholinergic antiemetic that can precipitate acute urinary retention.
cyclopentolate: Short-acting cycloplegic and mydriatic eye drop.
cyproterone acetate: An anti-androgen used to prevent tumour flare when starting a GnRH agonist.
cystic duct: The duct draining the gallbladder into the common bile duct.
cystic fibrosis: Inherited CFTR defect causing thick secretions and pancreatic insufficiency.
cystography: X-ray of the bladder after filling it with contrast, to show leaks or fistulas.
cystoscopy: Looking inside the bladder with a camera passed up the urethra.
cytoadherence: Falciparum-infected red cells sticking to blood vessel walls.
cytokine storm: An excessive inflammatory response that damages the body's own tissues.
cytology: Looking at cells under a microscope; in cervical screening it is read only if hrHPV is positive.
cytoreduction: Using drugs to lower blood cell counts.
cytoreductive therapy: Drugs that lower blood cell production in the marrow.
cytotoxic T-cells: Immune cells that kill virus-infected cells; they cause most of the liver damage in hepatitis B.
dB HL: Decibels hearing level; thresholds under 20 dB are normal.
dP/dt: The rate of rise of arterial pressure with each heartbeat; lowering it reduces shear on the aortic wall.
dacrocytes: Teardrop-shaped red cells seen in myelofibrosis.
dacryocystitis: Infection of the tear sac, causing a red swelling at the inner corner of the eye.
dactylitis: Painful swelling of the hands and feet from bone infarction, typical in sickle toddlers under 3.
dantrolene: Muscle relaxant used for malignant hyperthermia, not for heat stroke.
dapagliflozin: An SGLT2 inhibitor used with metformin first-line in type 2 diabetes.
dapsone: An antibacterial drug that rapidly controls the itch of dermatitis herpetiformis.
deamidation: Chemical change of glutamine to glutamate that makes gliadin bind HLA-DQ2/DQ8 more strongly.
debridement: Surgical or endoscopic removal of dead tissue.
decompensation: When a cirrhotic liver can no longer cope, causing jaundice, ascites, bleeding or encephalopathy.
decompression: Surgery to remove the structure pressing on nerve roots.
decompressive craniectomy: Removing part of the skull and leaving it off to relieve pressure.
deconditioning: Loss of physical fitness from prolonged inactivity.
decussate: To cross to the other side.
deep brain stimulation: Implanted electrodes stimulating the thalamus to suppress severe tremor.
deep inguinal ring: The internal opening of the inguinal canal, just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.
deep peroneal: Branch of the common peroneal nerve supplying dorsiflexors and the first web space.
defibrillation: An electric shock to stop VF or pulseless VT; less effective in a cold heart.
dehydration: A deficit of body water that reduces circulating volume and disturbs electrolytes.
delayed cerebral ischaemia: Stroke-like deterioration from vasospasm, typically 7 to 14 days after SAH.
delirium tremens: Severe alcohol withdrawal 48 to 72 hours after the last drink with tremor, sweating and hallucinations.
demarcation: The visible line between dead and living tissue.
demyelination: Loss of the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, slowing or blocking conduction.
dendritic ulcer: Branching corneal ulcer of herpes simplex; worsened by steroid drops.
denervation: Loss of nerve supply to muscle fibres.
dengue fever: Mosquito-borne viral fever with a 'white islands in a sea of red' rash.
denosumab: Monoclonal antibody against RANKL; lowers calcium and is safe in renal impairment.
dentate line: The line in the anal canal dividing visceral (painless) above from somatic (painful) below.
dentition: The condition and arrangement of a person's teeth.
dependence: Needing a drug to function normally, with withdrawal symptoms on stopping.
dependent rubor: Redness of the foot when it hangs down, from maximally dilated ischaemic vessels.
depolarisation: The change in membrane charge that fires a nerve or muscle cell.
dermatitis herpetiformis: Intensely itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces, specific to coeliac disease.
dermatomal: Following the distribution of one dermatome.
dermatome: The area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.
dermis: The layer of skin beneath the epidermis, containing vessels and collagen.
desmoplastic stroma: Dense fibrous tissue that surrounds pancreatic tumour cells.
desmopressin: Synthetic ADH analogue that acts on V2 receptors; treats cranial DI.
detrusor: The smooth muscle of the bladder wall that contracts to empty it.
dexamethasone: Corticosteroid given at 6 mg daily to Covid-19 patients needing oxygen.
dexamethasone suppression test: Gives dexamethasone then measures cortisol; failure to suppress suggests Cushing's.
dextrose: Another name for glucose in IV fluids.
diabetes insipidus: Lack of, or resistance to, ADH, causing large volumes of dilute urine.
diabetic retinopathy: Damage to retinal vessels from diabetes, screened annually.
diagnosis of exclusion: A diagnosis made only once other likely causes have been ruled out.
diaphragmatic crura: Muscle bands of the diaphragm that encircle the hiatus and squeeze the LOS.
diaphragmatic hernia: Abdominal contents pass into the chest through a diaphragm defect; in neonates causes respiratory distress.
diclofenac: An NSAID; first-line analgesia for biliary colic.
dietary recall: Patient's report of everything eaten and drunk over a set period.
diffuse type: Gastric cancer of signet ring cells that infiltrates the wall without a discrete mass.
diffusion-weighted imaging: MRI sequence that detects acute ischaemia within minutes.
digital retinal photography: Photographs of the retina used in annual diabetic eye screening.
diltiazem: A calcium channel blocker used topically to relax the anal sphincter.
direct antiglobulin test: Coombs test: detects antibodies on red cells in autoimmune haemolysis.
direct inguinal hernia: Pushes straight through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
disaccharidase: Brush border enzyme splitting sugars such as lactose.
disc herniation: Another name for a disc prolapse.
disc prolapse: Herniation of the soft disc centre through its outer ring, which can press on a nerve root.
disconnection hyperprolactinaemia: Raised prolactin because a mass compresses the stalk and blocks dopamine.
disseminated intravascular coagulation: Widespread activation of clotting in small vessels, consuming platelets and clotting factors and causing bleeding.
distributive shock: Shock from widespread vasodilation, so blood pools in the periphery.
diurnal variation: The normal daily rhythm of cortisol: high in the morning, lowest at midnight.
diverticula: Small outpouchings of the bowel wall, usually in the sigmoid colon.
diverticular disease: Diverticula that cause symptoms such as pain, bloating or bowel habit change.
diverticulitis: Inflammation or infection of one or more diverticula, with fever and raised inflammatory markers.
diverticulosis: Diverticula are present but cause no symptoms.
diverticulum: A single outpouching of the bowel wall.
docusate sodium: Stool softener and weak stimulant, used for opioid-induced constipation.
dopamine agonist: Drug that mimics dopamine, suppressing prolactin and shrinking prolactinomas.
dorsal root ganglia: Clusters of sensory nerve cell bodies beside the spinal cord where VZV lies latent.
dorsiflexion: Lifting the foot upwards at the ankle (L4/L5).
dot-blot haemorrhages: Small round bleeds within the deeper layers of the retina.
double duct sign: Dilation of both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct on imaging.
double hump: Barium appearance of two gas-filled bulges, stomach above and below the diaphragm.
downstage: Reduce a tumour's stage, usually with neoadjuvant therapy.
doxycycline: Tetracycline antibiotic; first-line for acute bronchitis when antibiotics are indicated.
drip and suck: Conservative obstruction care: IV fluids (drip) and NG tube drainage (suck), nil by mouth.
drug-eluting stent: A metal coronary stent coated with a drug that slows tissue regrowth, reducing re-narrowing.
dry gangrene: Ischaemic tissue death without infection: dry, black, painless and clearly demarcated.
dry tap: A bone marrow aspiration that yields no fluid because the marrow is fibrosed.
dual antiplatelet: Two antiplatelets together (e.g. aspirin plus clopidogrel) for a short time in high-risk patients.
duloxetine: SNRI antidepressant, an alternative second-line drug in GAD.
dumping syndrome: Symptoms after eating post-gastrectomy as food rushes into the small bowel.
duodenal biopsy: Tissue sample from the duodenum at endoscopy; gold standard for coeliac.
duodenal ulcer: Ulcer in the first part of the duodenum; pain eased by eating.
duplex ultrasound: Ultrasound combining an image of the vein with Doppler flow measurement.
dura: The tough outer membrane covering the brain.
dura mater: The tough outer membrane covering the brain, stuck to the skull at the sutures.
dural venous sinuses: Venous channels within the dura that drain blood from the brain.
dysdiadochokinesia: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements, a cerebellar sign.
dyskaryosis: Abnormal-looking cervical cells on cytology, graded low or high.
dyspepsia: Indigestion: upper abdominal burning or discomfort, often after meals.
dysplasia: Disordered, abnormal cell growth that can progress to cancer.
dysuria: Pain or burning on passing urine.
eGFR: Estimated glomerular filtration rate, calculated from creatinine, age and sex; used to stage CKD.
early morning waking: Waking two or more hours earlier than usual and being unable to get back to sleep.
early satiety: Feeling full after eating only a small amount.
ectopic ACTH: ACTH made by a tumour outside the pituitary, usually small cell lung cancer or carcinoid.
ectopic pregnancy: A pregnancy outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube.
ejection fraction: The percentage of blood the left ventricle pumps out per beat; below 40% means significant systolic dysfunction.
embolectomy: Surgical removal of an embolus from an artery.
embolise: When a clot breaks off and travels in the blood to block a vessel elsewhere.
embolus: A clot or other material carried in the blood that blocks a distant artery.
embryonal carcinoma: An aggressive non-seminomatous germ cell tumour.
emollient: A moisturiser that softens and protects dry skin.
empagliflozin: An SGLT-2 inhibitor used in type 2 diabetes and heart failure.
empyema: A collection of pus within a body cavity, here the gallbladder.
encapsulated organisms: Bacteria with a sugar capsule, such as pneumococcus, normally cleared by the spleen.
end colostomy: The cut end of the colon brought out on the abdomen as a stoma.
end-expiratory: Occurring at the end of breathing out.
endolymph: Potassium-rich fluid filling the membranous labyrinth of the cochlea and vestibular system.
endolymphatic hydrops: Excess endolymph fluid inside the inner ear membranes, raising pressure on the hair cells.
endolymphatic sac: Pouch draining the inner ear where endolymph is resorbed.
endoneurium: Connective tissue around each nerve fibre that guides regrowth.
endoscopic stent: A metal mesh tube placed across a tumour to keep the oesophagus open.
endoscopic ultrasound: Ultrasound from inside the gut, allowing pancreatic biopsy.
endoscopy: Camera test of the gut; for a GI bleed it finds and treats the bleeding point.
endothermal ablation: Closing a leaky vein from inside using heat from a laser or radiofrequency.
endovascular coiling: Filling the aneurysm with platinum coils via a catheter to seal it off.
endovenous ablation: Closing a refluxing vein from inside using laser or radiofrequency heat.
enema: Fluid given into the rectum to soften and clear stool.
energy management: Planning activity and rest to stay within the energy available.
enhanced physiological tremor: Exaggerated normal tremor from caffeine, anxiety, thyroid disease or drugs such as salbutamol.
entecavir: A nucleoside analogue antiviral used for chronic hepatitis B.
enteral feeding: Feeding liquid nutrition directly into the gut through a tube.
enteral nutrition: Feeding into the gut, by mouth or tube, rather than into a vein.
enteric: Relating to the intestine, as in gut bacteria.
enteric nervous system: The gut's own nerve network controlling motility and secretion.
enterocytes: Absorptive cells lining the small intestine.
enterotomy: A surgical cut into the bowel, used to remove a stone.
enterotoxin: A toxin that acts on the intestine to cause secretion, vomiting or diarrhoea.
enveloped: A virus wrapped in a lipid membrane taken from the host cell.
enzyme inducer: A drug that speeds up liver metabolism of other drugs, lowering their levels.
epidermis: The outer layer of the skin.
epididymal cyst: A benign fluid-filled swelling in the epididymis, separate from the testis.
epididymis: The coiled tube behind the testis that stores and carries sperm.
epididymitis: Inflammation of the epididymis, usually from infection.
epididymo-orchitis: Infection and inflammation of both the epididymis and the testis.
epidural: Local anaesthetic infusion around the spinal cord; speeds bowel recovery after surgery.
epidural steroid injection: Steroid injected near the nerve root to reduce inflammation.
epigastric: The upper central abdomen, just below the sternum.
epigastric hernia: A hernia through the linea alba above the umbilicus.
epiphyseal fusion: Closure of the growth plates at the end of growth.
episclera: The thin, nerve-rich vascular layer between the conjunctiva and the sclera.
episcleritis: Mild, often painless redness of the eye surface; tracks IBD activity.
eplerenone: An aldosterone antagonist added after MI when ejection fraction is below 40%.
erect chest X-ray: Chest X-ray taken with the patient upright, so free gas rises under the diaphragm.
erysipelas: A superficial skin infection with a sharply demarcated, raised red edge.
erythema: Redness of the skin from increased blood flow.
erythema infectiosum: Fifth disease: parvovirus B19 infection with slapped cheeks then a lacy rash.
erythema nodosum: Tender red nodules on the shins from inflamed fat.
erythrocytosis: An increase in red blood cells.
erythrogenic exotoxin: Streptococcal toxin that causes the scarlet fever rash.
erythroid progenitor cells: Bone marrow cells that mature into red blood cells.
erythromelalgia: Burning pain and redness of the hands and feet from dysfunctional platelets.
erythropoietin: A kidney hormone that drives red cell production; low in PV, raised in secondary polycythaemia.
eschar: Thick, dry, black dead tissue covering a wound.
escitalopram: An SSRI closely related to citalopram.
essential thrombocythaemia: An MPN with a persistently raised platelet count causing clots and bleeding.
essential tremor: A benign, often inherited postural and action tremor without parkinsonian features.
ethambutol: TB drug that can cause optic neuropathy; acuity and colour vision need monitoring.
ethmoid sinus: Sinus between the eyes, separated from the orbit by a very thin bone wall.
ethylene glycol: Toxic alcohol in antifreeze; causes raised anion gap acidosis and kidney injury.
eversion: Turning the sole of the foot outwards (superficial peroneal nerve).
exanthem: A widespread skin rash that comes with a systemic, usually viral, infection.
exchange transfusion: Removing the patient's blood while replacing it with donor blood; second-line in select severe cases.
excitotoxicity: Nerve cell damage from excessive stimulation by glutamate.
exogenous: Coming from outside the body, such as prescribed steroid tablets.
exophthalmos: Protrusion of the eye; often used for thyroid eye disease.
exotoxins: Toxins released by bacteria that damage tissue and cause shock.
exposure keratopathy: Damage to the cornea from drying when the eye does not close.
external haemorrhoids: Haemorrhoids below the dentate line; painful, especially if thrombosed.
extra-articular: Affecting organs outside the joints in an arthritis such as RA.
extra-axial: Outside the brain tissue itself, such as extradural or subdural.
extradural: Between the skull and the dura; bleeds are usually from the middle meningeal artery.
extradural haemorrhage: Bleeding between the skull and the dura, usually from the middle meningeal artery.
extramedullary haematopoiesis: Blood cell production outside the marrow, in the liver and spleen.
extraocular muscles: The six muscles that move the eye.
extravasated: Leaked out of a blood vessel into the surrounding tissue.
extravasation: Tumour cells leaving a vessel to enter tissue at a distant site.
extrinsic pathway: Clotting pathway triggered by tissue factor from damaged tissue.
exudate: White or yellow material on inflamed tonsils.
eye-opener: An alcoholic drink first thing in the morning to steady nerves or ease withdrawal.
facial canal: The narrow bony tunnel in the temporal bone through which the facial nerve runs.
facial nerve: Cranial nerve VII; supplies the muscles of facial expression.
factor VII: The clotting factor with the shortest half-life, so it falls first in liver failure.
factor Xa: Activated factor X, the clotting factor that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
faecal calprotectin: A stool test for bowel inflammation; raised in inflammatory bowel disease.
faecal elastase: Pancreatic enzyme measured in stool; low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
faecal fat: Measure of fat in stool, confirming steatorrhoea.
faecal impaction: A large, hard mass of stool stuck in the rectum or colon that cannot be passed.
faecal-oral: Spread by swallowing traces of infected faeces, usually on hands.
faeco-oral: Spread when traces of faeces reach the mouth via hands, food or water.
faecolith: A hard lump of stool that can block the appendix lumen.
false negative: A negative test in someone who has the disease.
false positive: A positive test in someone without the disease.
famciclovir: An alternative oral antiviral for shingles.
famotidine: H2 receptor antagonist added for persistent, often night-time, reflux.
fascia: Sheets of connective tissue that wrap muscles; infection spreads quickly along them.
fasciculations: Visible, irregular twitches of small groups of muscle fibres from denervation.
fat necrosis: Death of fat tissue as lipase digests it, releasing fatty acids.
fat stranding: Hazy streaks in the fat on CT, showing inflammation next to the bowel.
fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E and K, absorbed with fat.
febrile convulsions: Seizures triggered by fever in young children.
femoral canal: A small, narrow, rigid space medial to the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament.
femoral hernia: A hernia through the femoral canal, below the inguinal ligament and inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
ferritin: Blood marker of iron stores; low in iron deficiency.
fibrin: Protein strands that form the mesh of a clot.
fibrinogen: Clotting protein converted to fibrin to form clots; low in DIC.
fibrinolysis: Clot-dissolving drug treatment for STEMI when PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes.
fibromyalgia: Chronic widespread pain with tender points; pain rather than PEM dominates.
fibrosis: Scar tissue laid down after repeated injury.
fidaxomicin: A narrow-spectrum oral antibiotic for C. difficile, used second-line or for recurrence.
finasteride: A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that shrinks the prostate over about 6 months.
finger drop: Inability to extend the fingers with the wrist spared, from posterior interosseous nerve injury.
first-void urine: The first part of the urine stream, which carries urethral organisms for NAAT.
fissure in ano: Another name for an anal fissure.
fistula: An abnormal connection between two hollow organs or an organ and the skin.
fistula in ano: An abnormal track between the anal canal and perianal skin.
five F's: Gallstone risk factors: female, forty, fat, fertile and family history.
fixed-rate insulin: IV insulin at a set dose per kg per hour; 0.05 units/kg/hour in HHS.
flatulent dyspepsia: Bloating, belching and discomfort after fatty food.
flatus: Gas passed from the bowel; absence suggests obstruction.
flatus tube: A soft tube passed into the rectum to let gas out of a distended large bowel.
flexible sigmoidoscopy: Camera examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
flexor retinaculum: Fibrous band forming the roof of the carpal tunnel; divided in surgery.
flucloxacillin: Narrow-spectrum penicillin active against Staphylococcus aureus.
fluctuating consciousness: Conscious level that varies over hours to days, classic of subdural haemorrhage.
fluoxetine: An SSRI with a long half-life, so switching away needs a gap.
flurbiprofen: An oral NSAID used at 100 mg three times daily for mild scleritis.
flutamide: An anti-androgen used to cover the goserelin flare.
foam dressing: An absorbent padded dressing that cushions and manages exudate.
foam sclerotherapy: Injecting a foam that irritates and scars a vein shut, guided by ultrasound.
focal cerebral ischaemia: Reduced blood supply to one area of the brain.
focal signs: Chest signs in one area, such as crackles, dullness or bronchial breathing, suggesting consolidation.
folate: B vitamin needed to make red cells.
follicular adenoma: Benign tumour of thyroid follicular cells; looks like carcinoma on FNA.
follicular carcinoma: Second commonest thyroid cancer; spreads through blood to bone and lung.
fomepizole: Antidote for ethylene glycol and methanol; blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.
fondaparinux: An injectable factor Xa inhibitor used as anticoagulation in ACS and alongside fibrinolysis.
food fortification: Adding extra energy and protein to normal food, e.g. cream, butter, milk powder.
food poisoning: Gut infection from contaminated food, e.g. Campylobacter or Salmonella; routinely notifiable.
food-first: Improving intake with normal and fortified food before adding supplements.
foot drop: Inability to dorsiflex the ankle, giving a high-stepping gait.
forced-air warming: A blanket that blows warm air over the patient.
forehead sparing: Preserved forehead movement despite lower-face weakness; a sign of an UMN (central) lesion.
four-layer compression bandage: Graduated multilayer bandage system that applies sustained pressure to heal venous ulcers.
fovea: Pit at the centre of the macula with the sharpest vision.
free fluid: Fluid seen in the abdomen on imaging; a small amount can be normal or reactive.
free light chains: Kappa or lambda antibody fragments measured in blood; the ratio becomes abnormal in myeloma.
fresh frozen plasma: Plasma frozen soon after donation, containing all clotting factors.
friction: Rubbing of skin against a surface, damaging the outer layers.
frontotemporal dementia: Dementia with early behaviour, personality or language change, linked to MND.
full thickness: Skin loss through the whole dermis into the tissue beneath.
full-thickness: Through every layer of the bowel wall, so contents can leak out.
fulminant: Sudden and severe, as in rapid-onset liver failure.
functional: Symptoms from abnormal gut function with no structural or biochemical disease.
functional asplenia: A spleen that is present but no longer works, after repeated infarction.
fundoplication: Surgery wrapping the gastric fundus around the lower oesophagus to stop reflux.
fundoscopy: Examination of the back of the eye with an ophthalmoscope.
fundus: The dome-shaped top part of the stomach.
furosemide: A loop diuretic added to spironolactone for ascites.
gabapentin: Anticonvulsant sometimes used for essential tremor.
gaiter area: The lower leg between the ankle and mid-calf, where venous ulcers form.
gaiter region: The lower leg between the ankle and mid-calf, where a gaiter would sit.
galactorrhoea: Milky nipple discharge not related to breastfeeding.
gallstone ileus: Small bowel obstruction by a gallstone that passed through a fistula into the gut.
gallstones: Hard deposits of cholesterol or pigment formed in the gallbladder.
gamma-carboxylation: Vitamin K-dependent change that makes clotting factors II, VII, IX and X work.
gamma-herpesvirus: A herpesvirus subfamily that infects lymphocytes and stays latent for life.
ganglion cells: Enteric nerve cell bodies that coordinate bowel movement.
gangliosides: Glycolipids on nerve cell membranes and myelin, targeted in Guillain-Barré syndrome.
gangrene: Death of body tissue from loss of blood supply, sometimes with infection.
gas gangrene: Life-threatening muscle infection by Clostridium perfringens producing gas in tissues.
gastrectomy: Surgical removal of all or part of the stomach.
gastric aspirate: Stomach fluid aspirated in the morning to find swallowed TB bacilli, used in young children.
gastric outlet obstruction: Blockage at the pylorus causing vomiting of undigested food.
gastric ulcer: Ulcer in the stomach; pain worsened by eating and more often malignant.
gastric volvulus: Twisting of the stomach, causing obstruction and ischaemia; a surgical emergency.
gastrinoma: A gastrin-secreting tumour, usually pancreatic or duodenal, causing excess acid.
gastritis: Inflammation of the stomach lining without ulceration.
gastroduodenal artery: Branch of the common hepatic artery behind the first part of the duodenum.
gastroenteritis: Infection of the gut causing diarrhoea and vomiting.
gastrografin: Water-soluble contrast used to look for leaks.
gastroparesis: Delayed stomach emptying from autonomic nerve damage, causing vomiting and early satiety.
gemcitabine: Nucleoside analogue chemotherapy drug, paired with cisplatin for advanced NSCLC.
generalised anxiety disorder: Chronic excessive worry about many everyday areas causing distress or impairment, lasting at least 6 months.
genitofemoral nerve: L1 to L2 nerve whose branches carry both limbs of the cremasteric reflex.
gentamicin: An IV aminoglycoside antibiotic covering Gram-negative bacteria.
germ cell tumour: A tumour arising from sperm-forming cells; most testicular cancers.
germinal epithelium: The sperm-producing lining of the seminiferous tubules.
giardiasis: Infection with Giardia lamblia, causing greasy diarrhoea and bloating after drinking untreated water.
glandular fever: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus; a classic trigger of CFS.
glaucoma: Optic nerve damage, usually from raised intraocular pressure.
gliadin: The part of gluten that the immune system reacts to in coeliac disease.
gliclazide: A sulfonylurea; main risk is hypoglycaemia.
globe rupture: A full-thickness break in the wall of the eyeball.
glove-and-stocking: Sensory loss starting in the feet and hands, the longest nerves first.
glucagon: Hormone that releases glucose from liver glycogen; given IM when there is no IV access.
glucocorticoid: Steroid hormone like cortisol that affects glucose, protein, fat and immunity.
gluconeogenesis: Making new glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, mainly in the liver.
glutamate: The main excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.
glutathione: A liver antioxidant that neutralises NAPQI.
gluten: Protein in wheat, barley and rye that triggers coeliac disease.
gluten challenge: Eating gluten daily for at least 6 weeks so that tests can be interpreted.
glyceryl trinitrate: A nitric oxide donor used as 0.2% ointment for chronic fissures.
goblet cells: Mucus-secreting cells in the gut lining; lost in UC.
goserelin: A GnRH agonist implant used for advanced prostate cancer.
gout: Painful joint inflammation from urate crystals; urate rises with high cell turnover.
graded exercise therapy: Fixed, increasing exercise programme; NICE now advises against it in ME/CFS.
granuloma: A cluster of activated macrophages and lymphocytes that walls off an organism.
great saphenous vein: The long superficial vein running up the inner leg into the femoral vein.
greater palatine artery: Maxillary artery branch reaching the anterior septum through the incisive canal.
greater trochanter: The bony bump on the outer upper thigh at the hip.
ground-glass: Hazy lung shadowing on imaging through which vessels are still visible.
group and save: Blood group and antibody screen so blood can be issued quickly.
guarding: Involuntary tensing of the abdominal muscles when pressed, a sign of peritonism.
guided self-help: Low-intensity therapy using structured CBT materials with brief practitioner support.
gut-brain axis: Two-way signalling between the gut and the brain via nerves, hormones and immune signals.
gut-directed hypnotherapy: Hypnotherapy focused on reducing gut symptoms.
hCG: Human chorionic gonadotrophin; raised in some testicular tumours.
haemagglutinin: Influenza surface protein that binds sialic acid to let the virus enter cells.
haematemesis: Vomiting blood, fresh red or coffee-ground.
haematocrit: The proportion of blood volume made up of red cells; rises when the blood is concentrated.
haematoma: Collection of blood; in the neck after surgery it can compress the airway.
haematopoietic stem cell: A marrow cell that gives rise to all the blood cell lines.
haemochromatosis: Inherited iron overload that can cause cirrhosis.
haemodynamic instability: Low blood pressure or high pulse showing the circulation is failing.
haemoglobin electrophoresis: Separates haemoglobin types by charge; gold-standard test that detects HbS.
haemoglobinopathy: An inherited disorder of the structure or amount of haemoglobin, such as sickle cell disease or thalassaemia.
haemolysis: Breakdown of red blood cells, releasing bilirubin.
haemolysis screen: Tests for red cell breakdown: bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocytes and blood film.
haemorrhagic transformation: Bleeding into infarcted tissue, especially after reperfusion.
haemorrhoidectomy: Surgical excision of haemorrhoids; definitive for severe grade 3 or 4.
haemorrhoids: Swollen anal vascular cushions; typically cause painless bright red bleeding.
haemosiderin: Iron pigment from broken-down red cells that stains the skin brown in venous disease.
hair cells: Sensory cells in the cochlea and vestibular organs that convert movement into nerve signals.
half-life: Time for a drug's blood level to fall by half.
hamartomatous: Made of a disorganised overgrowth of normal tissue, not true neoplasia.
hand hygiene: Hand washing to stop spread; soap and water for norovirus.
hand, foot and mouth: Coxsackie A16 infection with vesicles on palms, soles and mouth.
haptoglobin: Protein that binds free haemoglobin; falls in haemolysis.
hard exudates: Yellow lipid deposits leaked from damaged retinal vessels.
haustra: Pouches of the colon wall; on X-ray their folds cross only part of the bowel width.
head impulse test: Rapid head turn while the patient fixes on your nose; a catch-up saccade shows a peripheral vestibular lesion.
head of the pancreas: The part of the pancreas in the curve of the duodenum, next to the bile duct.
health protection team: The local UKHSA team that receives notifications and manages outbreaks and contacts.
heartburn: Burning pain behind the breastbone caused by acid in the oesophagus.
heat exhaustion: Milder heat illness below 40°C with a normal mental state and sweating.
heat stroke: Core temperature above 40°C with CNS dysfunction, often with hot dry skin and no sweating.
hemianopia: Loss of half of the visual field.
heparin: Injectable anticoagulant that activates antithrombin III.
hepatic encephalopathy: Confusion and reduced consciousness caused by toxins the failing liver cannot clear.
hepatic glucose output: Glucose released by the liver from glycogen and gluconeogenesis.
hepatic stellate cells: Liver cells that, when activated by inflammation, produce collagen and cause fibrosis.
hepatitic: An LFT pattern where transaminases (ALT/AST) rise far more than ALP, meaning liver cell injury.
hepatitis B: A blood-borne viral liver infection; routinely notifiable.
hepatocellular: Relating to liver cells; a hepatocellular LFT pattern means ALT-dominant injury.
hepatocellular carcinoma: Primary liver cancer arising from hepatocytes.
hernia: Protrusion of a structure, usually bowel or fat, through a weakness in the wall that normally contains it.
herniation: Brain tissue forced from one compartment to another by high pressure; often fatal.
herniotomy: Operation that removes the hernial sac alone; the standard repair in children.
herpes zoster: Shingles, reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in a sensory nerve.
hesitancy: Delay before the urine stream starts.
heterophile antibodies: Non-specific antibodies that agglutinate horse or sheep red cells; detected by the monospot.
hexanucleotide repeat: A six-base DNA sequence repeated many times, as in C9orf72.
hiatus hernia: Part of the stomach pushed up through the diaphragm's oesophageal opening.
high-attenuating: Appearing bright on CT, as fresh blood does.
high-intensity psychological therapy: Individual therapy with a trained therapist, usually 12 to 15 sessions of CBT.
high-intensity statin: Statin at a dose that cuts LDL by over 40%, e.g. atorvastatin 80 mg.
high-riding: Testis sitting higher in the scrotum than the other side because the twisted cord is shorter.
high-stepping gait: Lifting the knee high to clear a dropped foot.
histamine: A chemical released by mast cells and basophils that causes itching.
histology: Examination of tissue under a microscope.
hoarseness: A rough or strained voice, here from acid irritating the larynx.
homonymous hemianopia: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, from a lesion behind the optic chiasm.
horizontal lie: Testis lying sideways rather than vertically, typical of Bell-Clapper anatomy.
hot nodule: Nodule taking up more isotope than the rest of the gland; usually benign and overactive.
hrHPV: High-risk human papillomavirus types (such as 16 and 18) that can cause cervical cancer.
hs-Troponin: High-sensitivity troponin assay, repeated after a few hours to look for a rise.
hs-troponin: High-sensitivity troponin assay that detects very small rises, so serial samples hours apart can confirm or exclude MI.
hyaluronidase: A bacterial enzyme that breaks down connective tissue so infection spreads.
hydrocele: Fluid around the testis giving a soft swelling that transilluminates.
hydrocephalus: Build-up of CSF with enlarged ventricles from blocked flow or absorption.
hydrocolloid: A moist, gel-forming dressing used for shallow uninfected wounds.
hydrocortisone: Synthetic cortisol, used for replacement and in adrenal crisis.
hydronephrosis: Swelling of the kidney's collecting system from back-pressure of urine.
hydroxyapatite: The calcium phosphate mineral that makes bone hard.
hydroxycarbamide: An oral cytoreductive drug that suppresses blood cell production by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase.
hyper-resonant: A hollow, drum-like percussion note over air, as in pneumothorax.
hyperacusis: Ordinary sounds feel abnormally or painfully loud.
hypercalcaemia: Raised blood calcium; causes constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion.
hypercalcaemia of malignancy: High calcium from cancer, via bone destruction or PTHrP.
hypercalcaemic crisis: Severe, symptomatic hypercalcaemia with dehydration, confusion, vomiting and arrhythmia risk.
hyperchloraemic: With a raised blood chloride, typical of normal anion gap acidosis.
hypercoagulable: More prone than normal to forming blood clots.
hyperdense: Brighter than brain on CT; fresh blood is hyperdense.
hyperemesis gravidarum: Severe, persistent vomiting in pregnancy causing dehydration, weight loss or electrolyte problems.
hyperosmolality: Abnormally concentrated blood, which pulls water out of cells.
hyperphosphataemia: A high blood phosphate; in hypoparathyroidism the kidney cannot excrete it.
hyperplasia: Enlargement of all the glands from too many cells; seen in MEN1 and secondary disease.
hyperresponsiveness: Airways that narrow too easily in response to triggers.
hyperthermia: Raised core temperature caused by failure of thermoregulation, not a raised set-point.
hyperthyroidism: Overactive thyroid causing tremor, sweating, weight loss and palpitations; the key GAD mimic.
hypertonic: Having a higher solute concentration than plasma.
hypertonic saline: Concentrated saline used to reduce cerebral oedema.
hypertriglyceridaemia: Very high blood triglycerides; a recognised cause of pancreatitis.
hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy: Clubbing with painful new bone formation at the wrists and shins, linked to squamous cell.
hyperuricaemia: High blood uric acid, which can cause gout.
hyperventilation: Breathing more than needed, which lowers CO2 and raises pH.
hyperviscosity: Thickened blood that flows sluggishly and clots more easily.
hypnozoites: Dormant liver stages of vivax and ovale that can reactivate months later.
hypoalbuminaemia: Low blood albumin, lowering oncotic pressure and causing oedema.
hypocalcaemia: A low blood calcium, below about 2.2 mmol/L.
hypochloraemic: With a low blood chloride, typical of vomiting.
hypodense: Darker than brain on CT, as with a chronic, liquefied subdural.
hypoechoic: Darker than surrounding tissue on ultrasound; a suspicious feature.
hypoglycaemia: Blood glucose below 4.0 mmol/L causing autonomic and neuroglycopenic symptoms.
hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis: Low potassium with high blood bicarbonate, caused here by mineralocorticoid action.
hypomagnesaemia: A low blood magnesium; it blocks PTH release and action.
hypomania: A milder form of mania without psychosis or severe impairment.
hyponatraemia: Low blood sodium; with small cell lung cancer think SIADH.
hypophosphataemia: A low blood phosphate; in primary hyperparathyroidism it is from urinary phosphate loss.
hypopituitarism: Deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.
hyposplenism: Reduced spleen function, raising the risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria.
hypotension: Low blood pressure, usually systolic below 90 mmHg.
hypothalamus: Brain region that makes ADH and senses plasma osmolality.
hypothenar: The muscle bulge at the base of the little finger.
hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid, causing tiredness, weight gain and cold intolerance; a CFS mimic.
hypotonic: Having a lower solute concentration than plasma.
hypoventilation: Breathing too little, which raises CO2 and lowers pH.
hypovolaemic shock: Circulatory failure from too little circulating volume to perfuse the organs.
hypoxia: Low oxygen levels in the blood or tissues.
iMAP: International Milk Allergy in Primary care guideline for diagnosing and managing milk allergy in infants.
iatrogenic: Caused by medical treatment or a procedure.
ileal pouch: A reservoir made from ileum joined to the anus after proctocolectomy.
