ileocaecal: Where the end of the small bowel joins the caecum; the usual site of GI TB.
ileostomy: Opening of the ileum onto the abdominal wall.
ileum: The last part of the small bowel, ending at the caecum.
ileus: Temporary paralysis of bowel movement without a mechanical block.
ilioinguinal nerve: Nerve running in the inguinal canal; injury numbs the upper inner thigh, base of penis and anterior scrotum or labia.
imatinib: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor that targets BCR-ABL in CML.
immune complex: Antibody bound to antigen; can deposit in vessel walls and trigger inflammation.
immune dysregulation: An immune system that responds abnormally or fails to switch off.
immunocompromised: Weakened immune system, for example after transplant or chemotherapy.
immunoglobulin: Pooled antibodies given to vulnerable contacts for short-term passive protection after exposure.
immunoparesis: Suppression of normal antibodies, causing infections.
immunosuppression: Reduced immune defences, e.g. from steroids, chemotherapy or HIV.
impaired hypoglycaemia awareness: Loss of the warning autonomic symptoms, so hypos go straight to confusion or coma.
inactivated vaccine: Vaccine made from killed virus; cannot cause infection.
incarcerated: A hernia that is stuck and irreducible but still has its blood supply.
incisional hernia: A hernia through the scar of a previous operation.
incompetent valve: A vein valve that no longer closes properly, letting blood flow backwards.
incompetent valves: Vein valves that no longer close properly, letting blood fall back down the leg.
incomplete evacuation: Feeling the bowel has not fully emptied after defecation.
incubation period: Time between exposure and the first symptoms.
indirect inguinal hernia: Enters the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, along a patent processus vaginalis.
induration: The firm, raised area of skin measured in a Mantoux test; redness is ignored.
indwelling pleural catheter: Tunnelled drain left in the chest so a recurring malignant effusion can be drained at home.
infarction: Tissue death from loss of blood supply.
infected necrosis: Dead pancreatic tissue that has become infected; an indication for antibiotics and drainage.
infectious colitis: Inflammation of the colon caused by bacteria, viruses or parasites.
infectious mononucleosis: Glandular fever: an acute EBV infection with sore throat, fever, nodes and fatigue.
inferior epigastric vessels: Artery and vein in the lower abdominal wall; the landmark separating direct from indirect hernias.
inferior olive: Brainstem nucleus linked to the cerebellum, thought to drive tremor oscillation.
inferior quadrantanopia: Loss of a lower quarter of the field; from a parietal lobe lesion.
infliximab: Anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody for refractory IBD.
influenza: Acute viral respiratory infection caused by influenza A or B virus.
infrared photocoagulation: Heat applied to a haemorrhoid to scar its blood supply.
inguinal canal: A passage through the lower abdominal wall carrying the spermatic cord or round ligament.
inguinal hernia: A hernia through the inguinal canal, above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
inguinal ligament: The band running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle.
inguinoscrotal: A hernia that has travelled down the inguinal canal into the scrotum.
insufficiency fracture: A fracture of weakened bone under normal stress.
insulin resistance: Reduced response of tissues to insulin, so more insulin is needed to control glucose.
insulin tolerance test: Insulin-induced hypoglycaemia to test GH and cortisol reserve; gold standard for hypopituitarism.
insulinoma: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour that secretes insulin and causes fasting hypoglycaemia.
intention tremor: Tremor that worsens approaching a target, typical of cerebellar disease.
intercostal space: The gap between two ribs; the 2nd is used for needle decompression.
interface hepatitis: Biopsy finding where inflammation spills from portal tracts into surrounding liver cells; typical of AIH.
intermittent claudication: Calf pain brought on by walking a predictable distance and relieved by rest.
intermittent pneumatic compression: Inflatable leg sleeves that squeeze the calves to keep blood moving after surgery.
intermittent torsion: Brief episodes of twisting that untwist by themselves; a warning sign of full torsion.
internal anal sphincter: The involuntary smooth muscle ring of the anal canal; its spasm stops fissures healing.
internal carotid: The branch of the common carotid that supplies the eye and anterior brain.
internal haemorrhoids: Haemorrhoids above the dentate line; painless, bleed bright red.
interval appendicectomy: Removal of the appendix weeks after an appendix mass or abscess has settled.
interventional neuroradiologist: Specialist who treats brain vessels through catheters.
intestinal metaplasia: Stomach lining replaced by intestinal-type cells; a precancerous change.
intestinal type: Gland-forming gastric cancer arising from intestinal metaplasia, linked to H. pylori.
intra-abdominal pressure: Pressure inside the abdomen, raised by obesity, pregnancy, cough and straining.
intra-epithelial lymphocytes: T cells within the gut lining; increased numbers are the earliest coeliac change.
intracranial haemorrhage: Bleeding inside the skull; the most dangerous anticoagulant bleed.
intratesticular: Within the substance of the testis.
intratympanic: Given by injection through the eardrum into the middle ear.
intravasation: Tumour cells breaking into blood or lymphatic vessels.
intrinsic pathway: Clotting pathway triggered when blood contacts exposed collagen.
intubation: Passing a tube into the trachea to protect the airway and ventilate.
intussusception: One segment of bowel telescoping into the next, causing obstruction.
inversion: Turning the sole of the foot inwards (L4/L5, tibial nerve).
inverted champagne bottle: Leg shape in chronic venous disease: narrow fibrosed ankle below a swollen calf.
ionised calcium: The free, active fraction of blood calcium; falls in alkalosis.
iris bombé: Forward bowing of the iris from trapped aqueous when synechiae seal the pupil.
iritis: Anterior uveitis: inflammation of the iris.
iron deficiency anaemia: Low haemoglobin with small red cells from lack of iron, often from chronic bleeding.
irreducible: Cannot be pushed back into the abdomen.
ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue, starving it of oxygen.
ischaemic colitis: Ischaemia of the colon causing crampy pain and bloody diarrhoea, often at the splenic flexure.
ischaemic necrosis: Tissue death from loss of blood supply.
ischaemic optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from poor blood supply, e.g. in giant cell arteritis.
isodense: The same density as brain on CT, as with a subacute subdural.
isolation: Separating an infectious person from others to stop spread.
isoniazid: TB drug that blocks mycolic acid synthesis; causes peripheral neuropathy.
isotonic: Having the same solute concentration as plasma.
isotonic crystalloid: Salt solution with the same concentration as plasma, such as 0.9% saline.
ispaghula husk: A bulk-forming laxative (fibre supplement) that softens stools.
jaundice: Yellow skin and eyes from raised bilirubin; here from red cell breakdown.
jaw jerk: Reflex closing of the jaw when the chin is tapped; tests the trigeminal pathway.
kPa: Kilopascal, the unit used for blood gas pressures in the UK.
kappa: One of two types of antibody light chain.
keratin pearls: Whorls of keratin on histology that identify squamous cell carcinoma.
ketoacidosis: Acidosis caused by ketone bodies, as in DKA or alcoholic ketoacidosis.
ketogenesis: Production of ketones in the liver from fatty acids.
ketones: Acids made from fat breakdown when insulin is very low; minimal in HHS.
kissing disease: Nickname for glandular fever because EBV spreads through saliva.
koilonychia: Spoon-shaped nails, a sign of iron deficiency.
labetalol: IV alpha and beta blocker used to lower blood pressure quickly in stroke.
labyrinthitis: Inflammation of the inner ear causing vertigo plus hearing loss, usually after a virus.
lactase: Enzyme splitting lactose; lost temporarily after rotavirus.
lactate: Blood marker of poor tissue perfusion; above 4 mmol/L signals severe sepsis.
lactic acidosis: Acidosis from lactate, usually from poor tissue perfusion (sepsis, ischaemia).
lactose intolerance: Diarrhoea and bloating after milk due to lack of lactase.
lactulose: Osmotic sugar laxative, also fermented by gut bacteria.
lagophthalmos: Inability to fully close the eyelids.
lambda: One of two types of antibody light chain.
lamina papyracea: Paper-thin medial orbital wall over the ethmoid sinus; infection crosses it easily.
lansoprazole: Proton pump inhibitor preferred with clopidogrel because it interacts less via CYP2C19.
laparoscopic: Keyhole surgery through small incisions with a camera.
laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Keyhole surgical removal of the gallbladder.
laparotomy: An open operation through a large incision in the abdominal wall.
large cell carcinoma: Poorly differentiated non-small cell lung cancer with a poor prognosis.
laryngospasm: Spasm of the vocal cords that can block the airway.
latency: A dormant phase where the virus persists without causing disease.
latent TB: Contained TB infection: positive screening test, no symptoms, not infectious.
latent phase: A detectable stage of disease before symptoms appear.
lateral flow: Rapid antigen test; quick but less sensitive than PCR.
lateral internal sphincterotomy: Surgery that divides part of the internal anal sphincter to reduce its tone.
lateral malleolus: The bony bump on the outer side of the ankle (end of the fibula).
lateral rectus: Eye muscle that moves the eye outwards; supplied by the sixth cranial nerve.
lateralising signs: Findings that point to one side of the brain, such as one-sided weakness.
laxatives: Medicines that soften stool or help it pass.
lead-time bias: Apparent longer survival from screening only because diagnosis was earlier.
lecithinase: Enzyme that breaks down lecithin in cell membranes, killing cells.
ledipasvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks NS5A.
left axis deviation: The heart's overall electrical axis pointing further left than normal, seen on ECG; can accompany inferior MI.
left gastric artery: Coeliac trunk branch along the lesser curve; bleeds from gastric ulcers.
left hemicolectomy: Removal of distal transverse and descending colon.
left main: The short left main coronary artery before it splits into the LAD and circumflex; disease here threatens most of the left ventricle.
letrozole: Aromatase inhibitor used after breast cancer; causes bone loss.
leucocytes: White cells; positive on dipstick in infection such as epididymo-orchitis.
leukoerythroblastic: A blood film with immature white and nucleated red cells, from marrow infiltration or fibrosis.
leuprorelin: A GnRH agonist used for advanced prostate cancer.
levodopa: Dopamine precursor used in Parkinson's disease, not essential tremor.
levothyroxine: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) used as replacement.
lidocaine: A local anaesthetic that can numb the anus before defecation.
ligation and stripping: Surgery tying off the vein at the junction and pulling it out.
likelihood ratio: How much a test result changes the odds of disease; does not depend on prevalence.
linea semilunaris: The curved line along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle.
linitis plastica: Stiff, thickened 'leather bottle' stomach from diffuse-type infiltration.
lipase: A pancreatic enzyme that digests fat; more specific than amylase and stays raised longer.
lipodermatosclerosis: Hard, tight, inflamed skin of the lower leg from chronic venous disease.
lipolysis: Breakdown of stored fat into fatty acids; suppressed by small amounts of insulin.
lipooligosaccharide: Sugar-lipid molecule on the Campylobacter surface that resembles nerve gangliosides.
liquefaction: Breakdown of clot into fluid over weeks.
lithium: Mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder; the classic cause of nephrogenic DI.
lithotomy position: Lying on the back with hips and knees flexed; used for clock-face positions.
livedo reticularis: A net-like purple mottling of the skin.
lobectomy: Surgical removal of one lobe of the lung; curative for early NSCLC.
long saphenous vein: Another name for the great saphenous vein.
long thoracic nerve: Supplies serratus anterior; injury causes scapular winging.
longitudinally extensive: A spinal cord lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments, typical of NMO.
loop ileostomy: A loop of ileum opened on the skin to divert stool, usually temporarily.
loperamide: Opioid antidiarrhoeal that does not cross into the brain; dangerous in impaction.
low FODMAP: Diet low in fermentable oligo-, di- and monosaccharides and polyols.
low-grade fever: A mildly raised temperature, roughly 37.5 to 38.3°C.
low-intensity psychological intervention: Brief therapy such as guided self-help or psychoeducation groups.
low-intensity psychological therapy: Brief, structured therapy such as guided self-help or group CBT for milder depression.
lower motor neurone: The nerve from the brainstem nucleus to muscle; damage weakens the entire ipsilateral face.
lower oesophageal sphincter: Muscle ring at the bottom of the oesophagus that stops stomach contents flowing back up.
lucid interval: A period of apparent recovery after head injury before deterioration.
lumbar puncture: Sampling CSF with a needle between lumbar vertebrae.
lumen: The hollow inside of a tube-shaped organ.
lung abscess: A pus-filled cavity from necrosis of lung tissue, usually after aspiration of anaerobes.
lupus vulgaris: The commonest form of skin TB: papules enlarging into scaly red plaques.
lymphatic spread: Spread through lymph vessels to lymph nodes, common in breast cancer.
lymphoid hyperplasia: Swelling of lymphoid tissue in the appendix wall, often after a viral illness.
lymphopenia: A low lymphocyte count; typical in Covid-19.
lytic: Holes in bone on imaging where it has been destroyed.
lytic lesions: Areas where bone has been destroyed, seen as holes on imaging.
mOsm/kg: Milliosmoles per kilogram, the unit of osmolality.
mPAP: Mean pulmonary artery pressure; above 20 mmHg at rest defines pulmonary hypertension.
maceration: Softening and breakdown of skin kept wet for too long.
macrocytic: Large red cells (high MCV), seen in B12 or folate deficiency.
macrocytosis: Red cells larger than normal (raised MCV), common with heavy alcohol use.
macrovascular: Affecting large arteries: coronary, cerebral and peripheral.
macula: Central part of the retina responsible for detailed vision.
macular oedema: Fluid build-up in the macula that blurs central vision.
macular sparing: Preserved central vision despite a hemianopia, typical of occipital (PCA) strokes.
macules: Flat, coloured spots on the skin.
maculopapular: A rash with both flat (macules) and raised (papules) red spots.
maculopapular rash: A rash of flat red patches and small raised bumps.
maculopathy: Diabetic damage at the macula, usually oedema or exudates, threatening central vision.
malabsorption: Failure to absorb nutrients from the gut, causing deficiencies and weight loss.
malaria: Parasitic infection of red blood cells by Plasmodium, spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes.
malnutrition: Deficiency of calories, protein and nutrients causing weight loss, wasting and loss of function.
mamillary bodies: Small paired structures under the brain, part of the memory circuit, damaged in Wernicke's and Korsakoff's.
mammography: Low-dose breast X-ray used in breast screening.
mania: A period of elevated or irritable mood, overactivity and reduced need for sleep.
mannitol: Osmotic diuretic that temporarily lowers ICP.
manometry: Pressure measurement of oesophageal muscle contraction, used for motility disorders like achalasia.
manual reduction: Pushing a prolapsed haemorrhoid back in with a finger.
massive PE: PE with systolic BP below 90 mmHg for over 15 minutes, or collapse.
maxillary artery: A terminal branch of the external carotid artery.
mean deviation: Perimetry summary of how far a field is below normal, in decibels.
measles: A highly contagious paramyxovirus infection causing fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and a spreading rash.
mebeverine: Antispasmodic that relaxes gut smooth muscle; first-line for IBS pain.
mecA: Gene that gives MRSA its resistance by encoding PBP2a.
mechanical mitral valve: Artificial metal heart valve in the mitral position; target INR 3.5.
mechanical obstruction: A physical blockage of the bowel lumen, such as adhesions, a hernia or a tumour.
meconium: A newborn's first, dark sticky stool, normally passed within 48 hours.
meconium ileus: Newborn bowel obstruction from thick meconium, strongly linked to cystic fibrosis.
media: The muscular middle layer of an artery wall.
medial malleolus: The bony bump on the inner side of the ankle (end of the tibia).
median sulcus: The groove between the two prostate lobes; kept in BPH, often lost in cancer.
mediastinal shift: Movement of the heart and trachea away from a high-pressure side of the chest.
medullary carcinoma: Thyroid cancer from C cells that secretes calcitonin; linked to MEN 2.
megakaryocyte: The large marrow cell that makes platelets.
melaena: Black, tarry stool from upper GI bleeding.
melancholic: A 'biological' depression with early morning waking, weight loss and marked anhedonia.
melphalan: An alkylating chemotherapy drug used in myeloma.
meningism: Neck stiffness, photophobia and headache from irritation of the meninges.
meningitis: Infection and inflammation of the membranes around the brain.
meningococcal septicaemia: Bloodstream infection with Neisseria meningitidis, causing shock and a non-blanching rash.
mental state exam: Structured assessment of appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, thought, perception and cognition.
meralgia paraesthetica: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh giving burning lateral thigh pain.
mercaptopurine: Thiopurine related to azathioprine, used for IBD maintenance.
meropenem: A very broad-spectrum carbapenem IV antibiotic.
merozoites: Stage released from the liver or burst red cells that invades new red cells.
mesalazine: A 5-ASA drug for ulcerative colitis; a recognised cause of pancreatitis.
mesenteric adenitis: Inflamed abdominal lymph nodes after a viral illness, mimicking appendicitis.
mesenteric ischaemia: Reduced blood flow through the mesenteric arteries to the bowel.
mesenteric lymph nodes: Lymph nodes in the mesentery that drain the bowel.
mesentery: The fold of tissue that attaches the bowel to the back of the abdomen and carries its vessels and lymph nodes.
mesh repair: Hernia repair using a synthetic mesh to reinforce the weak wall.
mesothelioma: Malignant tumour of the pleura linked to asbestos, causing effusion and pleural thickening.
metabolic acidosis: Low blood pH with low bicarbonate, from acid build-up such as lactate.
metacarpals: The long bones of the hand; short 4th and 5th suggest pseudohypoparathyroidism.
metaplasia: One mature cell type replaced by another better suited to a hostile environment.
metastases: Secondary deposits of cancer spread from the original site.
metastasis: A secondary tumour formed when cancer cells spread from the primary to a distant site.
metformin: Oral diabetes drug that rarely causes lactic acidosis, especially in renal failure.
methanol: Toxic alcohol in screenwash; causes raised anion gap acidosis and blindness.
methotrexate: Folate antagonist used for Crohn's maintenance.
methylprednisolone: High-dose intravenous corticosteroid used for acute optic neuritis and MS relapses.
metoclopramide: An antiemetic given with morphine to stop opioid-induced nausea and vomiting.
metyrapone: Drug that blocks cortisol synthesis in the adrenal; used before surgery.
micelle: Bile-salt cluster that carries fats and fat-soluble vitamins to the gut wall.
micelles: Tiny bile acid clusters carrying fat and fat-soluble vitamins to be absorbed.
microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia: Red cell destruction as cells are cut by clots in small vessels, giving schistocytes.
microbiota: The community of bacteria and other microbes living in the gut.
microcalcifications: Tiny bright calcium spots on ultrasound; suggest papillary carcinoma.
microcytic anaemia: Anaemia with small red cells, usually from iron deficiency.
micrometastases: Tiny deposits of cancer spread too small to see on scans.
microsatellite instability: Changes in length of repetitive DNA sequences when mismatch repair fails.
microthrombi: Tiny clots in small blood vessels that block flow and damage organs.
microvascular: Affecting small vessels: retina, kidney and nerves.
mid-clavicular line: A vertical line down from the middle of the clavicle.
middle meningeal artery: Branch of the maxillary artery running inside the temporal bone; tears with temporal fractures.
midgut: Embryological gut from the duodenum to two-thirds along the transverse colon; its pain is felt periumbilically.
midline shift: Displacement of brain structures across the midline by a mass on one side.
migratory thrombophlebitis: Inflamed, clotted superficial veins appearing in different places over time.
miliary TB: Bloodstream spread of TB seeding many tiny millet-seed granulomas through the organs.
mimic: A condition that imitates TIA or stroke, such as hypoglycaemia, migraine or seizure.
mineralisation: Deposition of calcium phosphate into the bone matrix.
mineralocorticoid: Hormone like aldosterone that retains sodium and excretes potassium.
mismatch repair: The system that corrects copying errors in DNA; faulty in Lynch syndrome.
mitochondrial: Relating to mitochondria, the parts of cells that produce energy.
modified Rankin: Scale of disability and dependence, 0 (none) to 6 (dead).
molecular mimicry: Antibodies against a microbe cross-react with similar-looking host molecules.
monoamine: Neurotransmitters such as serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine.
mononeuritis multiplex: Damage to two or more separate named nerves, e.g. causing foot drop.
monospot: Rapid heterophile antibody test for glandular fever.
monospot test: Rapid heterophile antibody test for glandular fever.
mood-congruent: Psychotic content that matches the mood, such as delusions of guilt in depression.
moon face: Round, full, often red face from fat redistribution in cortisol excess.
morphine: Opioid painkiller used for ongoing ischaemic chest pain.
mottled: Blotchy, patchy skin from poor circulation.
mouth ulcers: Painful sores in the mouth, seen in coeliac and Crohn's.
mu-opioid receptors: Opioid receptors in the gut wall that slow motility when activated.
mucin: Mucus protein; glandular spaces with mucin identify adenocarcinoma.
mucociliary clearance: Hair-like cilia sweeping mucus out of the airways.
mucous membranes: Moist linings such as the inside of the mouth and tongue; dry in dehydration.
multi-organ failure: Failure of two or more organ systems in severe illness.
multinodular goitre: An enlarged thyroid with many nodules.
multiparametric MRI: MRI combining several sequences to find and score suspicious prostate lesions.
multiple myeloma: Cancer of plasma cells causing bone destruction, anaemia, renal failure and a paraprotein.
multiple sclerosis: Immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the brain and spinal cord with episodes separated in time and space.
multisystem: Affecting several body systems at once.
mummified: Dried out, shrunken and hard, as in dry gangrene.
mumps: A paramyxovirus infection causing parotid swelling; can spread to the testis.
mural invasion: How deep the tumour has grown into the oesophageal wall.
muscle wasting: Visible loss of muscle bulk, e.g. at the temples, shoulders and hands.
muscularis propria: The main muscle layer of the bowel wall; key landmark in Duke's staging.
myasthenia gravis: Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease with fatigable weakness, often of eye muscles.
mycolic acid: Waxy fatty acid in the mycobacterial cell wall, target of isoniazid.
myelofibrosis: Scarring of the bone marrow by collagen, leading to marrow failure.
myeloma kidney: Kidney damage from light chain casts blocking the tubules.
myeloproliferative: Describes clonal marrow disorders that overproduce blood cells.
myelosuppression: Reduced bone marrow production of blood cells.
myocarditis: Inflammation of the heart muscle, sometimes after viral infection.
myoglobin: Muscle protein that turns urine dark and gives a positive dipstick for blood without red cells.
myotome: The group of muscles supplied by one spinal nerve root.
napkin-ring: A tumour growing all the way round the bowel, narrowing it.
nasal endoscopy: Examination of the nasal cavity with a rigid camera, done by ENT.
nasal packing: Material placed in the nose to compress a bleeding vessel.
nasociliary nerve: Branch of the ophthalmic nerve supplying the nose tip and the eye.
nasolabial fold: The skin crease running from the side of the nose to the corner of the mouth.
nasopharyngeal swab: Swab taken from the back of the nose to test for respiratory viruses.
nasopharynx: The upper part of the throat behind the nose.
near-syncope: Feeling about to faint without losing consciousness.
necrosis: Death of cells or tissue from injury or loss of blood supply.
necrotising: Causing tissue death; necrotising scleritis is the most severe form.
necrotising fasciitis: Rapidly spreading infection of the fascia with pain out of proportion; a surgical emergency.
necrotising soft tissue infection: Rapidly spreading infection destroying skin, fat and fascia; a surgical emergency.
needle aspiration: Removing air from the pleural space through a cannula; first-line for symptomatic primary pneumothorax.
needle decompression: Emergency cannula into the chest to release trapped air in tension pneumothorax.
needle thoracocentesis: Another name for needle decompression of the chest.
negative feedback: When a hormone switches off the signals that cause its own release.
negative-pressure room: An isolation room whose air flows inwards, stopping airborne spread.
neoadjuvant: Treatment such as radiotherapy given before surgery to shrink a tumour.
neomembrane: New fibrous membrane forming around a chronic subdural, with fragile vessels that rebleed.
neonatal hypoglycaemia: Low blood glucose in a newborn; prematurity is a key risk factor.
neovascularisation: Growth of new, fragile blood vessels.
nephrogenic DI: DI because the kidney does not respond to ADH.
nephrolithiasis: Stones in the kidney or urinary tract.
nerve root: The part of a spinal nerve where it leaves the spinal canal.
neural crest: Embryonic cells that migrate to form the gut's nerve plexuses, among other tissues.
neuraminidase: Influenza surface enzyme that cleaves sialic acid to release new virions.
neuraminidase inhibitor: Antiviral class that stops new influenza virions leaving infected cells.
neurapraxia: Temporary nerve conduction block without axon damage; full recovery expected.
neuroendocrine tumour: A tumour of hormone-producing cells, which can secrete active hormones such as insulin.
neuroglycopenic: Symptoms caused by the brain lacking glucose, such as confusion, drowsiness and seizures.
neuroleptic malignant syndrome: Reaction to antipsychotics with fever, rigidity, confusion and high CK.
neuromuscular junction: The synapse where a motor nerve releases acetylcholine onto muscle.
neuromyelitis optica: Antibody-mediated disease causing severe optic neuritis and long spinal cord lesions.
neuropathic pain: Burning, shooting or electric pain from damaged nerves.
neuropathic ulcer: Painless ulcer on pressure points of the sole due to loss of sensation, often diabetic.
neuroplasticity: The brain's ability to change its connections over time.
neurosecretory granules: Hormone-containing granules seen in small cell (neuroendocrine) tumours.
neurotmesis: Complete cutting of a nerve; needs surgical repair.
neurovascular: Relating to both nerves and blood vessels; checked after any limb injury.
neutrophilia: Raised neutrophil count, typical of bacterial infection.
newborn blood spot: Heel-prick test between day 5 and 9 screening for conditions such as PKU and sickle cell.
niacin: Vitamin B3; needed to make NAD and NADP for energy metabolism.
nifedipine: A calcium channel blocker that can be used orally or topically for fissures.
night blindness: Poor vision in dim light from vitamin A deficiency.
nihilism: A delusional belief that oneself, one's organs or the world do not exist or are dying.
nimodipine: Cerebral-selective calcium channel blocker that reduces vasospasm-related ischaemia after SAH.
nirmatrelvir: Antiviral that inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 main protease.
nitric oxide: A signalling molecule that relaxes smooth muscle and widens blood vessels.
nitrites: Made by many Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli; a positive dipstick suggests UTI.
nocturia: Waking at night to pass urine.
non-Hodgkin lymphoma: A group of lymphomas without Reed-Sternberg cells, including EATL.
non-blanching: A rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass; suggests bleeding into the skin.
non-blanching erythema: Redness that does not fade when pressed; the sign of stage 1 damage.
non-caseating granulomas: Clusters of macrophages without central necrosis; the Crohn's hallmark.
non-contrast CT: CT scan without injected dye; the first test for bleeding in the head.
non-enveloped: A virus without an outer lipid layer, so it resists alcohol.
non-functioning: Describes a pituitary tumour that secretes no active hormone.
non-seminomatous germ cell tumour: Germ cell tumours other than seminoma, e.g. teratoma, yolk sac, embryonal; more aggressive.
noradrenaline: Neurotransmitter driving the sympathetic fight-or-flight response.
normocytic: Red cells of normal size (normal MCV).
norovirus: A highly infectious virus causing outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea, often in care homes.
notifiable: Must be reported to public health by law, such as food poisoning and typhoid.
notifiable disease: An infection that a doctor must legally report to public health authorities when it is suspected.
nucleus pulposus: The soft gel centre of an intervertebral disc.
nutcracker effect: Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA.
nystagmus: Involuntary rhythmic jerking movement of the eyes.
obstipation: Severe constipation with no passage of stool or gas; absolute constipation.
obstructive jaundice: Yellowing from blocked bile flow, with dark urine, pale stools and itch.
obstructive shock: Shock from blocked venous return or cardiac filling, as in tension pneumothorax.
obturator hernia: A hernia through the obturator canal of the pelvis; may be felt as a tender mass on rectal examination.
obturator sign: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip, suggesting a pelvic appendix.
occipital cortex: Primary visual cortex at the back of the brain.
occult bleeding: Blood loss not visible to the eye, found by tests or as anaemia.
occult blood loss: Bleeding too slow to be seen, detected by anaemia or tests.
octreotide: Somatostatin analogue used to lower GH in acromegaly.
oculomotor: Third cranial nerve: moves most eye muscles, lifts the lid and constricts the pupil.
oculomotor nerve: CN III: moves most eye muscles, lifts the lid and constricts the pupil.
oesophageal hiatus: The opening in the diaphragm through which the oesophagus passes.
oesophageal manometry: Pressure measurement along the oesophagus to assess muscle and sphincter function.
oesophageal probe: A temperature sensor passed into the oesophagus to measure core temperature accurately.
oesophagectomy: Surgical removal of part or all of the oesophagus.
ofloxacin: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for urinary-organism epididymitis.
oliguria: Reduced urine output, usually under 0.5 mL/kg per hour in adults.
omental cake: Thickened omentum infiltrated by tumour, typical of ovarian cancer spread.
omental patch repair: Closing a perforated ulcer by stitching a piece of omentum over the hole.
omentum: A fatty apron hanging from the stomach that can wall off infection.
omeprazole: Proton pump inhibitor that inhibits CYP2C19 and so reduces clopidogrel's effect.
oncotic pressure: Pull exerted by plasma proteins that keeps fluid in blood vessels.
opening pressure: CSF pressure measured at the start of a lumbar puncture.
ophthalmia neonatorum: Conjunctivitis in a newborn's first month; recently removed from the notifiable list.
ophthalmic artery: First branch of the internal carotid, supplying the eye.
ophthalmic zoster: Shingles of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, which can damage the eye.
ophthalmoplegia: Weakness or restriction of eye movements.
opioid: A morphine-like painkiller; constipation is a common side effect.
opioids: Drugs such as codeine and morphine acting on opioid receptors; a common cause of constipation.
optic atrophy: Pale optic disc from loss of nerve fibres, a late sign after optic neuritis.
optic chiasm: Where the optic nerves cross, directly above the pituitary.
optic nerve: Cranial nerve II, carrying visual signals from the retina to the brain.
optic neuritis: Inflammation of the optic nerve, causing painful loss of vision in one eye.
optic neuropathy: Damage to the optic nerve causing blurred vision or loss of colour vision.
optic radiations: Fibres running from the lateral geniculate nucleus through the temporal and parietal lobes to the occipital cortex.
optic tract: Carries fibres from the same half of both retinas from the chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus.
oral fluid swab: A sponge rubbed along the gums to collect fluid for measles PCR and antibody tests.
oral hairy leucoplakia: White, corrugated, 'hairy' patch on the side of the tongue linked to EBV.
oral nutritional supplements: Prescribed high-energy, high-protein drinks taken alongside food.
oral rehydration solution: Water with set amounts of salt and glucose that the gut absorbs efficiently.
orbit: The bony eye socket, made of seven bones.
orbital apex: Back of the orbit where the optic nerve and eye-movement nerves enter.
orbital cellulitis: Infection behind the orbital septum involving orbital fat and muscles; an emergency.
orbital septum: Thin fibrous sheet from the orbital rim to the eyelids that walls off the orbit.
orchidopexy: Surgery to bring an undescended testis down and fix it in the scrotum.
organogenesis: Formation of the organs in the first trimester.
orthopnoea: Breathlessness lying flat; in MND a sign of diaphragm weakness.
orthostatic intolerance: Symptoms such as dizziness and racing heart on standing that ease on lying down.
oseltamivir: Oral neuraminidase inhibitor (Tamiflu) for high-risk patients with influenza.
osmolal gap: Measured minus calculated osmolality; raised by toxic alcohols.
osmolality: The concentration of dissolved particles in a fluid.
osmotic: Drawing water into the bowel, as osmotic laxatives do.
osmotic demyelination: Brainstem damage from correcting a low sodium too quickly.
osmotic diarrhoea: Watery diarrhoea caused by unabsorbed solutes pulling water into the gut.
osmotic diuresis: Increased urine output because a solute such as glucose drags water into the urine.
osteoblastic: Bone-forming; prostate cancer metastases stimulate osteoblasts and make sclerotic lesions.
osteoclast: Bone cell that breaks down bone and releases calcium.
osteoid: The protein matrix of bone, laid down before it is mineralised.
osteolysis: Destruction of bone, as by metastases or myeloma.
osteolytic: Causing bone destruction, seen as lytic lesions on imaging.
osteomalacia: Soft bones from poor mineralisation, usually due to vitamin D deficiency.
osteoporosis: Low bone density with a raised risk of fracture.
otoconia: Calcium carbonate crystals in the utricle; displaced ones cause BPPV.
outbreak: More cases of a disease than expected in a place or group over a time period.
overdiagnosis: Diagnosing disease that would never have caused harm in the person's lifetime.
overflow diarrhoea: Liquid stool leaking around a hard impacted faecal mass, mimicking diarrhoea.
overflow incontinence: Dribbling leakage from an over-full bladder.
oxybutynin: An antimuscarinic for urgency and frequency.
p-ANCA: Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis.
p24 antigen: An HIV core protein detected early in infection by 4th generation tests.
p53: Tumour suppressor lost late, as an adenoma becomes a carcinoma.
pCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in blood; normal 4.7 to 6.0 kPa.
pacing: Energy management: balancing activity and rest to stay within energy limits and avoid crashes.
pack-years: Packs of 20 cigarettes smoked per day multiplied by years smoked.
painless jaundice: Jaundice without biliary colic, a classic sign of malignant obstruction.
palatal petechiae: Tiny red spots of bleeding on the soft palate.
palliative care: Care focused on symptom control and quality of life when cure is not possible.
palliative chemotherapy: Chemotherapy to control symptoms and extend life, not to cure.
pamidronate: IV bisphosphonate used in hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
pan-retinal laser photocoagulation: Laser burns to the peripheral retina to stop new vessel growth.
pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: The commonest pancreatic cancer, arising from the cells lining the pancreatic ducts.
pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy: Oral pancreatic enzymes (e.g. pancreatin) to replace missing digestive enzymes.
pancreatic insufficiency: Too little pancreatic enzyme to digest food properly.
pancreatic necrosis: Dead, non-viable pancreatic tissue, developing in the first week of severe disease.
pancreatic protocol CT: A multiphase CT designed to show the pancreas, tumour and nearby vessels.
pancreaticoduodenectomy: The Whipple operation for pancreatic head tumours.
pancreatin: Pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals to treat steatorrhoea.
pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas; hypercalcaemia is one cause.
pancytopenia: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together.
pandemic: A new infection spreading worldwide because few people are immune.
panic attack: A sudden surge of intense fear peaking within minutes, with physical symptoms such as palpitations.
panic disorder: Recurrent sudden attacks of intense fear with breathlessness and palpitations.
pansystolic murmur: A murmur lasting through the whole of systole, heard with septal rupture or mitral regurgitation.
papillary carcinoma: Commonest thyroid cancer; young women, spreads to lymph nodes.
papilloedema: Optic disc swelling caused specifically by raised intracranial pressure.
papules: Small raised solid spots on the skin.
papulovesicular: Describes a rash of small raised bumps and tiny fluid-filled blisters.
para-aortic lymph nodes: Retroperitoneal nodes beside the aorta; the first site of testicular cancer spread.
para-oesophageal: Beside the oesophagus; a rolling hernia where the fundus herniates alongside it.
paradoxical embolism: A venous clot crossing a heart defect to the arterial side, causing a stroke.
paradoxical thrombosis: Clotting despite a low platelet count, as seen in HIT.
parafollicular C cells: Neural crest-derived thyroid cells that make calcitonin.
paralytic ileus: Another name for ileus: the bowel stops contracting, typically after surgery.
paranasal sinuses: Air spaces around the nose: frontal, ethmoid, maxillary and sphenoid.
paraneoplastic: Effects of a cancer caused by hormones or antibodies it triggers, not by local spread.
paraprotein: A single monoclonal antibody band on electrophoresis, as in myeloma.
parasitaemia: Percentage of red blood cells containing parasites; 2% or more suggests severe disease.
parasternal heave: A lifting impulse beside the sternum from an enlarged right ventricle.
parathyroid adenoma: A benign tumour of one parathyroid gland; the usual cause of primary hyperparathyroidism.
parathyroid glands: Four small glands behind the thyroid that make PTH.
parathyroidectomy: Surgical removal of parathyroid tissue; the definitive treatment.
parenchyma: The functional lung tissue: alveoli and their walls, as opposed to airways.
parenteral nutrition: Intravenous feeding that bypasses the gut, used when the gut cannot be used.
paresis: Partial weakness of a limb or muscle group.
parietal cells: Stomach lining cells that secrete acid and intrinsic factor.
parietal peritoneum: The peritoneum lining the abdominal wall; it has somatic nerves, so pain is well localised.
parietal pleura: The membrane lining the inside of the chest wall.
parkinsonism: Bradykinesia with rigidity, rest tremor or postural instability.
parotid: Salivary gland in front of the ear; the facial nerve runs through it.
parotitis: Inflammation and swelling of the parotid salivary glands.
pars compacta: Part of the substantia nigra containing the dopaminergic neurones lost in Parkinson's.
partial thickness: Skin loss through the epidermis and part of the dermis only.
partner notification: Informing and treating sexual partners of someone with an STI.
parvovirus B19: Virus that infects red cell precursors and causes slapped cheek in children and aplastic crisis in sickle cell.
passive external rewarming: Blankets and a warm room, letting the patient's own heat restore temperature.
patellar reflex: Knee jerk reflex, tested by tapping the patellar tendon (L3/L4).
patent foramen ovale: A persistent hole between the atria that lets venous clots reach the brain.
pathological fracture: A fracture through bone weakened by disease, often after trivial force.
pellagra: Niacin deficiency causing diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia and death.
penumbra: Hypoperfused brain tissue that is not yet infarcted and can be saved.
peppermint oil: Natural antispasmodic used for IBS cramps.
peptic ulcer: A break in the stomach or duodenal lining; aspirin and NSAIDs are common causes.
percutaneous cholecystostomy: A drain placed through the skin into the gallbladder, used when surgery is unsafe.
percutaneous drainage: Draining a collection with a tube placed through the skin under image guidance.
percutaneous transluminal angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery with a balloon passed through the skin into the vessel.
perforation: A hole through the wall of an organ, spilling its contents.
perianal abscess: A pus collection near the anus causing constant throbbing pain and swelling.
periaqueductal grey: Grey matter around the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain; often affected in Wernicke's.
pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium causing sharp pleuritic chest pain eased by sitting forward, with saddle ST elevation.
pericholecystic fluid: Fluid around the gallbladder on ultrasound, a sign of inflammation.
pericytes: Support cells around capillaries; their loss weakens vessel walls.
perilymph: Sodium-rich fluid around the membranous labyrinth, separate from endolymph.
perimetry: Formal machine test that maps the visual field precisely.
perineural invasion: Tumour spreading along nerves, causing back pain.
perioperative chemotherapy: Chemotherapy given both before and after an operation.
perioral paraesthesia: Tingling around the mouth; classic sign of low calcium.
periorbital cellulitis: Infection of the eyelid and skin in front of the orbital septum; also called preseptal cellulitis.
peripheral arterial disease: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the legs, reducing blood flow.
peripheral neuropathy: Nerve damage causing tingling, numbness or burning in the hands and feet.
peripheral zone: The posterior outer prostate, felt on DRE, where most cancers arise.
peritoneal cavity: The space inside the abdomen lined by peritoneum.
peritoneal lavage: Washing the abdominal cavity with fluid; warmed saline rewarms when ECMO is unavailable.
peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound and rigidity.
peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum lining the abdomen, giving a rigid, very tender abdomen.
peritrochanteric: Around the trochanters of the upper femur; the highest-risk Mirels site.
periventricular: Next to the brain's ventricles; a classic site for MS plaques.
pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells causing B12 deficiency and achlorhydria.
pertussis: Whooping cough, caused by Bordetella pertussis, with paroxysmal coughing fits.
petechiae: Pinpoint red or purple spots from bleeding into the skin; do not blanch.
petechial rash: A rash of tiny non-blanching red spots, typical of low platelets.
phaeochromocytoma: Adrenal tumour making adrenaline, causing episodes of palpitations, sweating and hypertension.
phenoxymethylpenicillin: Oral penicillin V, given as daily prophylaxis to young children with sickle cell disease.
phenylephrine: Alpha-1 agonist vasoconstrictor used as a nasal spray.
phenytoin: An enzyme-inducing anticonvulsant linked to osteomalacia.
phosphate: Mineral excreted more under PTH or PTHrP action, so it falls.
phrenico-oesophageal ligament: Connective tissue anchoring the oesophagus to the diaphragm; weakens in sliding hernias.
pigment gallstones: Gallstones made of bilirubin, formed when chronic haemolysis floods the bile with pigment.
pigment stones: Gallstones made of bilirubin, typical of chronic haemolysis.
pill-rolling: Thumb-and-finger rest tremor of Parkinson's disease.
pioglitazone: Thiazolidinedione; contraindicated in heart failure and linked to fractures.
piperacillin-tazobactam: Very broad-spectrum IV penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (Tazocin).
pitting oedema: Swelling that keeps a dent after you press it with a finger.
pituitary adenoma: Benign tumour of the anterior pituitary gland.
pituitary apoplexy: Sudden haemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary adenoma; an emergency.
pituitary incidentaloma: Pituitary lesion found by chance on a scan done for another reason.
pituitary stalk: Connects the hypothalamus to the pituitary; carries dopamine to the lactotrophs.
placental abruption: Separation of the placenta from the uterus before delivery; a classic obstetric DIC trigger.
plantarflexion: Pointing the foot down, as in standing on tiptoes (S1).
plaque rupture: Tearing of the cap over an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing material that triggers platelet clumping and clot formation.
plasma cell dyscrasia: Any disorder of a clone of plasma cells making abnormal antibody.
plasma cells: Fully mature B cells that make antibodies.
platelet factor 4: Platelet protein that binds heparin; antibodies against the complex cause HIT.
platelets: Small cell fragments that plug damaged vessels; also a transfused blood product.
plethoric: Red, flushed appearance of the face.
pleural cavity: The thin space between the visceral pleura on the lung and the parietal pleura on the chest wall.
pleural effusion: Fluid collecting between the visceral and parietal pleura.
pleural line: The thin white edge of the collapsed lung seen on a chest X-ray.
pleuritic: Chest pain that is sharp and worse on breathing in.
pleuritic chest pain: Sharp pain worse on breathing in or coughing, from inflamed pleura.
pleurodesis: Sticking the pleural layers together mechanically or chemically to prevent recurrence.
pneumaturia: Passing gas bubbles in the urine.
pneumobilia: Air in the biliary tree, seen on imaging.
pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine: PPV23 vaccine against Strep. pneumoniae, repeated every 5 years in sickle cell disease.
pneumonia: Infection of the lung tissue with alveolar consolidation.
pneumoperitoneum: Free air in the abdominal cavity, usually from a perforated viscus.
pneumothorax: Air in the pleural space, between the lung and chest wall, causing the lung to collapse.
point-of-care: A test done at the bedside or in the surgery with a result within minutes.
polyarteritis nodosa: Medium-vessel vasculitis causing hypertension, renal impairment, mononeuritis multiplex and livedo; linked to hepatitis B.
polyclonal: Coming from many different B-cell clones, giving a diffuse rise in antibodies.
polycystic kidney disease: Inherited condition with multiple kidney cysts, associated with berry aneurysms.
polycythaemia: An abnormally increased red cell mass, raising the haemoglobin and haematocrit.
polycythaemia vera: An MPN with a raised red cell mass, usually JAK2 positive.
polymerisation: HbS molecules joining into long rigid fibres when deoxygenated, which distorts the cell.
polymicrobial: Caused by several different bacteria at once (type 1 necrotising fasciitis).
polyuria: Passing abnormally large volumes of urine, often over 3 L a day.
popliteal vein: The deep vein behind the knee; a clot here is a proximal DVT.
portal hypertension: Raised pressure in the portal venous system, usually from cirrhosis.
portal vein: Carries blood from the gut to the liver; why colorectal cancer spreads to the liver first.
post-cholecystectomy syndrome: Ongoing abdominal pain, diarrhoea or jaundice after gallbladder removal.
post-exertional malaise: Disproportionate worsening of symptoms, often delayed, after even minor physical, mental or emotional effort.
post-exposure prophylaxis: Treatment or vaccine given after contact with an infection to stop the disease developing.
post-herpetic neuralgia: Nerve pain that persists in the dermatome after the shingles rash has healed.
post-infectious IBS: IBS that starts after an episode of gastroenteritis.
post-thrombotic: Describes leg damage, especially valve failure, that follows a previous DVT.
post-thrombotic syndrome: Chronic leg aching, swelling, pigmentation and ulcers after DVT from damaged vein valves.
post-tussive vomiting: Vomiting straight after a coughing fit, typical of whooping cough.
post-void residual: Urine left in the bladder after passing urine, measured by bladder ultrasound.
posterior cervical lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
posterior circulation stroke: Stroke in the vertebrobasilar territory, including the occipital lobe.
posterior communicating artery: Artery linking internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries; a common aneurysm site.
posterior epistaxis: Bleeding from the back of the nasal cavity, usually the sphenopalatine artery; typically severe.
posterior interosseous nerve: Motor branch of the radial nerve in the forearm; injury causes finger drop.
posterior midline: The back of the anal canal, in line with the natal cleft; the usual fissure site.
posterior packing: Pack or balloon placed at the back of the nasal cavity for posterior bleeds.
posterior pituitary: Back lobe of the pituitary that stores and releases ADH.
posterior synechiae: Adhesions between the iris and the front of the lens, giving an irregular pupil.
posterior uveitis: Inflammation of the choroid, often with floaters and retina involvement.
posterolateral: Behind and to the side; the commonest direction of disc prolapse.
postseptal: Behind the orbital septum, inside the orbit.
postural hypotension: A fall in blood pressure on standing, causing dizziness and falls.
postural tremor: Tremor present when holding a position against gravity, such as arms outstretched.
ppb: Parts per billion, the unit for FeNO.
prasugrel: A P2Y12 antiplatelet given with aspirin before PCI in patients not on an anticoagulant.
pre-renal: Kidney impairment from poor blood flow to the kidneys, such as dehydration.
pre-renal AKI: Kidney injury caused by reduced blood flow to the kidneys rather than kidney damage itself.
pre-test probability: The chance of disease before the test, often equal to prevalence.
precipitant: The trigger that tipped the patient into the emergency.
prediabetes: HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol: raised risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes.
prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid; first-line in Bell's palsy if started within 72 hours.
prednisolone acetate: Steroid eye drop used first-line in anterior uveitis.
preformed toxin: Toxin made in the food before eating, so symptoms start within hours.
prefrontal cortex: Front part of the brain that regulates emotion and worry.
pregabalin: A gabapentin-like drug for neuropathic pain.
preseptal cellulitis: Another name for periorbital cellulitis: infection anterior to the orbital septum.
pressure sore: Skin and tissue breakdown over a bony area from prolonged pressure.
pressure ulcer: Skin and tissue damage from prolonged pressure over a bony prominence.
prevalence: The proportion of a population that has the disease at a given time.
primaquine: Drug that kills liver hypnozoites to prevent vivax and ovale relapse.
primary PCI: PCI performed as the first reperfusion treatment for STEMI, without fibrinolysis beforehand.
primary hyperparathyroidism: Overactive parathyroid (usually an adenoma) causing high calcium with high or normal PTH.
primary lateral sclerosis: MND variant with UMN signs only.
primary myelofibrosis: An MPN in which the marrow scars, causing pancytopenia and a massive spleen.
primary polydipsia: Drinking too much water, often psychiatric; urine is dilute but sodium is low-normal.
primary prevention: Stopping disease before it starts, such as vaccination or stopping smoking.
primary sclerosing cholangitis: Chronic scarring of the bile ducts, linked to UC; diagnosed on MRCP.
primary spontaneous pneumothorax: Pneumothorax with no underlying lung disease, usually from an apical bleb in a tall thin young man.
primary tumour: The original cancer from which metastases come.
primidone: Anticonvulsant used for essential tremor when propranolol is unsuitable.
principal cells: Collecting duct cells that respond to ADH and aldosterone.
processus vaginalis: A fold of peritoneum that follows the testis into the scrotum; if it stays open, an indirect hernia can form.
prochlorperazine: Dopamine D2 antagonist anti-sickness drug used briefly for acute vertigo.
proctitis: Inflammation of the rectum, e.g. after radiotherapy: bloody diarrhoea and tenesmus.
proctocolectomy: Removal of the entire colon and rectum.
proctoscope: A short rigid tube used to inspect the anal canal.
proctoscopy: Viewing the anal canal and lower rectum through a short rigid tube.
prodrome: Early symptoms before the main illness appears.
prodrug: A drug given in inactive form that the body must convert to its active metabolite.
progesterone: Pregnancy hormone that relaxes smooth muscle, including the LOS.
progressive bulbar palsy: MND variant affecting cranial nerves IX, X and XII, with the worst prognosis.
progressive muscular atrophy: MND variant with LMN signs only.
proinsulin: The precursor molecule that is split into insulin and C-peptide in beta cells.
prokinetic: A drug that increases gut movement.
prolactin: Pituitary hormone that stimulates milk production and suppresses GnRH.
prolactinoma: Pituitary adenoma that secretes prolactin; the commonest functioning type.
prolapse: Slipping down and out of normal position, here through the anus.
prophylactic fixation: Surgically stabilising a bone before it fractures.
prophylaxis: Medicine taken to prevent a disease, here before, during and after travel.
propranolol: Non-selective beta-blocker used to reduce palpitations and tremor in anxiety.
proptosis: Forward bulging of the eye, caused by something filling the orbit.
prostaglandins: Local hormones that maintain gastric mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow.
prostatitis: Inflammation of the prostate, usually infective, with a tender gland and pain.
prostration: Extreme exhaustion that stops someone getting out of bed.
protamine sulphate: Drug that binds and neutralises heparin.
protease: Viral enzyme that cuts long proteins into working parts; blocked by nirmatrelvir.
protective factors: Things that lower suicide risk, such as close family, children or future plans.
protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins to detect a paraprotein band in myeloma.
prothrombin time: Clotting test of the extrinsic pathway; prolonged by warfarin.
provoked DVT: A DVT with a clear trigger such as surgery, travel or immobility.
provoked PE: A PE with an identifiable trigger such as surgery, travel or pregnancy.
proximal DVT: A clot in the popliteal vein or above; the highest risk of PE.
proximal leg vein ultrasound: Ultrasound of the popliteal and femoral veins, where dangerous clots sit.
proximal muscle weakness: Weakness of muscles near the trunk, such as the hips and shoulders.
proximal myopathy: Weakness of muscles near the trunk, such as hips and shoulders; hard to stand up.
proximal tubule: First part of the kidney tubule, where most water, sodium and urea are reabsorbed.
pruritus: Itching, caused here by retained bile salts.
psammoma bodies: Round calcified bodies seen in papillary carcinoma.
pseudo-Cushing's: Cushing-like features and tests from chronic alcohol excess, resolving with abstinence.
pseudo-obstruction: Symptoms of bowel obstruction without a physical blockage.
pseudoappendicitis: Illness that mimics appendicitis, classically from Yersinia mesenteric adenitis.
pseudocyst: A walled-off fluid collection with no epithelial lining, forming about 4 weeks after pancreatitis.
pseudodementia: Severe depression that looks like dementia, with apparent memory loss that improves when mood is treated.
pseudofractures: Bands of unmineralised bone that look like incomplete fractures on X-ray.
pseudohypoparathyroidism: Body tissues resist PTH, so calcium is low despite a high PTH.
pseudomembranes: Raised yellow plaques of fibrin, mucus and dead cells on the inflamed colon.
pseudomembranous colitis: Severe C. difficile colitis with yellow plaques of fibrin and debris on the colonic lining.
pseudopolyps: Islands of regenerating mucosa between ulcers, seen in UC.
pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism: The skeletal look of pseudohypoparathyroidism with normal blood tests.
psoas sign: Pain on hyperextension of the right hip, suggesting a retrocaecal appendix.
psychoeducation: Teaching patients about their condition and how to manage it.
psychomotor agitation: Restless, purposeless movement driven by inner tension.
psychomotor retardation: Visible slowing of thought, speech and movement.
psychosocial morbidity: Psychological and social harm such as anxiety, depression and withdrawal.
psychotic depression: Severe depression with delusions or hallucinations, usually themed around guilt, sin or worthlessness.
pterion: H-shaped junction of four skull bones at the temple, where the skull is thinnest.
pubic tubercle: The bony bump at the inner end of the inguinal ligament; the key landmark for groin lumps.
punched out: Describes an ulcer with sharp, well-defined, vertical edges, like a hole punch.
pupil-sparing: Third nerve palsy with a normal pupil, typical of diabetic microvascular causes.
purpura: Larger purple patches of bleeding under the skin that do not blanch.
purpuric: Describes purple spots from bleeding under the skin that do not blanch.
pyoderma gangrenosum: Painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge, linked to IBD.
pyrazinamide: TB drug active in acidic macrophages; causes hepatitis and gout.
pyridoxine: Vitamin B6, given with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
pyruvate dehydrogenase: Thiamine-dependent enzyme converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, linking glycolysis to the Krebs cycle.
quadrantanopia: Loss of one quarter of the visual field.
quadruple therapy: Bismuth-based regimen of PPI, bismuth and two antibiotics for resistant H. pylori.
quinine: Older antimalarial; causes insulin release and hypoglycaemia.
quinsy: Peritonsillar abscess, causing trismus, uvula deviation and a muffled voice.
rabies: A fatal viral encephalitis spread by animal bites; urgently notifiable.
radical inguinal orchidectomy: Removing the testis and cord through a groin incision; diagnoses and treats testicular cancer.
radical prostatectomy: Surgical removal of the whole prostate and seminal vesicles.
radiculopathy: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root causing pain, numbness or weakness in its territory.
radioactive iodine: Iodine-131 taken up by thyroid tissue; ablates remnants or treats hyperthyroidism.
radiofrequency ablation: Closing a vein from inside using radiofrequency heat.
radiolucent: Appearing dark on X-ray because it lets X-rays through.
radionuclide scan: Scan of isotope uptake showing whether a nodule is hot or cold.
radiotherapy: Treatment with ionising radiation to shrink tumours or relieve pain.
raindrop skull: Skull X-ray with many punched-out lytic holes in myeloma.
raised ICP: High pressure in the skull: headache worse in the morning, vomiting, papilloedema.
ramipril: An ACE inhibitor started within 24 hours of MI to limit ventricular remodelling.
ranibizumab: An anti-VEGF drug given by intravitreal injection.
re-expansion pulmonary oedema: Fluid in a lung that has been re-expanded too quickly after collapse.
reactive lymphoid hyperplasia: Enlargement of lymph nodes as they respond to infection, without being primarily infected.
reactive thrombocytosis: A raised platelet count caused by infection, inflammation, bleeding or iron deficiency.
reassortment: Swapping of gene segments when two influenza strains infect the same cell.
rebleed: A second rupture of the aneurysm, most often within 12 hours, causing sudden deterioration.
rebound anxiety: Anxiety worse than before, appearing when a drug is stopped.
rebound tenderness: Pain when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released, a sign of peritoneal irritation.
reciprocal: ST depression in leads facing the opposite side of the heart to an area of ST elevation, supporting a true STEMI.
reconstructive surgery: Surgery, such as a flap, to close a large tissue defect.
rectal stump: The closed-off top of the rectum left behind in a Hartmann's procedure.
rectosigmoid junction: Where the sigmoid colon meets the rectum; a second watershed zone.
recurrent laryngeal nerve: Nerve to the vocal cords that can be injured in thyroid surgery, causing hoarseness.
red desaturation: Red objects appear faded or washed out in the affected eye.
red flags: Warning features (weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding, anaemia) needing urgent endoscopy.
red reflex: Orange-red glow seen through the pupil with an ophthalmoscope; dull when blood fills the vitreous.
reducible: Can be pushed back into the abdomen.
refeeding syndrome: Dangerous fall in phosphate, potassium and magnesium when a starved patient is fed too quickly.
referred pain: Pain felt away from its source, such as testicular pain felt in the lower abdomen.
reflux: Backward flow of blood through leaky vein valves.
regurgitation: Stomach contents coming back up into the mouth without vomiting.
relative afferent pupillary defect: Pupil dilates when light swings to the affected eye, showing optic nerve damage.
relative bradycardia: A pulse slower than expected for the height of the fever.
relative insulin deficiency: Some insulin is present, but not enough for the body's needs.
relook laparotomy: A planned second operation to check the bowel left behind is still alive.
remdesivir: IV antiviral that inhibits viral RNA replication.
remodelling: Harmful changes in ventricular size and shape after MI that lead to heart failure.
renal cell carcinoma: The commonest kidney cancer; can secrete PTHrP.
renal colic: Severe loin-to-groin pain from a stone moving down the ureter.
renal tubular acidosis: Failure of the kidney tubules to excrete acid or keep bicarbonate, giving a normal gap acidosis.
reperfusion injury: Damage caused when blood flow returns to ischaemic tissue.
repositioning: Regularly changing a patient's position to relieve pressure.
respiratory alkalosis: Raised blood pH from blowing off too much CO2 by overbreathing.
respiratory failure: Low blood oxygen (with or without high CO2) because the lungs cannot exchange gas well enough.
rest pain: Ischaemic pain at rest, often at night, a sign of critical limb ischaemia.
resting tremor: Tremor when the limb is relaxed and supported, typical of Parkinson's disease.
reticulocyte count: Blood test of young red cells; low in aplastic crisis, high in haemolysis and sequestration.
reticulocytes: Young red cells; a high count shows the marrow is replacing lost cells.
reticuloendothelial system: Phagocytic cells in liver, spleen, bone marrow and lymph nodes.
retinal detachment: Separation of the retina, causing flashes, floaters and a curtain over vision.
retinal haemorrhages: Bleeding in the retina seen on fundoscopy, which can accompany SAH.
retrobulbar: Behind the eyeball; retrobulbar optic neuritis leaves the disc looking normal.
retrobulbar haemorrhage: Bleeding behind the eye after trauma, causing sudden proptosis and visual loss.
retrocardiac: Behind the heart on a chest X-ray.
retrograde amnesia: Loss of memories formed before the brain injury.
retrograde ejaculation: Semen passing back into the bladder; the commonest complication after TURP.
retrograde spread: Infection travelling backwards up a duct, here from urethra to epididymis.
retrograde venous flow: Blood flowing back down a vein through incompetent valves; also called reflux.
retroperitoneal: Lying behind the peritoneum, at the back of the abdomen.
reuptake: Return of a released neurotransmitter into the nerve ending that released it.
revascularisation: Restoring blood flow to a limb by angioplasty or bypass surgery.
rewarming shock: A fall in blood pressure during rewarming as vessels dilate before cardiac output rises.
rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin, potassium and CK; can cause AKI.
rhinoscopy: Looking inside the nose with a light and speculum.
rhinovirus: The common cold virus; the most common cause of acute bronchitis.
rhonchi: Low-pitched rattling sounds from mucus in large airways, often clearing after a cough.
ribavirin: An antiviral sometimes added to hepatitis C treatment.
ribonucleotide reductase: The enzyme that makes DNA building blocks; blocked by hydroxycarbamide.
rickets: Defective mineralisation in children before the growth plates fuse.
rifabutin: A rifamycin with fewer drug interactions, used in place of rifampicin.
rifampicin: TB drug that inhibits RNA polymerase; turns urine orange and induces liver enzymes.
rifaximin: A poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.
right heart strain: Overload of the right ventricle from a sudden rise in pulmonary pressure.
right hemicolectomy: Removal of caecum, ascending and proximal transverse colon.
right lower quadrant: The right lower quarter of the abdomen, overlapping the RIF.
rigidity: A board-like abdomen from constant muscle spasm; suggests generalised peritonitis.
rigors: Violent shaking with a feeling of cold as the temperature rises.
riluzole: Antiglutamatergic drug that modestly slows MND progression.
ring-shaped inclusions: Ring forms inside red cells on a film; typical of P. falciparum.
ritonavir: Booster that inhibits nirmatrelvir's metabolism (CYP3A4) to raise its levels.
rivaroxaban: DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa.
rolling hernia: Para-oesophageal hernia: fundus rolls up beside the oesophagus, GOJ stays below the diaphragm.
rose spots: Faint pink macules on the trunk in typhoid fever.
roseola infantum: HHV-6 infection in infants: high fever for 3 days, then rash as fever settles.
rotavirus: Virus causing severe gastroenteritis in under 5s; prevented by a UK routine vaccine.
rotavirus vaccine: Oral vaccine in the UK infant schedule preventing severe rotavirus.
rouleaux: Red cells stacked like coins on a blood film, caused by excess protein.
rubber band ligation: A tight band placed at the base of an internal haemorrhoid so it dies and falls off.
rubella: German measles: a mild viral rash illness, dangerous to the fetus in pregnancy.
sacroiliitis: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints causing low back pain.
sacrum: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, the commonest pressure ulcer site.
saddle anaesthesia: Numbness of the perineum, buttocks and inner thighs.
safety-net: Clear advice on which changes mean coming back urgently.
safety-netting: Telling a patient which warning signs should prompt them to return.
salbutamol: Short-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler that opens narrowed airways.
salicylate: Aspirin and related drugs; overdose causes respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis.
salivary cortisol: Late-night saliva cortisol; raised in Cushing's because the night-time dip is lost.
salvage: Saving the testis so it can be kept rather than removed.
saphena varix: A swelling of the great saphenous vein at the groin with a cough impulse.
saphenofemoral junction: Where the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein in the groin.
saponification: Fatty acids from fat necrosis combining with calcium, lowering serum calcium.
sarcoidosis: Inflammatory disease with granulomas that can infiltrate the pituitary and hypothalamus.
scalloping: A notched, saw-tooth look to the duodenal folds at endoscopy, seen in coeliac disease.
scapular winging: Medial border of the scapula lifting off the chest wall.
scarlet fever: Group A Strep infection with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.
schistocytes: Fragmented red cells on a blood film, seen in microangiopathic haemolysis such as TTP.
schizogony: Asexual multiplication of the parasite, first in the liver then in red cells.
sciatic nerve stretch test: Straight leg raise test for L5/S1 root irritation.
sciatica: Pain radiating down the back of the leg from a lumbar or sacral nerve root, usually a disc prolapse.
sclera: The tough white outer wall of the eyeball.
scleromalacia perforans: Painless necrotising scleritis without inflammation, classically in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
sclerotherapy: Injection of a sclerosant to scar and shrink a haemorrhoid.
sclerotic: Dense, white-looking bone lesions on X-ray from extra bone formation.
scotoma: An area of lost or reduced vision within the visual field.
screening: Testing people without symptoms to find disease or risk early.
scrotal ultrasound: Imaging of the scrotum; Doppler shows testicular blood flow to exclude torsion.
secondary bacterial pneumonia: Bacterial lung infection that follows a viral illness such as flu.
secondary hyperparathyroidism: Appropriate PTH rise in response to low calcium, e.g. vitamin D deficiency or CKD.
secondary polycythaemia: Raised red cells driven by raised EPO, from hypoxia or an EPO-producing tumour.
secondary prevention: Finding disease early, before symptoms, such as cancer screening.
secondary spontaneous pneumothorax: Pneumothorax caused by underlying lung disease such as COPD.
secretory diarrhoea: Watery diarrhoea from active secretion of fluid by the gut lining.
segmented RNA genome: A viral genome split into separate RNA pieces, which can swap between strains.
self-limiting: Gets better on its own without specific treatment.
self-tolerance: The immune system's normal ability not to attack the body's own tissues.
sella: Sella turcica: the bony pocket in the skull base holding the pituitary.
semaglutide: A GLP-1 receptor agonist used when BMI is 37 or more.
seminiferous tubules: Tubules in the testis where sperm are made.
seminoma: A slow-growing, radiosensitive germ cell tumour; about half of testicular cancers.
senna: Stimulant laxative, usually taken at night.
sensitivity: The proportion of people with the disease who test positive: TP/(TP+FN).
sensorineural hearing loss: Hearing loss from the cochlea or auditory nerve rather than the outer or middle ear.
sensory level: A level on the trunk below which sensation is reduced; points to a cord lesion.
sentinel pile: Another name for the sentinel skin tag of a chronic fissure.
sentinel skin tag: A small tag of skin at the outer end of a chronic fissure.
sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
septic shock: Sepsis with low blood pressure needing vasopressors and a raised lactate despite fluids.
sequestration: Infected red cells trapped in small vessels of the brain, kidney and other organs.
serial CT: Repeated CT scans to watch whether a bleed grows.
serology: Blood tests that detect antibodies (e.g. IgM, IgG) to an infection.
serotonin: Neurotransmitter (5-HT) involved in mood and anxiety; raised by SSRIs.
serotonin syndrome: Excess serotonin activity causing hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, clonus and dilated pupils.
serotypes: Strains of a microbe distinguished by their surface antigens.
sertraline: SSRI antidepressant; first-line drug for GAD.
serum osmolality: Measured particle concentration of serum; above 320 mOsm/kg in HHS.
serum protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins to show a monoclonal paraprotein band.
sestamibi: Technetium-99m sestamibi scan; nuclear imaging that lights up an overactive parathyroid gland.
seton: A loose thread placed through a fistula to keep it draining.
severe hypoglycaemia: A hypo where the person needs help from someone else to treat it.
severe malaria: Malaria with organ dysfunction, e.g. glucose below 2.2, reduced GCS, AKI, acidosis or severe anaemia.
shear: Force when skin stays still while deeper tissue slides, tearing small vessels.
shifting dullness: Dullness to percussion that moves when the patient rolls; a sign of ascites.
shingles: Painful, one-sided, dermatomal blistering rash from reactivated varicella zoster virus.
shivering: Involuntary muscle contractions that generate heat; stops in severe hypothermia.
shock: Inadequate tissue perfusion: prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia, cold peripheries, low BP.
short bowel syndrome: Malabsorption after removal of a large length of small bowel.
short saphenous vein: Superficial vein of the back of the calf that drains into the popliteal vein.
shoulder dystocia: Baby's shoulder stuck behind the pelvis during delivery; can stretch the brachial plexus.
shunt: A tube that drains CSF from the ventricles to relieve hydrocephalus.
sialic acid: Sugar on host cell surfaces that influenza haemagglutinin binds.
sick day rules: Advice for illness: keep insulin going, check glucose often, drink fluids, pause metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors.
sick-day rules: Advice to double steroid replacement during illness to avoid adrenal crisis.
sickle cell disease: An inherited haemoglobin disorder causing chronic haemolysis and vaso-occlusive crises.
sickle cell trait: Carrying one sickle gene (HbAS); usually no symptoms.
sickle solubility test: Quick screening test for HbS; positive in both trait and disease.
side room: A single isolation room, ideally with its own toilet, to stop spread on the ward.
sigmoid colon: The S-shaped last part of the colon before the rectum, in the left iliac fossa.
sigmoidoscopy: Camera examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
signet ring cell: Cancer cell full of mucin that pushes the nucleus to one side, like a signet ring.
silent MI: A myocardial infarction without typical chest pain, more common in diabetics, women and the elderly.
silent hypoxia: Low oxygen saturation in a patient who does not feel very breathless.
silver nitrate cautery: Chemical cautery stick applied to a visible bleeding vessel to seal it.
simple transfusion: Giving donor red cells without removing any of the patient's blood.
sitagliptin: A DPP-4 inhibitor; rarely causes pancreatitis.
sitophobia: Fear of eating because food brings on pain.
skin turgor: How quickly pinched skin springs back; slow return suggests dehydration.
skip lesions: Patches of inflamed bowel separated by normal bowel, typical of Crohn's.
slapped cheek: Bright red cheeks of parvovirus B19 infection.
slapping gait: Foot slaps the floor on each step because of weak dorsiflexion.
sleep apnoea: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, often with loud snoring.
sliding hiatus hernia: Commonest type: the GOJ and upper stomach slide up into the chest, causing reflux.
slit lamp: A microscope with a bright light used to examine the eye in detail.
slough: Soft, yellow dead tissue in a wound bed.
small cell lung cancer: Aggressive lung cancer linked to smoking; the commonest source of ectopic ACTH.
small saphenous vein: Another name for the short saphenous vein.
smear-positive: Acid-fast bacilli seen on sputum microscopy; the patient is highly infectious.
sodium bicarbonate: IV alkali used in salicylate poisoning to alkalinise urine and speed excretion.
sodium tetradecyl sulfate: A sclerosant drug used to make foam for sclerotherapy.
sodium valproate: An antiepileptic drug that can cause acute pancreatitis.
sofosbuvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks the NS5B polymerase.
somatic: Relating to the body: physical symptoms such as palpitations or tremor.
somatic innervation: Nerve supply that senses sharp pain and touch precisely.
somatic pain: Sharp, well-localised pain from the body wall or parietal peritoneum.
somatostatin analogue: Drug such as octreotide that inhibits GH release.
spasticity: Velocity-dependent increase in tone from UMN damage.
specificity: The proportion of people without the disease who test negative: TN/(TN+FP).
spectrophotometry: Laboratory measurement of CSF bilirubin and oxyhaemoglobin to detect xanthochromia.
spent phase: Late PV when the marrow scars and counts fall, progressing to myelofibrosis.
sperm banking: Freezing sperm before treatment that may affect fertility.
spermatic cord: The bundle carrying the vas deferens, testicular vessels and nerves.
sphenopalatine artery: Terminal branch of the maxillary artery supplying the posterior nasal cavity.
sphenopalatine artery ligation: Endoscopic surgical tying or clipping of the sphenopalatine artery for refractory epistaxis.
sphincterotomy: Cutting the sphincter of Oddi during ERCP to let stones pass.
spider naevi: Small red skin lesions with radiating vessels, seen in chronic liver disease.
spike protein: Surface protein of SARS-CoV-2 that binds ACE2.
spinal cord compression: Pressure on the cord causing back pain, leg weakness, a sensory level and retention.
spiral groove: Groove on the back of the humerus where the radial nerve runs.
spironolactone: An aldosterone antagonist diuretic, the mainstay for ascites.
splenic flexure: The bend of the colon near the spleen; a watershed between SMA and IMA.
splenic rupture: Tearing of the spleen causing internal bleeding; a surgical emergency.
splenic sequestration: Red cells pool in the spleen, which enlarges fast, causing acute anaemia and shock in children.
spongiform: Sponge-like ultrasound appearance with many small cysts; a benign feature.
spores: Tough dormant bacterial forms that survive heat, drying and alcohol.
sporozoites: Infective stage injected by the mosquito; travels to the liver.
squamous cell carcinoma: Cancer of squamous epithelium; central, smoking-linked, cavitates and secretes PTHrP.
squamous cell lung cancer: Central lung cancer strongly linked to smoking and known for PTHrP secretion.
stable angina: Predictable chest pain on exertion relieved by rest or GTN, caused by fixed narrowing without thrombus.
stacked coins: AXR look of dilated small bowel with valvulae conniventes, like a pile of coins.
staggered overdose: Overdose taken over more than an hour, so the treatment nomogram cannot be used.
staging: Working out how far a cancer has spread to plan treatment.
stalk effect: Mild prolactin rise when a tumour compresses the pituitary stalk and blocks dopamine.
stapedius: Tiny middle-ear muscle, supplied by CN VII, that damps loud sounds.
stapled haemorrhoidopexy: Stapling procedure that lifts prolapsed haemorrhoids back into place.
statin: Cholesterol-lowering drug that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.
statutory duty: A legal obligation set out in law; it does not depend on the patient's consent.
steatorrhoea: Pale, bulky, offensive, greasy stools that float, from fat malabsorption.
stem cell transplant: Replacing the marrow with donor stem cells; the only curative option in PMF.
stent thrombosis: Clot forming inside a coronary stent, causing MI; the danger of stopping antiplatelets early.
stepped care: Starting with the least intensive effective treatment and stepping up if it fails.
