steroid-sparing: A drug added so that the steroid dose can be reduced or stopped.
stimulant laxative: Laxatives such as senna or bisacodyl that increase colonic motility via enteric nerves.
stony dull: Very dull percussion note typical of pleural fluid.
stool antigen test: Detects H. pylori proteins in faeces; shows active infection.
stool burden: The amount of stool felt in the abdomen or seen on imaging.
stool microscopy: Looking at stool under a microscope for parasites, cysts and cells.
straight leg raise: Raising the straight leg stretches the L5/S1 roots; leg pain between 30° and 70° is positive.
strangulated: A hernia whose blood supply is cut off, causing ischaemia; a surgical emergency.
strangulation: Cut-off blood supply to prolapsed tissue; an emergency.
strawberry tongue: Bright red tongue with prominent papillae in scarlet fever.
streptokinase: A streptococcal enzyme that breaks down clots, helping bacteria spread.
striae: Stretch marks; in Cushing's they are wide and purple.
stricture: An abnormal narrowing of a tube such as the bowel, often from scarring.
stridor: High-pitched noisy breathing from upper airway narrowing.
sub-Saharan Africa: Africa south of the Sahara; where most falciparum malaria is caught.
subacute: Developing over days, not seconds or months.
subarachnoid space: The CSF-filled space between the arachnoid mater and pia mater.
subcutaneous emphysema: Gas or air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling.
subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer beneath the dermis.
subdural: The space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.
subdural haematoma: Blood collecting between the dura and brain, often after a fall.
subdural haemorrhage: Bleeding beneath the dura from torn bridging veins, crescent-shaped on CT.
subendocardial: The inner layer of heart muscle, the first to become ischaemic when blood supply falls.
subperiosteal abscess: Collection of pus between the orbital bone and its periosteum, usually next to the ethmoid sinus.
succussion splash: Sloshing sound over the stomach when shaken, from retained fluid in outlet obstruction.
suicide risk assessment: Structured questions on thoughts, plans, intent, means, protective factors and previous attempts.
sulcal effacement: Loss of visible sulci on CT from brain compression.
sulfasalazine: An anti-inflammatory used in IBD and arthritis; can cause pancreatitis.
sulfonylureas: Drugs such as gliclazide that stimulate insulin release; cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain.
sulphonylurea: Oral diabetes drug class, such as gliclazide, that makes the pancreas release insulin.
superficial femoral artery: The main thigh artery, a common site of PAD occlusion.
superficial thrombophlebitis: Clot and inflammation in a superficial vein: a hard, tender, red cord.
superinfection: A second, often bacterial, infection on top of a first, often viral, one.
superior labial artery: Facial artery branch supplying the upper lip and anterior septum.
superior mesenteric artery: The artery supplying the small bowel and right colon; the usual site of embolus.
superior quadrantanopia: Loss of an upper quarter of the field; from a temporal lobe lesion.
supersaturated: Holding more of a substance in solution than it can stably dissolve, so it crystallises.
supinator reflex: Another name for the brachioradialis reflex (C5/C6).
suppository: A solid medicine inserted into the rectum, where it dissolves.
suprasellar: Above the sella turcica, where the pituitary sits.
supratentorial: Above the tentorium cerebelli, so involving the cerebral hemispheres.
surgical clipping: Open surgery placing a metal clip across the aneurysm neck.
surgical emphysema: Air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling (crepitus).
surgical exploration: Opening the scrotum in theatre to look at, untwist and assess the testis.
suture lines: Fibrous joints between skull bones where the dura is firmly attached.
swinging: Drain fluid moving up and down with breathing, showing the drain is patent.
swinging fever: A temperature that rises and falls repeatedly, typical of an abscess.
swinging light test: Moving a torch between the eyes to compare each optic nerve's pupil response.
sympathetic: The fight-or-flight part of the autonomic nervous system.
syncope: Brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.
tTG: Tissue transglutaminase: the enzyme that deamidates gliadin and the target of coeliac antibodies.
tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant used after transplant.
tamponade: Stopping bleeding by direct pressure on the vessel.
tamsulosin: An alpha-1 antagonist that relaxes prostate and bladder neck muscle to improve flow.
tear film: The thin fluid layer that keeps the cornea moist.
teardrop cells: Red cells deformed into a teardrop shape squeezing through a scarred marrow.
telangiectasia: Small dilated blood vessels visible on skin or mucosa.
temporal bone: Skull bone at the side of the head around the ear and temple.
tenecteplase: A clot-busting tissue plasminogen activator given as a single bolus.
tenesmus: A constant feeling of needing to open the bowels even when the rectum is empty.
tenofovir: A nucleotide analogue antiviral, first-line for chronic hepatitis B.
tension pneumothorax: Life-threatening pneumothorax where trapped air builds pressure, shifts the mediastinum and causes shock.
tentorial notch: The gap in the tentorium through which the brainstem passes.
tentorium: Fold of dura separating the cerebrum from the cerebellum.
teratogenic: Able to cause abnormalities in a developing baby.
teratoma: A germ cell tumour containing several tissue types; grows and spreads faster than seminoma.
terminal ileum: The last part of the small bowel, where bile salts and vitamin B12 are absorbed.
tertiary hyperparathyroidism: Autonomous PTH secretion after long-standing secondary disease, with a high calcium.
tertiary prevention: Reducing complications of established disease, such as rehabilitation.
test and treat: Testing for H. pylori and treating it before endoscopy in patients without red flags.
test of cure: HPV test and cytology 6 months after CIN treatment to confirm clearance.
testicular torsion: Twisting of the spermatic cord cutting off the testis's blood supply; a surgical emergency.
tetany: Involuntary sustained muscle spasm from irritable nerves.
thalamus: Central brain relay station; medial thalamic damage contributes to Korsakoff's amnesia.
thalidomide: An immunomodulatory drug used in myeloma.
thenar: The muscle bulge at the base of the thumb.
thermoregulation: The body's control of temperature, run by the hypothalamus.
thiamine: Vitamin B1; given before glucose in alcohol-related illness to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
thiazide: Diuretic acting on the distal tubule; paradoxically reduces urine in nephrogenic DI.
thiazides: Diuretics acting on the distal tubule; cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
thick film: Blood film that concentrates cells to detect parasites and count the burden.
thienopyridines: Class of P2Y12 blockers including clopidogrel and ticlopidine.
thin film: Blood film spread in a single layer to identify the Plasmodium species.
third space: Fluid lost into body cavities or tissues (gut, pleura, peritoneum) rather than the circulation.
third spacing: Fluid shifting out of the blood into the bowel lumen and wall, where it cannot be used.
thoracic duct: Main lymph vessel draining most of the body into the left subclavian vein.
thrombin: Enzyme (factor IIa) that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
thrombolysis: Drug treatment that dissolves a clot, such as alteplase.
thrombophilia: An inherited or acquired tendency to form clots, such as factor V Leiden.
thrombophlebitis: Inflammation and clot in a superficial vein, felt as a tender red cord.
thrombosed external haemorrhoid: A clotted haemorrhoid below the dentate line causing a tender purple lump.
thrombosed haemorrhoid: A haemorrhoid with clotted blood inside; purple, tense and very painful.
thrombosis: Formation of a blood clot inside a vessel.
thromboxane A2: Platelet-made signal that causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
thrombus: A blood clot formed inside a vessel.
thumb-printing: Thickened, oedematous colonic wall folds seen on imaging in severe colitis.
thumbprinting: Rounded indentations of the bowel wall on X-ray caused by mucosal oedema.
thunderclap headache: A severe headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute.
thyroglobulin: Protein made by thyroid cells; used to monitor differentiated thyroid cancer after surgery.
thyroglossal cyst: Midline neck cyst from the embryonic thyroid tract; rises on tongue protrusion.
thyroid eye disease: Autoimmune orbital inflammation in Graves' disease causing proptosis and lid retraction.
thyroid nodule: A discrete lump within the thyroid gland; most are benign.
thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
ticagrelor: A P2Y12 antiplatelet used with aspirin in ACS, given with caution over 75 because of bleeding risk.
tinkling bowel sounds: High-pitched bowel sounds of fluid and gas forced past a mechanical blockage.
tinnitus: Ringing in the ears; an early sign of salicylate toxicity.
tirzepatide: Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist used for early-onset type 2 diabetes and weight loss.
tissue factor: Protein from damaged tissue that starts the extrinsic pathway.
tissue transglutaminase: Enzyme that modifies gliadin, making it more immunogenic; the antigen in the coeliac blood test.
titubation: Rhythmic nodding ('yes-yes') or shaking ('no-no') tremor of the head.
tocilizumab: Antibody against the IL-6 receptor, used in ventilated Covid-19 patients.
tolerance: Needing a higher dose for the same effect.
tolterodine: An antimuscarinic for bladder storage symptoms.
tolvaptan: V2 receptor antagonist that blocks ADH; used for SIADH, not DI.
topical: Applied directly to the skin or affected area.
topiramate: Anticonvulsant used as a further option for essential tremor.
torsion: Twisting of an organ on its blood supply; here the testis rotating on its spermatic cord.
toxic megacolon: Acute, non-obstructive dilatation of the colon with systemic toxicity; risks perforation.
toxin A: C. difficile enterotoxin that damages the colonic lining.
toxin B: C. difficile cytotoxin, the main cause of colonic cell damage.
tracheal deviation: The trachea pushed off the midline; away from the side of a tension pneumothorax.
tracheobronchial: Relating to the trachea and bronchi together.
tranexamic acid: Drug that blocks fibrinolysis; generally avoided in DIC.
trans-sphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
transcoelomic: Spread across a body cavity such as the peritoneum or pleura, e.g. ovarian cancer.
transcoelomic spread: Spread of cancer cells across a body cavity such as the peritoneum.
transcranial Doppler: Ultrasound through the skull measuring cerebral artery blood flow velocity, raised in vasospasm.
transformation zone: The area of the cervix where cells change type, where most CIN arises.
transient outward potassium current: Early repolarising potassium current in heart cells; cold changes it, producing the J wave.
transilluminate: Light passing through a swelling, showing it contains fluid.
transilluminates: Lets light shine through, as fluid-filled swellings do.
transition point: The point on CT where dilated bowel changes to collapsed bowel; the site of obstruction.
transition zone: The part of the prostate surrounding the urethra, where BPH arises.
transketolase: Thiamine-dependent enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway.
transmissibility: How easily an infection spreads from person to person.
transmural: Affecting the full thickness of the heart wall, from endocardium to epicardium.
transperineal biopsy: Prostate biopsy through the skin between scrotum and anus, with lower infection risk.
transsphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery performed through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
traumatic tap: Blood in CSF from the needle itself; red cells fall across successive tubes.
treatment-resistant depression: Depression that has not responded to adequate trials of treatment.
trephine: A core biopsy of bone marrow, used when the aspirate is a dry tap.
tricyclic antidepressants: Older antidepressant class; low doses help pain and sleep.
trigeminal nerve: Cranial nerve V; its ophthalmic branch is the classic site of facial shingles.
triple therapy: PPI plus two antibiotics for 7 days to eradicate H. pylori.
triple vessel disease: Significant narrowing in all three main coronary arteries, often better treated by CABG than PCI.
tropism: The preference of a virus for particular cells or tissues.
troponin: A heart muscle protein released into the blood when cardiomyocytes die; the key blood test for myocardial infarction.
truss: A support belt that holds a reducible hernia in place.
trypsin: A protein-digesting enzyme that activates the other pancreatic enzymes.
trypsinogen: The inactive form of trypsin, normally activated only in the duodenum.
tumour flare: Temporary worsening of cancer from the testosterone surge when a GnRH agonist starts.
tunica vaginalis: Double layer of membrane surrounding the front and sides of the testis.
two-week wait: Urgent cancer referral: the patient is seen by a specialist within two weeks.
tympanic: Measured in the ear canal; unreliable at extremes of temperature.
tympanometry: Test of middle ear pressure and eardrum movement.
type 1 respiratory failure: Low oxygen (pO2 below 8 kPa) with a normal or low carbon dioxide.
type 2 respiratory failure: Low oxygen with high carbon dioxide from hypoventilation.
typhoid: Enteric fever caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread by contaminated food and water.
ulcerative colitis: Inflammatory bowel disease of the colon; classically associated with episcleritis.
umbilical hernia: A hernia at the umbilicus; common in babies and usually closes by 12 months.
uncal herniation: The uncus pushes through the tentorial notch, compressing CN III and the brainstem.
uncomplicated grief: A normal, time-limited reaction to loss with waves of sadness.
unconjugated bilirubin: Bilirubin not yet processed by the liver; raised in haemolysis.
unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: Raised bilirubin that the liver has not yet processed, typical of haemolysis.
uncus: The innermost part of the temporal lobe; herniates first when ICP rises.
underwater seal: Drain bottle where the tube sits under water so air escapes but cannot return.
unfractionated heparin: An anticoagulant given IV that boosts antithrombin; preferred when immediate PCI is planned as it is quickly reversible.
ungradable: A pressure ulcer whose depth cannot be judged because eschar or slough covers it.
unmeasured anions: Negative ions not included in routine tests, such as lactate, ketones and toxin acids.
unprovoked DVT: A DVT with no clear trigger; prompts a look for cancer or thrombophilia.
unrefreshing sleep: Sleep that does not restore energy despite adequate hours.
unstable angina: Ischaemic chest pain at rest or worsening, with normal troponin, so there is no infarction.
uraemia: Build-up of urea and other waste products from kidney failure.
urate: A breakdown product of DNA; raised with high cell turnover.
urea: Waste product of protein breakdown; the most sensitive U&E marker of dehydration.
urea breath test: Swallowed labelled urea is split by H. pylori; labelled CO2 in breath shows active infection.
urea cycle: Liver pathway that converts ammonia into urea for excretion.
urea:creatinine ratio: Urea divided by creatinine; a high ratio suggests a pre-renal, volume-depleted state.
urease: Enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
urgency: A sudden, hard-to-delay need to open the bowels.
urinary free cortisol: Cortisol measured in a 24-hour urine collection; raised in Cushing's.
urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder; often painless in cauda equina.
urine dipstick: A quick strip test for leucocytes, nitrites, blood and protein in urine.
uroflowmetry: A test measuring how fast urine flows; low peak flow suggests obstruction.
ursodeoxycholic acid: A bile acid used to treat primary biliary cholangitis.
uvea: The pigmented middle layer of the eye: iris, ciliary body and choroid.
uveitis: Inflammation of the iris, ciliary body or choroid, causing a red, photophobic eye.
valaciclovir: Oral prodrug of aciclovir with better absorption.
valveless veins: Orbital veins with no valves, so blood and infection can flow back to the cavernous sinus.
valvulae conniventes: Mucosal folds of the small bowel that cross its full width on X-ray.
vancomycin: Glycopeptide antibiotic; given orally it stays in the gut to treat C. difficile.
varicella: Chickenpox, the primary infection with varicella zoster virus.
varicocele: Dilated veins of the spermatic cord; feels like a 'bag of worms'.
varicose veins: Dilated, twisted superficial veins caused by leaky valves.
vas deferens: The duct carrying sperm from the epididymis to the urethra.
vasa recta: Small straight arteries that pierce the colonic muscle to supply the mucosa.
vascular cushions: Normal pads of blood vessels and connective tissue that help seal the anus.
vasculitis: Inflammation of blood vessel walls, causing narrowing, ischaemia or bleeding.
vaso-occlusive crisis: Sickled cells block small vessels, causing ischaemia and severe pain; the commonest presentation.
vasoconstriction: Narrowing of blood vessels to keep heat in the core.
vasoconstrictor: A drug that narrows blood vessels.
vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, which releases heat and lowers blood pressure.
vasospasm: Sudden tightening of a coronary artery causing ischaemia, classically triggered by cocaine.
velpatasvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks NS5A.
venesection: Removing blood from a vein to lower the red cell mass.
venlafaxine: SNRI used if an SSRI fails or is not tolerated in GAD.
venoarterial ECMO: ECMO that supports both heart and lungs by returning blood to an artery.
venous beading: Sausage-like irregular dilation of retinal veins; a sign of ischaemia.
venous congestion: Blood pooling because outflow is blocked; causes swelling in early torsion.
venous eczema: Itchy, scaly inflamed skin of the lower leg from venous hypertension.
venous hypertension: Raised pressure in the leg veins from reflux or obstruction.
venous reflux: Backward flow of blood in a vein because the valves leak.
venous stasis: Slow or pooled blood flow in the veins.
venous ulcer: Shallow, irregular ulcer over the medial malleolus caused by chronic venous hypertension.
ventricular fibrillation: Chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no output, the commonest cause of death early in ACS.
ventricular septal rupture: A tear in the wall between the ventricles days after MI, causing a new pansystolic murmur and heart failure.
vertical transmission: Spread of infection from mother to baby around birth.
vertigo: A false sense of movement, usually spinning, from vestibular disease.
vesicles: Small fluid-filled blisters under 5 mm across.
vestibular compensation: The brain's adaptation to a vestibular lesion; slowed by long-term sedatives.
vestibular neuritis: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve: days of vertigo without hearing loss.
vestibular schwannoma: Correct name for an acoustic neuroma.
vestibular suppressant: A drug that dampens vestibular signalling to reduce acute vertigo.
vestibulo-ocular reflex: Reflex keeping the eyes still in space when the head moves.
viable: Still alive and able to recover once the blood supply returns.
villi: Finger-like projections of the small bowel lining that absorb nutrients.
villous adenoma: A colonic polyp that can secrete large amounts of fluid and potassium.
villous atrophy: Flattening of the finger-like villi of the small bowel, cutting absorptive surface area.
villous tips: Ends of the villi, where mature absorptive enterocytes sit.
virions: Complete virus particles that can infect other cells.
visceral hypersensitivity: A lowered pain threshold to normal stretching of the gut.
visceral innervation: Autonomic nerve supply that senses stretch, not cutting or pinching.
visceral pain: Dull, poorly localised pain from stretched or inflamed organs, felt in the midline.
visceral pleura: The membrane covering the lung surface.
viscosity: How thick and sticky the blood is; higher viscosity slows flow and causes clots.
visible peristalsis: Waves of bowel contraction seen through a thin abdominal wall in obstruction.
visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart.
visual field: The whole area a person can see while looking straight ahead.
visual field defect: An area of lost vision within the visual field.
visual field testing: Formal mapping of the visual field (perimetry).
vitamin K: Vitamin needed to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X; reverses warfarin.
vitamin K epoxide reductase: Enzyme that recycles vitamin K; blocked by warfarin.
vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment, giving white patches.
vitreous: Clear gel filling the back of the eye.
vocal resonance: How clearly speech is heard through the chest wall; increased over consolidation, reduced over fluid.
volume depletion: Loss of circulating fluid, causing low BP and fast pulse.
volvulus: Twisting of a loop of bowel on its mesentery, causing closed-loop obstruction.
von Willebrand factor: Protein that helps platelets stick and carries and protects factor VIII in blood.
waddling gait: Side-to-side walk from weak hip muscles.
waiter's tip: Arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, wrist flexed: Erb's palsy.
warfarin: Oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant monitored with the INR.
washout: Rinsing the abdominal cavity during surgery to remove contamination.
watchful waiting: Monitoring without surgery, with advice on symptoms that need urgent review.
water deprivation test: Withholds fluid, then gives desmopressin, to confirm DI and its type.
watershed: Tissue at the far end of an arterial territory, most vulnerable to low flow.
watershed area: A region at the edge of two blood supplies with relatively poor perfusion.
wet AMD: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration, also treated with anti-VEGF.
wet beriberi: Thiamine deficiency causing high-output heart failure and oedema.
wet gangrene: Gangrene with infection: moist, swollen, painful, foul-smelling, no clear edge.
wheeze: High-pitched whistling from narrowed airways, usually on breathing out.
whole-body low-dose CT: CT of the whole skeleton at low radiation dose to find lytic lesions.
whooping cough: Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis infection with bouts of coughing and an inspiratory whoop.
wound swab: A sample from a wound sent to find the infecting organism.
wrist drop: Inability to extend the wrist, from radial nerve injury.
xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from bilirubin produced as red cells break down, proving an older bleed.
yolk sac tumour: A non-seminomatous germ cell tumour that produces AFP.
zanamivir: Inhaled (or IV) neuraminidase inhibitor; can cause bronchospasm in asthma or COPD.
zoledronic acid: Potent IV bisphosphonate used after rehydration in hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
γGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase, a liver enzyme raised with ALP in cholestasis.
